##### [26-A-19947-ACC ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ENHANCED ELECTROCARDIOGRAM (AI-ECG) TO PREDICT MORTALITY IN PATIENTS PRESENTING WITH ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.3024)

```
## Background

AI-ECG is rapidly becoming a useful tool in the diagnosis and risk stratification of patients with cardiovascular disease. However, its use in predicting mortality in patients with ACS, in real time workflow, has not been demonstrated.

## Methods

Our study utilized data from the EHR to identify patients admitted to one of 13 in-system hospitals with ACS. Three machine learning models were created to predict in-hospital mortality using ECG and clinical features. The models were meant to mimic real time workflow; the “triage” model uses demographics, vitals, and ECG features, the “intake” model adds medical history, and the “assessment” model adds labs. Model outputs cascaded into subsequent models, improving predictability.

## Results

A total of 4,782,850 ECGs were extracted and matched to 10,916 patients admitted for ACS. In testing sets, the “triage” model predicted mortality at a rate of 75% and no-mortality at a rate of 73% (AUC 0.82), the “intake” model predicted mortality at a rate of 77% and no-mortality at a rate of 72% (AUC 0.82), and the “assessment” model predicted mortality at a rate of 80% and no-mortality at a rate of 74% (AUC 0.79).

## Conclusion

Our AI-ECG model was able to predict mortality at a rate better than conventional risk stratification tools for ACS. All 3 models had similar performance despite incorporating more clinical data. As such, we conclude that the readily available ECG alone offers invaluable risk stratification capabilities when paired with our AI-ECG model.
```

##### [26-A-14063-ACC INTEGRATING CLINICAL, GENETIC, AND ELECTROCARDIOGRAM-BASED ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TO PREDICT RISK OF FUTURE ATRIAL FIBRILLATION](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.353)

```
## Background

It is unknown whether integrating clinical, genetic, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled electrocardiogram (ECG) risk signals improves AF risk estimation.

## Methods

We estimated AF risk in the population-based UK Biobank (UKB) and the hospital-based Mass General Brigham Biobank (MGBB) using the CHARGE-AF clinical score, an ECG-based AI model (ECG-AI), and an AF polygenic risk score (PRS). We estimated discrimination of 5-year incident AF using time-dependent AUROC and average precision (AP).

## Results

In the UK Biobank (mean age 65±8 years, 52% women) 825/49,293 (2.4%) and in MGBB (mean age 53±15 years,53% women) 1,034/12,812 (8.1%) developed AF within 5 years. In both datasets, CHARGE-AF (UK Biobank: AUROC 0.785, AP 0.053; MGBB: 0.710, AP 0.19), ECG-AI (AUROC 0.705, AP 0.085; AUROC 0.740; AP 0.23), and the AF PRS (AUROC 0.618, AP 0.038; AUROC 0.550; AP 0.098) discriminated incident AF. A combined score achieved the best discrimination (AUROC 0.817; AP 0.11; MGB AUROC 0.750, AP 0.23) and individuals at classified as high risk (i.e., 5-year predicted AF risk >2.5% in UKBB and >10% in MGBB) had a 5-year cumulative incidence of AF of 5.8% and 17.1%. At the same thresholds, 5-year AF incidence was highest when all 3 models predicted high risk (UKB 11.1%, MGBB 27.5%).

## Conclusion

Integration of clinical, genetic, and AI-derived risk signals improves discrimination of 5-year AF risk and have potential to improve prioritization of individuals for AF screening and preventive interventions.
```

##### [26-A-20260-ACC DEEP LEARNING ENABLES GENETIC ANALYSIS OF CARDIOVASCULAR AGING](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.402)

```
## Background

Artificial intelligence-enhanced ECG (AI-ECG) distinguishes chronological age (CA) from biological age (BA), defining distinct biological cardiovascular aging profiles. We examined genomic mechanisms of accelerated CV aging.

## Methods

We deployed an AI model to evaluate biological age on ECGs in the UK Biobank, stratifying individuals as accelerated or resilient agers based on whether their age gap (BA-CA) exceeded the mean absolute error. We conducted genome-wide association studies (GWAS) comparing accelerated vs resilient agers. We then queried significant GWAS hits in single-cell transcriptomic data of young vs aged myocardium to evaluate tissue-specific enrichment and define cell-cell interactions.

## Results

Among 58034 individuals with ECGs and genomic data (median age, 55y, 51% female), AI-ECG stratified 12382 as accelerated agers, 55373 normal, and 25510 as resilient agers. GWAS identified 140 significant single nucleotide polymorphisms mapping to 9 genes. Tissue-specific analyses revealed enrichment in cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, and pericytes. An aging-related signature of cardiomyocytes was associated with elevated expression of _TTN_, CAMK2D and _PTN_ signaling.

## Conclusion

AI-ECG, GWAS, and single-cell analyses identify genetic and cellular mechanisms of accelerated cardiac aging.
```

##### [26-YIA-7531-ACC ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ENHANCED ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHY META-MODEL FOR SHORT-TERM GENERALISED CARDIOVASCULAR RISK PREDICTION](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.4855)

```
## Background

Cardiovascular disease remains the leading global cause of mortality, yet existing risk stratification tools focus on single conditions. We developed an artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography (AI-ECG) platform to predict 1-year generalised cardiovascular risk.

## Methods

We trained eleven AI-ECG models using convolutional neural networks on ECG images from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (189,538 subjects). Models predicted future disease: mortality, atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure (HF), and others, as well as detection of left ventricular dysfunction (LVSD) and valvular diseases. An ensemble meta-model using XGBoost trained on all eleven disease-specific predictions generated 1-year cardiovascular risk scores. External validation used five international cohorts.

## Results

Individual models achieved strong performance: mortality (c-statistic: 0.818), AF (0.770), HF (0.809), LVSD (AUC: 0.896). External validation showed mortality prediction in CODE (c-statistic:0.764) and structural disease detection in Shanghai (AUC: 0.948). Meta-model performance: BIDMC (AUC: 0.847, PPV: 0.558), VUMC (AUC: 0.772, PPV: 0.616), UK Biobank (AUC: 0.716). Risk stratification hazard ratios: 13.4 (CI: 11.5-15.6) BIDMC, 2.69 (2.59-2.79) VUMC.

## Conclusion

The meta-model integrates eleven cardiovascular predictions into a single 1-year risk score, enabling targeted resource allocation and guiding high-risk patients toward appropriate interventions.
```

##### [26-YIA-7947-ACC AI-ENHANCED ECG ANALYSIS ENABLED DISCOVERY OF MECHANISTIC PATHWAYS FOR DRUG-INDUCED LONG QT SYNDROME](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.4868)

```
## Background

Drug-induced long QT syndrome (diLQTS) causes malignant arrhythmias, precluding the safe use of several medications. Well-powered genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been null due to challenging case definitions, varied exposures, and unknown risk in controls. We hypothesized that AI-ECG could learn a unified latent representation of diLQTS, enabling mechanistic discovery.

## Methods

We developed a deep-learning ECG classifier predicting diLQTS (defined as QTc >500 ms or ΔQTc ≥60 ms within 14 days of drug initiation) in 11,666 patients receiving 1 of 69 LQTS drugs in a large US health system and validated it in 1,459 patients. We conducted a GWAS in the UK Biobank, comparing high vs low AI-ECG risk groups. Baseline QTc >500 ms served as a comparator. Gene expression was assessed using the Human Protein Atlas and a dilated cardiomyopathy single-cell resource.

## Results

In the validation cohort, AI-ECG achieved AUROC 0.738 for diLQTS, outperforming QTc (AUROC 0.642) including in patients with normal baseline QTc. AI-defined case/control groups increased GWAS sample size (13,239/44,796; 100% power) vs. QTc (543/11,257; 64% power), identifying known (_SNTG1_) and novel loci (_NFIA_, _ERBB4_). Expression analyses confirmed cardiac enrichment; _NFIA_ localized to cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, and endocardium.

## Conclusion

A multimodal workflow linking AI-ECG risk with bulk and single-cell genomics depict molecular pathways for diLQTS. Future work may yield cardioprotective strategies.
```

##### [26-A-12144-ACC SUBSEQUENT ECG STEMI PREDICTED ON TIME ZERO ECG BY AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MODEL](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.4878)

```
## Background

Rapid and accurate recognition of ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) is essential. Having previously shown reduced false positive cath lab activations using an artificial intelligence (AI) electrocardiogram (ECG) model, we now evaluate its ability to detect STEMI equivalents on initial “nondiagnostic” ECGs in patients later diagnosed as subsequent ECG STEMI.

## Methods

In our STEMI database (3 STEMI centers, 30 referring sites) we included all Subsequent ECG Code STEMI patients with available initial ECG, subsequent STEMI ECG, and post-cath confirmed STEMI diagnosis. ECGs were retrospectively analyzed by the AI model.

## Results

In 3.3 years there were 380 Subsequent ECG Code STEMIs included (19% of all STEMIs, 72% male, mean age 61). Arrival method was 57% walk-in vs. 43% ambulance, and 42% direct vs. 58% transfer. Culprit arteries were 43% LAD, 33% RCA, 19% LCX, 4% other. 29 died within 2 months. Mean delay from initial “nondiagnostic” ECG to Subsequent STEMI ECG was 74 min. The AI model correctly identified 297/380 (78%) as STEMI equivalent on initial “nondiagnostic” ECG, in whom the mean delay to diagnostic ECG was 68 min and 28 deaths occurred. The model predicted the culprit artery in 77%, and the initial ECG leads that later developed diagnostic STE in the subsequent ECG in 94%.

## Conclusion

In addition to reducing false positive activations, the AI ECG model identified 78% of subsequent ECG STEMI patients a mean of 68 minutes earlier using ECGs initially nondiagnostic to clinicians.
```

##### [26-A-13841-ACC DEEP LEARNING-DERIVED ELECTROCARDIOGRAPHIC AGE IS ASSOCIATED WITH CARDIOVASCULAR RISK FACTORS IN CHILDREN](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.489)

```
## Background

Chronic cardiovascular risk begins in childhood and contributes to morbidity/mortality in adulthood. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) delta-age—the difference between AI-ECG predicted and chronological age—has shown promise to predict chronic disease in adults but remains underexplored in children.

## Methods

In this single-center study, we trained (75%) and tested (25%) a convolutional neural network to predict chronological age using ECGs from 2000 to 2022. AI-ECG delta-age absolute z-scores ≥1 and ≥2 were used as predictor variables. The primary composite cardiovascular risk outcome—including hypertension, dyslipidemia (high LDL or high triglycerides), diabetes, or obesity—was defined by institutional Fyler codes and pertinent lab values. Each individual outcome was defined as a secondary outcome. Associations between delta-age and outcomes were assessed via logistic regression.

## Results

The test cohort included 46,456 ECGs (median age 11.2 years) from 14,928 patients. Prevalence of risk factors was 2.9% hypertension, 1.6% dyslipidemia, 0.9% diabetes, 2.3% obesity, and 6.0% composite outcome. AI-ECG predicted age correlated well with chronological age (Figure 1A). AI-ECG delta-age absolute z-scores ≥1 and ≥2 were associated with higher risk of the composite and individual outcomes when adjusting for age (Figure 1B) and obesity (Figure 1C).

## Conclusion

AI-ECG delta-age is associated with cardiovascular disease in childhood.
```

##### [26-A-14345-ACC LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL VS. DEEP NEURAL NETWORK VS. PHYSICIANS: ACCURACY AND CONSISTENCY IN STEMI DETECTION](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.4902)

```
## Background

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for medical decision support; however, their reliability for electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation remains uncertain. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated superior performance in detecting ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and STEMI equivalents.

## Methods

Eighteen chest-pain ECGs (8 STEMI equivalents, 8 mimics, 1 STEMI, 1 normal) with adjudicated outcomes were selected. An LLM (ChatGPT-5) was queried 100 times per ECG. Performance was benchmarked against 95 physicians and a deterministic DNN (Queen of Hearts, PMcardio), which yields identical outputs on repeat runs and was trained specifically for STEMI/STEMI-equivalent detection. Accuracy and response consistency rate (agreement with majority) were assessed.

## Results

Among 18 ECGs (50% STEMI by outcome), the LLM achieved 55.4% accuracy (95% CI: 38.9-71.6%), compared with 88.9% (95% CI: 72.2-100%) for the DNN and 64.7% (95% CI: 51.2-77.1%) for physicians. LLM performance was significantly lower for STEMI mimics (19.9% accuracy; 95% CI: 11.7-29.1%) compared to DNN (87.5% accuracy; 95% CI: 62.5-100%) and physicians (72.5% accuracy; 95% CI: 61.3-83.0%). Response consistency was 84% for LLM (with unanimous agreement in only 6% of cases), 100% for the DNN and 77% for physicians.

## Conclusion

DNN demonstrated superior accuracy and perfect reproducibility compared with physicians and an LLM, supporting its implementation for improved STEMI detection.
```

##### [26-A-15705-ACC INTEGRATING PROGNOSTIC POWER OF CORONARY FLOW RESERVE AND AI-ENABLED ECG FOR LEFT VENTRICULAR FILLING PRESSURE IN ANOCA](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.4915)

```
## Background

Coronary flow reserve (CFR) reflects microvascular function, and a novel artificial intelligence-enabled ECG (AI-ECG) model for elevated filling pressure (EFP) could capture myocardial wall stress. Their combined prognostic value in angina with nonobstructive coronary artery disease (ANOCA) is less clear.

## Methods

ANOCA patients with invasive coronary function test were studied. EFP was defined by the AI-ECG algorithm, which was trained and validated against echocardiography parameters. Patients were classified by CFR (<2.5 vs. ≥2.5) and EFP status. Associations with outcomes (death, myocardial infarction, and heart failure hospitalization) were assessed by Cox regression and overlap weighting.

## Results

Of 1,957 patients, impaired CFR was observed in 26.4%, EFP+ in 6.6%, and 10.4% had events over 8 years. Both CFR (aHR 1.42 [1.13-1.78], p<0.01) and EFP (aHR 2.28 [1.67-3.11], p<0.01) independently predicted outcomes. In the 4-group model, impaired CFR/ EFP+ had the worst outcomes (aHR 3.12[2.05-4.74], p<0.01) compared to preserved CFR/ EFP-. Overlap weighted analysis after baseline covariate balance revealed distinct temporal risk patterns: impaired CFR/ EFP+ had the highest 1-year risk (12.7%), while both EFP+ groups had the highest cumulative 8-year risk (57% in preserved CFR, 52% in impaired CFR).

## Conclusion

Integrating AI-ECG EFP with CFR improves risk prediction in ANOCA, potentially identifying distinct phenotypes with divergent short-term and long-term prognosis.
```

##### [26-A-16672-ACC PROGNOSTICATION OF CHRONIC AORTIC REGURGITATION WITH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ENHANCED ELECTROCARDIOGRAM ASSESSMENT OF LEFT VENTRICULAR DIASTOLIC FUNCTION](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.5025)

```
## Background

Left ventricular diastolic function (LVDF) is an early marker of myocardial damage (MD) in chronic volume overload and may have prognostic value in significant (>moderate) aortic regurgitation (AR). We recently validated an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) algorithm to assess LVDF.

## Methods

We included patients with echocardiography-confirmed significant AR (09/2001-06/2022) who were not part of the AI-ECG LVDF training cohort and had both an ECG and echocardiogram performed within seven days. AI-ECG classified patients as MD- (no MD; normal/LVDF grade 1) or MD+ (MD present; LVDF grades 2/3). The primary outcome was all-cause mortality during medical management.

## Results

Among 1,148 patients with significant AR (median age 70; 49.2% female), 40.8% were MD- and 59.2% MD+. Over 3.5 years, 25.6% died under medical management and 18.6% underwent valve replacement. MD+ was independently associated with higher mortality under medical management [adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) 1.42, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03-1.96] and long-term (aHR 1.56, 95% CI 1.15-2.10), adjusted for age, sex, comorbidities, LV ejection fraction (LVEF), and heart failure symptoms. The effect tended to be stronger in LVEF>50% (aHR 3.0, 95% CI 0.8-4.1) than LVEF<50% (aHR 1.8, 95% CI 2.2-4.1; p-interaction = 0.07).

## Conclusion

AI-ECG-derived MD, reflecting LVDF, is independently associated with increased mortality in significant AR, especially among patients with preserved LVEF.
```

##### [26-A-19569-ACC DEVELOPMENT AND MULTINATIONAL VALIDATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ENABLED ASCVD RISK STRATIFICATION USING ELECTROCARDIOGRAMS](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.557)

```
## Background

Validated clinical risk scores for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) exist, however, their use is limited as individuals do not undergo testing of their components. We developed and validated ECG-ASCVD, a widely scalable ECG-based risk prediction paradigm to inform targeted risk factor assessment.

## Methods

We used data from 363,877 adults aged 30-79 years with an ECG and no prior CVD in a large US health system. ECG data were combined with age and sex to train residual neural networks to predict time-to-ASCVD from 12-lead signals (ECG-ASCVD-12) and wearable-adapted 1-lead signals (ECG-ASCVD-1). Model performance was evaluated and compared with the Predicting Risk of CVD Events (PREVENT) equations in a held-out test set and across 4 diverse external cohorts. We then simulated the deployment of ECG-ASCVD in 100,000 randomly selected adults at YNHHS.

## Results

ECG-ASCVD-12 and ECG-ASCVD-1 demonstrated robust discrimination with C-indices of 0.63-0.75 and 0.61-0.74, respectively. Discrimination was comparable to the full estimated PREVENT equations (C-index: 0.60-0.0.78). In simulation, ECG prescreening reduced the number of individuals who needed to undergo risk assessment by 44% at an 80% sensitivity threshold.

## Conclusion

ECG-ASCVD predicts ASCVD risk and identifies subpopulations that will benefit from a formal risk assessment. Deploying ECG-ASCVD in the EHR and on increasingly common ECG-enabled wearables could streamline ASCVD risk factor assessment.
```
##### [26-A-15731-ACC SOCIAL RECONNECTION REVERSES BIOLOGICAL AGING ACCELERATION DETECTED BY ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ENABLED-ECG AT 3 YEARS FOLLOW-UP](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.784)

```
## Background

Social isolation (SI) contributes to cardiovascular disease (CVD) partly by accelerating biological aging. We investigated whether longitudinal changes in SI influence aging trajectories, measured by artificial intelligence-enabled-electrocardiography (AI-ECG).

## Methods

In 17,663 individuals without significant CVD, SI was assessed twice by the Berkman Social Network Index questionnaire, with paired ECGs within one year which underwent AI-enabled analysis. SI status was categorized as persistently connected, became connected, became isolated or persistently isolated. The aging trend was measured as the change over time in the age gap between AI-ECG-predicted age and chronological age.

## Results

Despite being chronologically older [median 63.1 (52.1,70.6) years] and having more comorbidities, persistently connected individuals demonstrated relative slower aging [median change in age gap= -0.69 (-4.22,3.08) years]. Similarly, those who became connected showed a modest attenuation of accelerated aging. [median change in age gap= -0.48 (-4.33,3.38) years, pairwise-p=ns]. Instead, persistent isolation [β= +0.406 years, p<0.01] or becoming isolated [β= +0.430 years, p=0.01] predicted accelerated aging at multivariable linear regression.

## Conclusion

Social connections slow the pace of biological aging independent of comorbidities, supporting the recognition of SI as a modifiable CVD risk factor and the role of AI-ECG in the biological monitoring of these individuals.
```
##### [26-A-15749-ACC LONGITUDINAL SOCIAL ISOLATION STATUS PREDICTS MORTALITY IN COMBINATION WITH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ESTIMATED BIOLOGICAL AGING TRAJECTORY](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.785)

```
## Background

Social isolation (SI) is linked to accelerated aging and adverse outcomes. We explored if longitudinal changes in SI and biological aging measured by artificial intelligence enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) predict mortality.

## Methods

In 17,663 subjects without significant cardiovascular (CV) disease, SI was assessed twice by the Berkman Social Network Index, with paired ECGs within 1 year. SI status was categorized as persistently connected, became connected, became isolated or persistently isolated. Aging trend was measured as change over time in the age gap between AI-ECG predicted age and chronological age. All cause mortality was recorded for Kaplan Meier (KM) and Cox analyses.

## Results

In our population the median chronological age was 63 years and 53% were females. KM curves revealed that persistently connected individuals had the highest survival followed by those who became connected, while persistent or new isolation showed worse survival (log rank p<0.001). Persistently isolated (HR=1.81, 95%CI 1.44-2.27) and newly isolated individuals (HR=1.88, 95%CI 1.36-2.60) had a higher mortality risk after adjusting for clinical variables. Having an age gap change above median also independently predicted mortality (HR=1.25, 95%CI 1.03-1.52).

## Conclusion

Persistent and incident social isolation predict excess mortality. AI-ECG derived aging trajectories provide additive prognostic value, supporting integration of social and biological metrics in CV risk assessment.
```

##### [26-A-20645-ACC DEEP LEARNING-DERIVED PERICARDIAL ADIPOSE TISSUE BY ECG-GATED COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY PREDICTS CARDIOVASCULAR RISK IN NORMAL WEIGHT INDIVIDUALS](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.826)

```
## Background

Body mass index (BMI) does not distinguish body composition, potentially misclassifying cardiovascular (CV) risk in normal-weight individuals with excess visceral adiposity, called “normal-weight obesity”. Pericardial adipose tissue (PAT), a cardiac-specific visceral fat, has been linked to adverse outcomes. We evaluated whether deep learning (DL)-based PAT volume provides independent prognostic value beyond BMI.

## Methods

We analyzed 12,044 Olmsted County, MN, residents without prior ASCVD who underwent standard non-contrast, ECG-gated CT. PAT was quantified using a validated automated DL segmentation model (Dice score 0.94). Cox proportional hazard models evaluated associations with the composite outcome of total CVD (fatal and nonfatal myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke, cardiac death, and heart failure), adjusting for CV risk factors across BMI categories. CVD outcomes were previously adjudicated and validated in the Rochester Epidemiology Project.

## Results

Baseline characteristics are described in Fig. A. PAT volume increased as BMI increased (Fig. A). Over 16.3 ± 6 years,11.1% experienced CVD. Those in the highest PAT tertile had significantly greater CVD risk (Fig. B), driven primarily by the normal/underweight group (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.02-2.17), with no significant association in overweight or obesity groups (Fig. C).

## Conclusion

DL-PAT volume identifies visceral adiposity and independently predicts CVD events, particularly in normal weight individuals.
```
##### [26-A-20963-ACC DEEP LEARNING-DERIVED PERICARDIAL ADIPOSE TISSUE BY ECG-GATED COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY PREDICTS CARDIOVASCULAR EVENTS BEYOND CORONARY CALCIUM](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.832)

```
## Background

Pericardial adipose tissue (PAT) is an emerging imaging biomarker of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. We evaluated whether PAT volume improves prediction of cardiovascular events beyond Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) score and the AHA Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events (PREVENTTM) equation.

## Methods

We analyzed 11,897 Olmsted County, MN, residents without prior ASCVD who underwent non-contrast, ECG-gated CAC scans. PAT was measured using a validated automated deep learning (DL) segmentation model (Dice score 0.94). We stratified patients into groups based on PAT volume (cut-off: top quartile 319 cm3) and CAC score (cut-off: 100 AU). Cox proportional hazard models evaluated associations with the composite outcome total CVD (fatal and nonfatal myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke, cardiac death, and heart failure), while adjusting for cardiovascular risk factors, and CAC score across PREVENT risk categories.

## Results

Baseline characteristics are shown in Fig. A. Over a median 16.4 years, 11.1% experienced CVD. Kaplan-Meier curves demonstrate progressively worse CVD-free survival across PAT and CAC groups (p < 0.001, Fig. B). PAT volume stratified risk across CAC categories, with higher volume conferring incremental risk even at low CAC (Fig. D), conferring increased risk across borderline and intermediate PREVENT categories, independent of CAC score, Fig. C.

## Conclusion

PAT volume provides prognostic value for CVD events beyond PREVENT and CAC scoring.
```
##### [26-A-10457-ACC AUTOMATED INTERPRETATION OF PEDIATRIC ECG PRINTOUTS USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.863)

```
## Background

Artificial intelligence-enabled ECG (AI-ECG) models typically rely on digital waveform inputs, which may limit widespread real-world application. To address this problem, we aimed to develop an AI-ECG model capable of interpreting digital photos of ECG printouts.

## Methods

A convolutional neural network (EfficientNet-B4 architecture) was trained (90% of patients) and tested (10% of patients) on synthetic images of ECGs to predict a comprehensive list of ECG diagnoses (including primary outcomes of prolonged QTc and WPW). The synthetic images were augmented to account for common ECG printout (e.g., layouts and lead name fonts/sizes) and picture quality (e.g., rotation, zoom, blur, contrast, noise) variants. In addition, 100 ECG printouts (50 positive and 50 negative cases) of WPW and prolonged QTC were photographed with a smartphone camera. Model performance was examined on synthetic images and digitized printouts using AUROC.

## Results

The main cohort comprised of 201,620 patients (583,134 ECGs at median age 11.7 [IQR, 3.1-16.9 years]) with 1.0% WPW and 5.3% prolonged QTc. The AI-ECG model achieved similar performance when using synthetic ECGs (AUROC 0.92 and 0.93 for WPW and prolonged QTc) and smartphone pictures of printouts (AUROC 0.95 and 0.94 for WPW and prolonged QTc) as inputs (Figure).
```
##### [26-A-17090-ACC ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-ENABLED ELECTROCARDIOGRAMS PREDICT MORTALITY AND SUDDEN CARDIAC EVENTS IN FONTAN PATIENTS: A MULTI-CENTER STUDY](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.900)

```
## Background

The growing Fontan population remains at high risk of mortality and sudden cardiac death, underscoring the need for accessible and cost-effective risk stratification. Artificial intelligence-enabled ECG (AI-ECG) shows promise to predict mortality, but remains underexplored in Fontan patients.

## Methods

We utilized an established AI-ECG 5-year mortality risk model to predict mortality and sudden cardiac events after Fontan in five external participating FORCE sites. The primary outcome was 5-year mortality or transplant, with a secondary outcome of 5-year sudden cardiac events (cardiac arrest, cardioversion, or sustained ventricular arrhythmias). Performance was benchmarked to MRI single ventricle end-diastolic volume (SV EDV) ≤1 year of ECG. Transplant-free survival analysis was performed using Cox analysis.

## Results

The external test cohort included 11,759 ECGs (median age 14.6 [IQR, 9.4-20.6] years) from 683 patients (median age at Fontan 2.8 years; 8.3% mortality or transplant; 8.8% sudden cardiac events). AI-ECG performed comparably to SV EDV to predict 5-year mortality or transplant (AUROC 0.71 vs 0.70) and sudden cardiac events (AUROC 0.66 vs 0.68). During survival analysis (Figure), AI-ECG achieved a c-index of 0.67 and remained an independent predictor (p=0.0036) when added to SV EDV with improved performance (c-index of 0.74).

## Conclusion

AI-ECG may enable more accessible risk stratification of Fontan patients, and complement establish imaging biomarkers.
```
##### [26-A-10982-ACC DIAGNOSTIC ACCURACY OF ELECTROCARDIOGRAM-BASED ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR ST-ELEVATION MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW AND META-ANALYSIS](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.968)

```
- [Information & Authors](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.968#core-collateral-info "Information & Authors")
- [Metrics & Citations](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.968#core-collateral-metrics "Metrics & Citations")

- [Figures](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.968#core-collateral-figures "Figures")

- [Share](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2026.02.968#core-collateral-share "Share")

## Background

Rapid, accurate recognition of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is critical. Artificial intelligence (AI) for ECG interpretation could accelerate detection, yet no meta-analysis has assessed its diagnostic performance.

## Methods

Following PRISMA-DTA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane and Google Scholar (2010-2025) for studies evaluating ECG-based AI for STEMI diagnosis against a pre-specified composite clinical reference standard (incorporating ECG findings, clinical data, and coronary angiography). Data were analyzed using a bivariate random-effects model to pool sensitivity and specificity (PROSPERO: CRD420251090323).

## Results

From 23 included studies (n=9,832 STEMI-positive; n=530,097 STEMI-negative ECGs). AI demonstrated an area under the summary ROC curve of 0.98 (95% CI: 0.97-0.99). Pooled sensitivity was 0.94 (0.90-0.97) and specificity was 0.95 (0.90-0.97), with a diagnostic odds ratio of 317 (100-1005). Positive likelihood ratio was 18.5 (9.2-37.0) and negative likelihood ratio 0.06 (0.03-0.10). Heterogeneity was high (I2 = 100%), but influence analysis showed stable results. Deeks’ test showed no small-study effects (p=0.15). At 2% pretest probability, AI+ yields ∼27% post-test probability, whereas AI- lowers it to ∼0%.

## Conclusion

ECG-based AI shows high accuracy for STEMI, supporting its potential as a clinical decision-support tool. Prospective workflow-integrated studies are essential.
```
##### [Performance of Artificial Intelligence–Powered ECG Analysis in Suspected ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.102671)

```
### Background

Artificial intelligence (AI)–based electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis has emerged as a promising adjunct to human ECG interpretation in suspected ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).

### Objectives

To expand knowledge in this evolving field, the authors retrospectively analyzed the performance of a novel AI-ECG model in patients with cardiac catheterization laboratory activation for suspected STEMI.

### Methods

Consecutive patients were gathered from a multicenter U.S. STEMI registry (2018-2022) and categorized into 3 clinical cohorts based on the presence or absence of angiographic culprit and troponin elevation: acute myocardial infarction (AMI) with culprit, AMI without culprit, and no-AMI. Cardiac catheterization laboratory-activating ECGs were analyzed using an AI-ECG model trained to identify acute coronary occlusion and classified as occlusion myocardial infarction, OMI(+) or not, OMI(−).

### Results

The study included 2,523 patients, 68.3% male, with a median age of 63 years. AMI with culprit was present in 2076 (82.3%), AMI without culprit in 314 (12.4%), and no-AMI in 133 (5.3%). Among AMI with culprit patients, the model correctly identified 93.8% as OMI(+). Sensitivity for TIMI flow 0/1, 2, and 3 was 96.3%, 93.1%, and 86.9% respectively; _P_ < 0.001. The model correctly identified 79.7% of no-AMI patients as OMI(−). The AUCROC was 0.952 (95% CI: 0.924-0.966). The AMI without culprit cohort included takotsubo syndrome OMI(+) = 78%, MI with nonobstructive coronary arteries OMI(+) = 61%, and myopericarditis OMI(+) = 67%.

### Conclusions

In suspected STEMI, this AI-ECG model correctly identified nearly all patients with acute coronary obstruction and most of those without AMI. If prospectively validated, this approach could improve management of patients with suspected AMI.
```
##### [Deep Learning Echocardiographic Trajectories of Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: A Retrospective Cohort Study](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.102659)

```
### Background

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a dynamic chronic disease. Specific disease trajectories remain unclear.

### Objectives

This study aims to investigate cardiac structure and function trajectories measured by echocardiography and their relationship with clinical outcomes.

### Methods

This was a retrospective cohort from a single center of HFpEF patients with follow-up echocardiogram at ≥ 1 year. Seven longitudinal echocardiographic variables of cardiac geometry and function were utilized to identify trajectory. Longitudinal phenomapping analysis was conducted with machine and deep learning longitudinal clustering. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, while the secondary outcome consisted of changes in B-type natriuretic peptide levels overtime. A panel of longitudinal laboratory biomarkers was used for exploratory outcomes.

### Results

In total, 1,626 HFpEF cases were included; training and validation sets were randomly derived. Echocardiographic trajectories were identified: Echo-Trajectory #1, a stable remodeling trajectory; Echo-Trajectory #2, an increased remodeling course; and Echo-Trajectory #3, decreased remodeling trajectory with right ventricular dysfunction. Baseline clinical characteristics varied significantly among Echo-Trajectories by sex, age, blood pressure, obesity, comorbidities, and left ventricular mass index (_P_ < 0.05). Compared to Echo-Trajectories #2 and #3, Trajectory #1 had a better all-cause mortality outcome (_P_ < 0.001). Similarly, Echo-Trajectory #1 presented favorable trajectories of natriuretic peptides, sodium, and renal function (_P_ < 0.05).

### Conclusions

Longitudinal phenomapping resulted in echocardiographic trajectories of cardiac structure and function with different clinical, laboratory, and survival characteristics. HFpEF is a dynamic condition, and longitudinal phenomapping may improve trajectory characterization and guide treatment strategies.
```
##### [Artificial Intelligence–Driven Electrocardiogram Screening for Asymptomatic Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction in the General Population](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.102660)

```
### Background

Asymptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD) is a well-established precursor of overt heart failure (HF), yet it often remains undiagnosed in the general population. Artificial intelligence–enabled electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis offers a scalable approach for early detection.

### Objectives

The purpose of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic performance of an artificial intelligence–enabled ECG model (AiTiALVSD) for identifying asymptomatic LVSD in a large health screening population.

### Methods

In this retrospective, single-center study, we evaluated the AiTiALVSD model among 40,713 self-referred adults who underwent a total of 60,711 ECG-transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) pairs between 2011 and 2023. LVSD was defined as a left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40%. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC), and diagnostic performance metrics were compared with established HF risk scores.

### Results

Among 60,711 ECG–TTE pairs, 32 cases (0.054%) met the criteria for LVSD. The AiTiALVSD model demonstrated excellent discrimination (AUROC 0.973; AUPRC 0.328), with a sensitivity of 90.6%, specificity of 99.4%, positive predictive value of 7.7%, and a negative predictive value of 100%. Established HF risk scores, including the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) 5-year HF score and Pooled Cohort Equations to Prevent HF score, showed inferior discrimination (AUROC: 0.696 and 0.672, respectively). The MESA score was not designed to detect prevalent LVSD and was calculated without natriuretic peptide data, which may have disadvantaged its performance in this comparison. Simulation analyses suggested that approximately 1,841 ECGs and 13 confirmatory TTEs would be required to detect one case of LVSD.

### Conclusions

In a real-world screening population with an extremely low prevalence of LVSD, the AiTiALVSD model demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy, supporting its potential role as a rule-out screening tool for HF prevention. Prospective validation is warranted.
```
##### [Artificial Intelligence–Enabled Electrocardiographic Detection of Severe Aortic Stenosis Leading to Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jaccas.2026.107184)

```
### Background

EchoNext is an artificial intelligence (artificial intelligence)-enabled electrocardiographic (ECG) model validated to detect unrecognized structural heart disease.

### First-in-Human/Early Reports Summary

An 84-year-old woman presented after a fall and was found to have a left femur fracture. An ECG was ordered which was analyzed by EchoNext. Despite the absence of cardiac symptoms, the ECG was flagged to suggest structural heart disease, prompting cardiology consultation and evaluation. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and severe aortic stenosis (AS). After orthopedic surgery with cardiac anesthesia, the patient underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement.

### Discussion/Novelty

Early identification of severe AS altered perioperative management in an otherwise asymptomatic patient. To our knowledge, this is the first report of an artificial intelligence–enabled ECG algorithm detecting undiagnosed severe AS that led to transcatheter aortic valve replacement.

### Take-Home Message

AI-enabled ECG models may enable earlier detection of clinically silent structural heart disease.
```
##### [200.13 Performance Of Machine Learning Models in Predicting Incident and Recurrent Atrial Fibrillation After Catheter Ablation: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Meta-Regression Analysis](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jcin.2026.01.096)

```
## background

Machine learning (ML) may improve prediction of incident and recurrent atrial fibrillation (AF), but performance varies across models and data types. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of contemporary ML models for AF prediction and identify which algorithms demonstrate the highest discriminative performance.

## methods 

MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and IEEE Xplore were searched without time restriction for original adult studies developing or validating ML models for incident, recurrent, or post-operative AF that reported AUROC from testing or external validation sets. Studies were included if they evaluated patients >18 years using ECG, clinical, or imaging data. Exclusions were non-human studies, non-English manuscripts, reviews, editorials, and studies lacking AUROC. Two reviewers independently performed screening, data extraction, and ROBINS-I assessment. Random-effects meta-analysis, meta-regression, Bayesian modelling, and subgroup analyses were conducted.

## results

Twenty-one studies (512,045 patients) met criteria. The pooled AUROC for ML models was 0.774 (95% CI 0.730–0.818). Support Vector Machine (SVM) showed the highest performance (frequentist AUROC 0.793; Bayesian 0.781), followed by XGBoost, Random Forest, ResNet, and CNN. Bayesian comparison indicated a credible AUROC advantage of SVM over Random Forest. Recurrent AF models performed slightly better (AUROC 0.798) than incident AF (0.765), though without statistical significance.

## conclusion

ML models provide good accuracy for predicting incident and recurrent AF and outperform traditional clinical risk scores. SVM demonstrates the most consistent performance. Larger, prospectively validated datasets are needed to confirm clinical applicability.
```
##### [800.01 Artificial Intelligence Analysis of A 12-Lead Digital ECG Predicts Angiographically Significant Left Main Coronary Artery Disease](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jcin.2026.01.201)

```
## backgroud

The gold standard of coronary artery disease diagnosis is invasive angiography; however it is not employed until late in the diagnostic pathway. Left main (LM) disease is of particular interest due to the difficulty of early detection and associated increased risk or mortality. In this project, we assess a novel deep learning model’s ability to detect LM disease based on a 10-second, 12-lead ECG.

## methods 

 We analyzed the ability of ECGio—a proprietary artificial intelligence algorithm—to identify the presence of clinically significant LM disease (angiographic diameter stenosis ≥50%) in 7,302 patients collected between 2019–2021 from the Allegheny Health Network using just a 12 lead digital ECG. All patients had a resting 12-lead digital ECG recorded within a 90-day window prior to coronary angiography. 10-fold cross-validation was used to analyze the performance of the AI model. Relevant performance metrics were sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and area under the receiver curve (AUC). Secondly, we analyzed ECGio for sources of bias, focusing on number of patient risk factors, age, and sex. Performance metrics and AUC were calculated and reported for each subgroup.

## results

Overall, 1,288 patients (18%) had clinically significant LM disease that was predicted by ECGio with a sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and AUC of 84.2%, 89.2%, 56.1%, 96.2%, and 92.4%, respectively. Patient demographics of sex and age had little effect on model performance, with the number of patient risk factors being the largest source of model performance variation.

## conclusion

This deep learning model is able to accurately detect and exclude clinically significant LM CAD. Model performance appears unaffected by number of risk factors, age, or sex.
```
##### [800.02 The Optimal Interval for Coronary Artery Disease Assessment from A 12 Lead Digital ECG To the Coronary Angiogram: Implications for Diagnostic Test Accuracy](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jcin.2026.01.202)

```
## backgroud

The time interval between a non-invasive test and performance of coronary angiography (CAG) has the potential to impact the ability of a non-invasive algorithm to accurately predict angiographic coronary artery disease (CAD). We developed a proprietary artificial intelligence based ECG algorithm —ECGio— to detect anatomically significant CAD as verified by CAG (diameter stenosis ≥70% in the left anterior descending, left circumflex, or right coronary or ≥50% in the left main); the overall area-under-the curve (AUC) was 90%.

## methods 

Using longitudinal ECG data from 16,476 patients collected between 2019–2021 from the Allegheny Health Network, we assessed a deep-learning model’s ability to detect clinically significant CAD. All patients had a resting 12-lead digital ECG recorded within a 90-day window prior to coronary angiography, with the majority having more than one. Collected ECGs were used to train and test the AI model using a 10-fold cross-validation methodology. In this analysis, we evaluated whether the time interval between the recorded ECG and diagnostic CAG affected the performance metrics of ECGio.

## results

Overall, 61.8% of patients were male and 38.2% were female; CAD prevalence was 64.5%. No patient developed acute symptoms between the date(s) of the recorded ECG and the diagnostic CAG. The ability of the model to predict the presence of clinically significant disease averaged an AUC of 0.90, regardless of whether the ECG was recorded within 1 week or 90 days of CAG.

## conclusion

This deep-learning model was able to accurately detect CAD given an ECG that was recorded within 90 days of CAG. Model performance appears unaffected by length of time between ECG recording and CAG verification. This has implications for all technologies seeking to predict angiographic CAD.
```
##### [Use of Electrocardiograms to Identify Coronary Artery Disease: Cross-Validation of an Artificial Intelligence Model](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacadv.2025.102573)

```
### Background

The current gold standard for the diagnosis of coronary artery disease (CAD) is invasive angiography; however, it is an invasive procedure. Therefore, we developed an artificial intelligence model designed to predict significant CAD from a resting digital 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG).

### Objectives

This retrospective study assessed the model’s ability to predict clinically significant CAD in a patient population presenting for coronary angiography.

### Methods

From 2019 to 2021, 16,476 patients had a resting 12-lead digital ECG recorded within 90 days prior to coronary angiography. The artificial intelligence model was developed using 10-fold cross-validation methodology. Clinically significant disease was defined as angiographic diameter stenosis ≥70% in the left anterior descending, left circumflex, or right coronary artery or ≥50% in the left main coronary artery. We then applied the model to an external validation set.

### Results

In the cross-validation cohort, the prevalence of clinically significant CAD was 64.5%; the model achieved a positive predictive value of 91.7% (95% CI: 89.9%-93.4%), negative predictive value of 72.8% (95% CI: 69.6%-76.0%), and area under the curve of 91.4% (95% CI: 89.4%-94.4%) in predicting clinically significant CAD. In external validation, the prevalence of clinically significant CAD was 36.0%; the model achieved a positive predictive value of 82.5% (95% CI: 75.9%-89.2%), negative predictive value of 88.1% (95% CI: 84.0%-92.1%), and area under the curve of 92.4% (95% CI: 89.7%-95.1%) in predicting clinically significant CAD.

### Conclusions

This study demonstrated the clinical utility of a deep learning artificial intelligence algorithm to analyze a digital 12-lead ECG to predict the presence of clinically significant CAD as determined by coronary angiography.
```
##### [Artificial Intelligence–Enhanced Electrocardiogram Models for Detection of Left Ventricular Dysfunction: A Comparison Study](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacadv.2025.102572)

```
### Background

Several artificial intelligence–enhanced electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) models have shown promise in detecting left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD), but their head-to-head agreement and performance have not been independently compared within the same cohort.

### Objectives

This study aimed to compare the performance of published AI-ECG models for LVSD detection in a standardized external cohort and evaluate the field’s transparency and reproducibility.

### Methods

We systematically reviewed AI-ECG models predicting LVSD and assessed the risk of bias. Authors were invited to share models for external validation in a well-phenotyped registry of patients undergoing routine clinical cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with cardiologist-adjudicated reports and paired ECGs. Model performance was evaluated in all consecutive patients and a lower-complexity subgroup with 15% LVSD prevalence.

### Results

We identified 35 studies describing 51 models, reporting high (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve [AUROC] >0.80) or excellent (AUROC >0.90) performance. The risk of bias is high and primarily attributed to the limited description of development and validation cohort characteristics, as well as the lack of independent external validation. Four groups (from Korea, the United States, Taiwan, and the Netherlands) shared models for independent testing. AUROCs ranged from 0.83 to 0.93 in all patients (n = 1,203; mean age 59 ± 15 years; 450 [35%] female) and from 0.87 to 0.96 in the lower-complexity subset. Performance remained consistent across subgroups, with slight decreases in ECGs showing wide QRS complexes or atrial fibrillation.

### Conclusions

In this first-in-kind independent validation and head-to-head comparison study, AI-ECG for LVSD detection demonstrated strong performance despite training on disparate populations. However, the limited-availability of models hinders independent validation.
```
##### [Multisite, External Validation of an AI-Enabled ECG Algorithm for Detection of Low Ejection Fraction](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacadv.2025.102537)

```
### Background

Low left ventricular ejection fraction (LEF) can progress undiagnosed. Artificial intelligence–based electrocardiogram (ECG-AI) screening may provide a scalable means to detect LEF.

### Objectives

The purpose of this study was to validate a complete ECG-AI software as a medical device for LEF detection.

### Methods

Four geographically diverse sites in the United States identified patients with both ECGs and transthoracic echocardiograms performed within 30 days of each other in clinical practice. Data were electronically extracted to specific guidelines and transmitted to the coordinating center for analysis.

### Results

Records of 16,000 subjects were extracted, resulting in an evaluable set of 13,960 subjects (mean age 66 years; 52% male). The device demonstrated excellent discrimination (AUROC: 0.92 [95% CI: 0.91-0.93]) and was 84.5% (95% CI: 82.2%-86.6%) sensitive and 83.6% (95% CI: 82.9%-84.2%) specific for LEF. The overall prevalence of LEF in the study data set was 7.9%, with LEF among 1.6% of the ECG-AI negative and 30.5% of ECG-AI positive subjects, contributing to positive and negative predictive values of 30.5% (95% CI: 28.8%-32.1%) and 98.4% (95% CI: 98.2%-98.7%), respectively.

### Conclusions

External validation studies such as this one provide a rigorous framework to validate an algorithm’s performance. This study demonstrated the algorithm’s strong diagnostic accuracy over a geographically diverse, independent set of patients. In this generally unselected population, the algorithm produced a test negative result in 78% of the cases, suggesting potential utility as a rule-out strategy to defer echocardiography when other clinical findings are absent.
```
##### [Predicting Heart Failure From 12-Lead ECGs Using AI: A HeartShare/AMP-HF Pooled Cohort Analysis](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.10.065)

```
### Background

Artificial intelligence applied to electrocardiograms (ECG-AI) offers a scalable approach to identify individuals at risk for heart failure (HF) and guide preventive interventions.

### Objectives

The purpose of this study was to assess whether ECG-AI designed to detect systolic and diastolic dysfunction enhances the prediction of incident HF over clinical risk estimation using the PREVENT-HF (Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs–Heart Failure) equation.

### Methods

Baseline clinical and electrocardiogram data were pooled from the Framingham Heart Study, Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, and Cardiovascular Health Study. Participants with data sufficient for both ECG-AI and PREVENT-HF assessment were included. Analyses were performed on the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute BioDataCatalyst from July to September 2025. Risk of incident HF was estimated using previously validated ECG-AI algorithms that detect systolic (ECG-AI LEF) and diastolic (ECG-AI DD) dysfunction. Discrimination and reclassification were evaluated using Harrell’s C-statistic and net reclassification improvement.

### Results

Of 14,126 participants, positive screening rates were 2.9% for ECG-AI LEF, 11.1% for ECG-AI DD, 11.9% for the composite ECG-AI model, 25.1% for PREVENT-HF score ≥10%, and 5.8% for PREVENT-HF score ≥20%. Incident HF or death occurred in 7.7% and 15.1% of participants, respectively. Participants with positive composite ECG-AI screens at baseline had 10- to 20-fold higher risk of developing HF compared with those with negative screens. At 1, 3, 5, and 10 years, the addition of ECG-AI to PREVENT-HF yielded 1-directional net reclassification improvements ranging from 0.086 to 0.125 at a PREVENT-HF threshold of 10%, and 0.327 to 0.403 at a threshold of 20%.

### Conclusions

The addition of ECG-AI to PREVENT-HF improved discrimination of near-term HF risk. ECG-AI may enable population-level HF risk stratification and facilitate targeted prevention strategies.
```
##### [The Emerging Role of ECG-AI as a Digital Risk Biomarker for Incident Heart Failure](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.11.039)

```
Electrocardiography (ECG) lies at the core of nearly every cardiovascular pathway.¹ For decades, its interpretation has relied on rule-based criteria and pattern recognition, reflecting the cumulative refinement of physiological knowledge and clinical practice. Despite this, diagnostic performance varies across readers, and ECGs are now understood to contain subtle signatures of structural heart disease that are not easily discernible to the human eye.¹ These limitations have motivated a new generation of artificial intelligence (AI) approaches capable of extracting “hidden” structural phenotypes directly from standard ECG signals and images.²,³ Yet, because most studies have emphasized cross-sectional detection, the utility of ECG-AI as a biomarker of future cardiovascular risk remains underexplored.
```
