##### [AI-enabled privacy-preserving cardiac diagnostics via electrocardiograms](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-47665-6)

```
## Abstract

Electrocardiogram (ECG) is a widely available, non-invasive diagnostic tool used for cardiovascular screening and provides essential insights into heart rhythm, structure, and function. However, the high dimensionality of ECGs and their entanglement with demographic information pose challenges for building fair and privacy-preserving machine learning models. ECG signals inherently encode soft biometric attributes such as sex, age, and race, which may introduce bias and raise privacy concerns in data-sharing environments. To address these challenges, we propose a deep learning framework that learns clinically relevant ECG representations while suppressing sensitive demographic information. We leverage a variational autoencoder (VAE) with a dual-discriminator architecture. One adversarial branch reduces soft biometric encoding, while the other preserves clinically important discrimination of reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). The privacy-preserving reconstructed ECGs reduced identifiability of soft biometrics by independent CNN models with AUROC for sex 0.59 (from original 0.79), age 0.63 (from 0.78), and race 0.57 (from 0.69), while retaining clinically-useful predictions like reduced LVEF 0.82 (from 0.86), left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) 0.72 (from 0.75), and 5-year mortality 0.67 (from 0.66). These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for retaining ECG data yet protecting patient privacy.

## Introduction

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide, accounting for approximately 19.8 million deaths annually, representing 32% of all global deaths according to the World Health Organization1.
Early and accurate diagnosis of cardiac conditions is essential for effective treatment planning and improved patient outcomes. Among the most widely used non-invasive tools in cardiac diagnostics is the electrocardiogram (ECG), which records the heart’s electrical activity and provides valuable insights into arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, conduction abnormalities, and other aspects of cardiac structure and function. ECGs are fast, cost-effective, and accessible across a wide range of clinical settings, making them indispensable in both acute and chronic cardiovascular care. Furthermore, ECG derived features have increasingly been explored in computational models for automated detection and prognostic assessments of cardiac dysfunction, including reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and heart failure risk2, 3. However, with the increasing evaluation of ECG data for purposes beyond clinical diagnosis, such as biometric authentication4 and medical data-sharing initiatives5, there has been a growing emphasis on addressing privacy and data security concerns6. Recent advancements in deep learning have shown that personal attributes, including biological sex and age, can be accurately inferred from ECG signals7.
This highlights a significant vulnerability: even anonymized ECG data can inadvertently disclose identifying information, potentially compromising patient confidentiality.
Recent studies have demonstrated that ECG signals can serve as biometric identifiers capable of re-identifying individuals across sessions and devices8. Such identity leakage poses serious privacy risks, including unauthorized record linkage, patient re-identification, and misuse of biometric health data9, 10. These risks are particularly concerning under modern data protection regulations such as GDPR11, where physiological signals used for identification are considered sensitive personal data. Therefore, developing privacy-preserving ECG representa- tions that suppress identity-related attributes while preserving clinical utility is both a technical and ethical necessity.
Conventional anonymization techniques such as data masking or removal of explicit identifiers often prove insufficient, as demographic attributes may remain inferrable from the signal data itself12. This paper by Kaissis et al.13 argues that existing anonymization strategies often focus on removing metadata, may be insufficient in the face of increasingly sophisticated AI models capable of extracting identifying features directly from the raw modality ECG signals. Evidence of this threat has already emerged. For instance, Packhäuser et al.14 demonstrated that deep learning models could achieve re-identification rates as high as 95% on chest X-ray datasets, despite standard anonymization. Similarly, Schwarz et al.15 successfully reconstructed recognizable facial images from cranial MRI data with 83% accuracy. In the context of ECGs, Ghazarian et al.16 reported that a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on ECG waveforms could re-identify patients with up to 99.7% accuracy in certain subgroups by mapping waveforms to individual identities. Collectively, these findings underscore the need to move beyond conventional anonymization paradigms, particularly in the context of data sharing in AI workflows. An ideal anonymized medical dataset should retain predictive value for clinically relevant outcomes while being futile for inferring demographic details such as age, sex, and race. The goal of this study is to support privacy-preserving data sharing and model training, not to replace demographic information during clinical decision making. In real clinical settings, demographic information should remain available to physicians.

## Results

We conducted a series of experiments to evaluate the PP-VAE’s ability to suppress demographic information while preserving clinically relevant features. To this end, we used the 30-dimensional latent representations learned by different VAEs as input to XGBoost classifiers for a set of downstream prediction tasks, providing empirical evidence for the suitability of the 30-dimensional latent space shown in Table 2. The prediction targets included clinical outcomes such as reduced LVEF, LVH, and 5-year mortality as well as demographic variables, e.g., age, sex, and race. To compare, we evaluated four models: a baseline VAE, a VAE with adversarial sex loss, the proposed PP-VAE, and the proposed PP-VAE trained with an additional LVEF prediction objective (PP-VAE+LVEF). The results show that adversarial training enables VAEs to suppress sensitive demographic information partially. For example, the VAE with adversarial sex loss reduced predictive accuracy not only for sex, but also for age and race, although to a limited extent. In contrast, the PP-VAE, which incorporates penalties for both age and race, achieved a more substantial removal of demographic information from the encodings. Importantly, PP-VAE and PP-VAE+LVEF preserved the clinical utility of the representations. These models yielded improved performance on reduced LVEF and LVH prediction tasks while keeping demographic predictability close to chance levels. The additional LVEF prediction objective in PP-VAE+LVEF further strengthened performance on clinical outcomes without compromising privacy preservation.
For an additional experiment. We then trained convolutional neural network (CNN) models to predict the same outcomes as Table 2 to see if the PP-VAEs were able to obscure the demographic information in the raw sig- nals themselves while maintaining the morphological and clinical data within the signals. Table 3 evaluates the prediction performance of the CNN models, and it demonstrates that the PP-VAE+LVEF is able to remove the demographic information while maintaining the clinical use, even for reconstructed ECGs. This is a major step in privacy-preserving data sharing between health centers, as the modified ECGs can be sent over without breaking HIPAA compliance guidelines in an anonymized way32.
We also measured the error between the raw signal and reconstructed signals. The reconstruction performance of the PP-VAE demonstrates robust signal recovery across all cardiac cycle components, with notable variations in performance characteristics that align with the inherent morphological properties of each waveform segment, showed in Figure 1. The QRS complex exhibits the strongest overall performance with an R2 value of 0.83 and Spearman correlation of 0.75, indicating excellent preservation of the high-amplitude, morphologically distinct ventricular depolarization patterns, despite registering the highest mean absolute error (MAE = 34.79 μV) due to its greater dynamic range. The T-wave reconstruction achieves the highest correlation coefficient (ρ = 0.79) with moderate error levels (MAE = 20.24 μV) and strong explained variance (R2 = 0.78), reflecting the model’s capacity to capture the smooth, predictable repolarization morphology. In contrast, P-wave reconstruction presents the most challenging scenario with the lowest R2 (0.54) and correlation (0.64) values, though maintaining the smallest absolute error (MAE = 14.75 μV), which is consistent with the inherently variable and low-amplitude nature of atrial depolarization that presents greater difficulty for autoencoder architectures to reliably reconstruct. All correlations demonstrate statistical significance (p < 0.001), confirming the model’s consistent ability to preserve essential ECG morphological features across the complete cardiac cycle.

## Discussion

In this work, we introduce a Privacy-Preserving Variational Autoencoder (PP-VAE) for ECG analysis. By integrating adversarial demographic obfuscation with clinically supervised representation learning, our framework produces latent embeddings that retain morphological and diagnostic information while suppressing sensitive demographic attributes. This dual objective enables the model to balance clinical utility with privacy preservation. While VAEs have demonstrated promise for dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, and generative tasks in ECG analysis, existing implementations have largely been restricted to single-lead or standard 12-lead recordings in controlled environments. By contrast, our approach demonstrates feasibility in 10-second ECG recordings, highlighting its potential scalability. Nonetheless, most VAE-based methods, including ours, remain limited by their reliance on fixed-length segments, which constrains applicability to continuous monitoring where arrhythmic events may occur sporadically over extended periods.
Despite recent advances in interpretable latent representations29, 33, the interpretability of VAE latent spaces continues to pose a barrier to clinical adoption. While certain dimensions can be aligned with canonical ECG features, the relationship between latent factors and specific pathophysiological processes often remains opaque.
This interpretability gap constrains the capacity of such models to provide explanatory insights alongside predictions, a critical requirement for decision support in clinical settings. Another related technical challenge is the choice of latent priors. The conventional Gaussian prior in VAE may not adequately capture the complex manifold structure of ECG signals, potentially limiting both generative performance and representation quality. Although alternative priors have been proposed34, systematic evaluation is required to determine appropriate distributional assumptions for cardiac data. An additional consideration concerns the entanglement of clinical and demographic information.
For example, age is strongly associated with reduced LVEF, meaning that ECG features predictive of age may also carry legitimate diagnostic value. Removing demographic correlates can therefore impair clinical prediction, not due to model failure but because of genuine biological associations. This highlights the importance of task- specific evaluation when attempting to mitigate demographic information. Moreover, the removal of demographic features does not inherently resolve issues of fairness; in some cases, it may exacerbate inequities. Differences in disease prevalence, phenotype expression, or comorbidity across demographic groups can alter conditional feature distributions, thereby harming subgroup performance or calibration. Careful fairness assessment, including subgroup error and calibration analyses, is therefore essential when applying privacy-preserving transformations.
Further limitations arise from the lack of evaluation on conventional ECG summary statistics (e.g., QRS duration, PR interval, QTc). Understanding how these clinically interpretable measures are altered by transformation is crucial, as such changes affect both human interpretability and compatibility with rule-based diagnostic workflows.
In the absence of correction or inverse mapping, transformed ECGs may become unintelligible to clinicians, presenting a significant challenge for deployment. Beyond interpretability, confidentiality and adversarial privacy risks also warrant consideration. Practical implementation requires strict protection of both the guiding classifiers and the original ECG data. Leakage of model weights, training data, or even aggregated statistics could enable adversaries to reconstruct demographic information. Furthermore, class imbalance in real-world datasets can implicitly encode demographic correlates, enabling partial re-identification. Addressing these vulnerabilities necessitates formal threat modeling and the integration of privacy-preserving techniques such as differential privacy and secure model hosting. Finally, the publication of de-identification methodologies presents a dual-use concern: while transparency promotes scientific progress, it may also enable adversaries with auxiliary datasets to replicate and invert de-identification pipelines. This underscores the need for complementary technical, procedural, and legal safeguards, rather than reliance on model-based transformations alone.
In summary, VAEs represent a powerful framework for ECG representation learning, yet their clinical translation depends on more than predictive accuracy. While the proposed framework significantly reduces demographic attribute leakage (age, sex, race), it does not claim complete protection against all forms of re-identification.
ECG morphology may encode subject-specific signatures. Therefore, our work is a step toward demographic de- identification rather than full identity anonymization. Progress in robustness to real-world artifacts, interpretability of latent spaces, and the integration of privacy- and fairness-preserving mechanisms will be critical for trustworthy adoption. Future work should focus on extending clinically supervised latent objectives to a broader range of outcomes, systematically evaluating the effect of transformations on standard ECG markers, and developing rigorous fairness and privacy assessments. Although the framework is trained with demographic suppression objectives, experimental results on independent clinical tasks such as LVEF and LVH prediction demonstrate that the anonymized ECG retains clinically relevant information without requiring retraining on original ECG data. High correlation coefficients between original and processed waveforms further confirms morphological preservation. These findings suggest that the approach generalizes beyond the specific training objectives. With these complementary advances, representation-learning frameworks such as PP-VAE can move from experimental demonstrations to reliable components of precision cardiology pipelines.
Future Directions The present study highlights the potential of privacy-preserving VAEs for ECG representation learning, but also reveals several avenues for advancing both the methodology and its clinical applicability. Building on our findings, we identify the following promising directions: • Privacy-Preserving Learning: Future work can integrate federated learning and differential privacy tech- niques to extend our framework beyond centralized datasets. This would enable multi-institutional collabora- tion while rigorously safeguarding sensitive patient data, a prerequisite for real-world deployment.
• Physiologically Informed Priors: Incorporating priors grounded in cardiac electrophysiology, such as distributions over RR intervals, QT durations, or QRS widths, has the potential to align the learned latent space with an interpretable, physiologically meaningful objective. This would improve model transparency and facilitate adoption by clinicians, who often demand correspondence between model features and known cardiac parameters.
• Personalized Monitoring: Current representations are optimized at the population level, yet clinical care often requires individualized assessment. Adaptive VAEs that establish patient-specific baselines could detect subtle deviations over time, particularly beneficial for monitoring individuals with chronic or high-risk cardiac conditions.
• Fairness under Privacy: While our work demonstrates that demographic attributes can be obfuscated, an open question remains: how do privacy-preserving constraints interact with fairness across demographic and clinical subgroups? Future efforts should design strategies to simultaneously mitigate bias in latent spaces and ensure equitable performance under privacy-preserving regimes.
Conclusion The results of this study demonstrate the potential of privacy-preserving deep learning for ECG analysis in clinical practice. Standard deep learning models achieve strong predictive performance for critical cardiovascular outcomes, including reduced LVEF, LVH, and 5-year mortality, yet inadvertently encode sensitive demographic information such as sex, age, and race, raising concerns about patient privacy and algorithmic fairness. To address this, we introduced Privacy-Preserving VAE and further extended it with task-relevant supervision (PP-VAE + LVEF). Our results demonstrate that the proposed model significantly reduces the encoding of sensitive attributes (e.g., Sex: 0.58 vs. 0.75 in classical VAE) while maintaining strong predictive performance on key clinical outcomes (e.g., LVEF: 0.82, matching classical VAE). This illustrates a favorable privacy-utility trade-off, showing that incorporating adversarial tasks into the VAE architecture and loss function can mitigate demographic leakage without sacrificing clinical relevance.
```
##### [Personalized artificial intelligence based left ventricular ejection fraction and systolic dysfunction assessment](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02462-3)

```
## Abstract

Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is a fundamental measure of cardiac function, typically assessed with resource-intensive imaging techniques such as transthoracic echocardiography (TTE). We evaluated the electrocardiogram (ECG) as alternative and accessible data to estimate LVEF, in a large cohort of 191,941 patients paired with 236,623 ECG/TTEs. Using either the ECG data alone or with structured features, we developed convolutional and probabilistic neural network models to estimate LVEF and quantify uncertainty. The ECG-only model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 7.71% and RMSE of 10.36%, while the hybrid model achieved an MAE of 7.84% and an RMSE of 10.52%. Personalized models significantly improved performance, achieving MAEs of 5.98% (ECG-only) and 6.75% (hybrid). Left-ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF ≤ 40%), was identified with an AUC of 0.88, sensitivity of 0.92 and negative predictive value of 0.98. The presented models demonstrated excellent performance in estimating LVEF and screening/triage of LV systolic dysfunction.

## Introduction

Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) is a central clinical prognostic parameter in assessing progression of heart failure 1, risk of sudden cardiac death 2, and complications from valvular heart dysfunction 3. There exist several methods for estimating LVEF, including invasive left-ventriculography during cardiac catheterization, and non-invasive imaging techniques such as transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), cardiac computed tomography, nuclear imaging and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI). However, each method has important limitations.
cMRI is expensive and limited to specialized settings, nuclear imaging involves radiation exposure, and TTE, while portable and more accessible, has high intra- and inter-observer variability 4 Given these challenges, as well as recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), there has been growing interest in estimating LVEF by applying AI algorithms to the electrocardiogram (ECG), 5,6 which is affordable and widely available in under-resourced settings. To that end, several studies have developed deep learning-based models to estimate the TTE-derived LVEF, from ECG signals 7-9. Using the ECG as an image has resulted in a mean absolute error (MAE) of 5.84% 10, while a 30-day interval limit between the ECG recording and the TTE date, achieved an MAE of 5.28%. 11, and an cMRI-based ground truth for estimating LVEF resulted in an MAE of 4.64% 12.
Despite various attempts in estimating LVEF, concerns regarding the reliability of these models still persist. Most prior studies have focused primarily on point estimates, often overlooking the uncertainty inherent in these estimates. A recent study employing a 82 layers CNN probabilistic neural network, reported an MAE of 7.5% employing the standard deviation (SD) of the estimation as the uncertainty metric13. However, uncertainty stems from various sources, including inter-observer measurement variability in clinical measurement14 and limitations in model's knowledge of personalized natural history factors 15, raising questions about the reliability of point estimates. Therefore, evaluating a model’s uncertainty in its estimations is imperative for making informed decisions about treatment and diagnosis 16-18. An alternative approach to reduce the estimation error, in the era of personalized medicine, is to obtain personalized predictions by developing models that learn to adapt to unique patient- specific characteristics.
In this study, we define two practical use cases for ECG-based LVEF estimation; first, the primary intended use is in settings where traditional imaging modalities are not available or are delayed, an ECG-based estimate of LVEF may serve as interim decision support to guide prioritization and care escalation until definitive imaging can be obtained; second, screening/triage, leveraging the low cost and ubiquity of ECG to help rule out LV systolic dysfunction and prioritize confirmatory imaging for higher-risk cases. To achieve these objectives we explore various convolutional neural network CNN architectures to estimate LVEF, using TTE derived LVEF as the ground truth. We also investigate the uncertainty quantification using a probabilistic neural network to derive prediction intervals for LVEF estimates across different LVEF ranges. Furthermore, we hypothesize that personalized deep learning improves LVEF estimation performance compared to a generalized model by learning from individual longitudinal ECG data. Additionally, the developed foundational CNN model is externally validated using the external MIMIC IV dataset.

## Results

### CNN Configurations and Architectures

CNN models were assessed using the initial data across eight different configurations, by varying the number of layers, fusion schemes, and input signal types. To obtain the optimal architecture, we employed a tuning mechanism using the Keras tuner that evaluated each of the eight configurations through 50 trials. We reported the MAE and RMSE for the training, testing, and validation datasets. The choice of number of filters, kernel size, activation functions used in the tuning process to obtain the optimal model are summarized in Table S1.
The results indicate that the configuration utilizing the median ECG signal as input outperformed the configuration using the full signal, as shown in Table S2. Additionally, Table S2 indicates that the model employing the 2-layer (2L) configuration demonstrates slightly better performance compared to the 1-layer (1L) and 10-layer (10L) configurations for the ECG-only architectures. We observed that the 2L early fusion configuration performs marginally better than the 2L late fusion configuration.
Furthermore, it is evident from Table S2 that the 2L early and late fusion configurations performed nearly identically in terms of MAE and RMSE, 8.46% and 11.26% vs 8.39% and 11.11%, respectively. However, favoring computational efficiency, we chose the 2L early fusion configuration, using the median ECG beat as the optimized architecture for further analysis. The results of the tuning process for each configuration are presented in Data S1-S12.

### CNN Model Performance

Once the optimized model configuration was obtained, we incorporated a fully connected layer in the optimized model (a 2L early fusion configuration, using the median ECG beat as an input). We ran the Keras tuner for this configuration over 50 trials, and the performance metrics, including MAE and RMSE improved to 7.68% and 10.35%, respectively; detailed results are presented in Data S13.
To evaluate the optimal configuration, we implemented a 5-fold stratified cross- validation approach. The training, testing, and validation datasets were concatenated into a single dataset, which was then split into five folds, maintaining a similar range of LVEF values in each fold. In each iteration, one fold served as the test set, while the remaining four served as the training set, allowing us to assess the model performance across different subsets of the data.
We observed consistency, with a mean ± SD of 7.72 ± 0.03, across the 5-folds, as shown in Data S14.
To investigate whether the extracted tabular features improved LVEF estimation, we built a hybrid model based on the selected optimal CNN configuration the 2L, the median ECG beat, and the early fusion configuration. This hybrid model utilized ECG as the input to the CNN, and tabular features as input to the MLP network, yielding an MAE and RMSE of 7.86% and 10.56%, respectively. The evaluation metrics suggest that the hybrid model performs similarly to the ECG- only model. This aligns with previous findings indicating that features extracted from the ECG signal contributed minimally to the overall model performance 10. The tuner results across 50 trials, are presented in Data S15.
We further optimized the network by performing a fine search of the hyperparameter space, described in Table S3, which resulted in an MAE of 7.83% and an RMSE of 10.64% for the ECG-only model, and an MAE of 7.66% and an RMSE of 10.30% for the hybrid model. The tuner results for both the ECG and hybrid models are detailed in Data S16-S17.
Given the wide distribution of LVEF values in the study population (Figure 1), we implemented L2 regularization to mitigate overfitting, and ensure equal importance is assigned to all labels. The Keras tuner results for 50 trials, yielded an MAE and an RMSE of 7.71% and 10.36% for the ECG-only model, and 7.84% and 10.52% for the hybrid model; while the detailed results are presented in Data S18-S19. Henceforth, we refer to the best performing models as the foundational ECG-only (Figure S1), and the foundational hybrid model (Figure S2) respectively. We also presented the error distribution box plots in Figures 2 and 3 for all LVEF ranges to assess the model's performance for both the ECG and hybrid models. It is observed that for both models, the MAE is higher in the extreme LVEF ranges (<25 and >75). This was attributed to the relatively limited number of samples in the very high and low LVEF values.
Additionally, we trained separate foundational ECG-only models, on either male-only or female-only cohorts to investigate the sex-based impact on LVEF estimation. The male cohort consisted of 128,118 ECGs, while the female cohort consisted of 100,681 ECGs. Overall, we observed a slightly better performance in the female-only cohort (MAE and RMSE: 8.27% and 11.29%, Data S20) compared to the male-only cohort (MAE and RMSE: 11.14% and 14.69%, Data S21).
We found the MAE distributions of the male and female cohorts to be significantly different (p < 0.05), using the independent t-test with equal variances. A possible explanation for this observation may lie in the differences of the LVEF value distributions, between females and males. Previous studies have shown that women tend to have higher LVEF values compared to men19, with the female distribution of LVEF values being shifted towards higher values compared to men (see also, Figure 1)20. In our study, the female cohort exhibited a similar pattern, with more LVEF values in the upper ranges, particularly in the 70-85% range, leading to a higher mean LVEF of 62.13%, compared to the male cohort's mean of 57.86%, as shown in Figure 1. The female cohort demonstrated a lower MAE, likely due to its higher number of values around the average LVEF, resulting in improved model’s performance. In contrast, the male cohort exhibits a greater proportion of LVEF values in the lower ranges which introduces more variability and makes the predictions less accurate, resulting in a higher MAE.
When both sexes are combined, the resulting broader distribution of LVEF values appears to mitigate sex-based performance differences, allowing the model to generalize better, manifested by an improvement of the foundational ECG-only model performance.

### Prediction Uncertainty Estimation

To quantify uncertainty through prediction intervals, we implemented the PNN architecture for both the foundational ECG-only and hybrid models, with hyperparameter tuning/optimization using the Keras Tuner, as presented in Data S22-23. We observed that the foundational ECG-only PNN model’s performance, was comparable to the CNN’s, with MAE and RMSE of 7.97% and 10.67%, respectively. Using the foundational hybrid PNN model, the MAE and RMSE were 7.89% and 10.58%, respectively.
We also observed that the prediction intervals were similar for both models, and that they were wider at the lower LVEF values and narrowed towards the mean of the LVEF distribution. The error distribution and prediction interval plots across the whole range of the LVEF for both ECG-only and hybrid models are shown in Figures S3-S6.
In the Online Supplement, Figures S3 and S5 present the MAE for LVEF values ranging from 5% to 90% along with the corresponding sample sizes for the ECG-only model and the hybrid models, of the PNN architectures. The MAE and RMSE for the ECG-only model are 7.97% and 10.67% respectively, and for the hybrid model 7.89% and 10.58% respectively (Data S22 and S23).
We observe similar prediction intervals for both the ECG-only and hybrid models, as shown in Figures S4 and S6, with LVEF values below 30% and above 70%, falling outside these prediction intervals (the box plots in Figures S4 and S6 illustrate the lower and upper bounds of the prediction intervals for each respective range). Interestingly, the prediction intervals are wider at the lower-end of the LVEF values, and narrow as the LVEF values approach the mean of the LVEF distribution. While for lower-end LVEF values we observe broader prediction intervals, the overlap between the upper and lower bounds indicates a high level of certainty that the LVEF values fall within these intervals, suggesting limited variability. Furthermore, in the 60-75% range, the data points are closely clustered, indicating greater precision in the prediction intervals around the true mean of the LVEF distribution. These observations highlight the fact that both the true mean and the number of samples of the distribution, influence the width of the prediction intervals.

### Model Interpretability

To gain insights into the significant contributions of each ECG lead during the model’s decision-making process, we performed a GRAD-CAM analysis. While the 2-layer early fusion approach delivered the best performance, we aimed to examine the contribution of each lead independently; therefore, we selected the 2-layer late fusion configuration, where each lead was processed individually through its corresponding CNN layer. This enabled us to generate heat- maps for each lead, highlighting the most influential ECG segments in the model's LVEF estimation. We then calculated the median heat-map for each lead’s corresponding median beat.
In the Echo cohort, we observed significant contributions from several regions of the ECG, from different leads, such as the PR interval of Lead I, the PR segment and QRS duration of aVL and V4, the QT interval of aVF, and the T-wave of V2 (Figure S7). Additionally, nearly all segments of Leads II, aVR, and V6 contributed to the model's performance. These findings are in agreement with those of a recent study that emphasized the importance of Leads I, II, and V2, in LVEF prediction 21 .

### Algorithm External Validation

The foundational ECG–only architecture was validated using the MIMIC-IV ECG records22, MIMIC-IV notes23, and MIMIC-IV Echo data24, as described in the Methods; the model achieved an MAE of 8.79 % and an RMSE of 11.83 % during external validation in a cMRI cohort, that were slightly higher than the corresponding values obtained in our own cohort (Data S18); a finding that may be attributed to this imaging modality shift or population demographic differences.

### Development and Testing of a Personalized CNN Model

The cohort for the personalized model was constructed by including all available records of all subjects. Subjects with a single report only were included in the training and validation datasets, while those with multiple records were allocated to the test cohort. The cohort was comprised of 306,319 ECG records, corresponding to 78,677 and 8,742 unique subjects in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. The test cohort was comprised of 218,888 ECG records corresponding to 64,988 unique subjects. We utilized the foundational ECG-only model and the Keras tuner for 50 trials was employed; the results are presented in Data S24-S25. The best generalized model was selected from Data S24. The generalized ECG-only model achieved an MAE of 8.98% and an RMSE of 12.21%.
For the personalized models, the training process was iterative: the best generalized model was trained on the first i samples and tested on the (i+1)th sample in the test cohort; that is initially, the model was trained on the first sample, and in each subsequent iteration, it added one more sample to the training set, while testing on the next sample for each subject. During each iteration, all layers of the model were fine-tuned by unfreezing them, and the model was recompiled with a learning rate of 1e-5. This approach allowed the model to continuously learn by incorporating new samples while being evaluated on previously unseen data. To prevent overfitting, early stopping was implemented by monitoring the relative error between the model's estimated value and the true label on the training data, requiring the training to stop if the relative error fell below a predetermined threshold of 1%. To compare the personalized model performance for each subject’s sample with the generalized model, we also tested each sample of the subject on the best generalized model.
The personalized model was then trained and tested for each subject in the test cohort.
To evaluate the performance of the generalized and personalized models, we calculated the relative error (between the model's estimated value and the true label) for each subject's sample during testing; where, the first sample from each subject was excluded, as it was used solely for training. The results are based on the second sample onwards in each subject for both the generalized and personalized models. The relative errors for all samples within each subject was grouped by sample number. This allowed us to test the hypothesis that as the number of sample number increases for each subject, the personalized model's error decreases.
Figure 4 shows the relative error across all the testing cohort subjects. Box plots have been modified such that the upper whisker indicates the 95th percentile. A linear fit of the 95th percentile values indicates a decrease of the 95th percentile error with each additional sample.
Figure 5 presents a comparison of the absolute error between the generalized and the personalized models across different LVEF values, showing that the personalized model yielded statistically significant (p < 0.0001) lower error, across all LVEF values, compared to the generalized model. Additionally, the overall MAE for the personalized model was 5.98%, compared to 8.98% for the generalized model.

### Development and Testing of a Personalized Hybrid CNN Model

We further developed a personalized hybrid CNN model. The cohort consisted of 282,478 ECG records, corresponding to 73,542 and 8,171 unique subjects with a single TTE report training and validation cohorts, respectively. The test cohort was comprised of 200,765 ECG records with 60,854 unique subjects. We utilized the foundational hybrid model and the results of the keras tuner for 50 trials are presented in Data S25. The personalized model was trained and evaluated individually for each subject in the test cohort. The overall MAE for the personalized hybrid CNN model was 6.75%, whereas the generalized hybrid CNN model yielded an MAE of 9.06% (the best model, from Data S25).
Figure 6 illustrates the relative error across all subjects in the test cohort, shown for each additional TTE report sample. One observes that the fitted line obtained from the 95% quantile of each box plot, shows a downward slope as the sample number increases, indicating the decreasing uncertainty with every additional new sample, consistent with the results of the personalized ECG-only model. However, the personalized hybrid CNN model did not demonstrate overall improvement in performance compared to the personalized ECG-only model.
Figure 7 presents a comparison of the absolute error between the generalized and personalized hybrid CNN models across different LVEF ranges. The personalized model consistently demonstrated statistically significant lower error (p < 0.0001) compared to the generalized model across all LVEF ranges.

### Assessment of Left Ventricular Dysfunction

An LVEF ≤ 40% is indicative of left ventricular systolic dysfunction25,19. To assess the models’ performance in identifying subjects with left ventricular systolic dysfunction, we used the same hyperparameters of the foundational ECG-only and hybrid CNN model architectures, modified the loss function to binary cross-entropy, changed the final layer to a sigmoid activation, and calculated confusion matrices using a predefined classification threshold of 0.05. The ECG- only classifier model achieved an AUC of 0.88 with a standard error of 0.0044, and an accuracy of 0.67. Similarly, the hybrid model achieved an AUC of 0.88 with a standard error of 0.0044, and an accuracy of 0.68, in predicting left ventricular dysfunction; this threshold was selected with the objective of minimizing false negative results by maximizing the product of sensitivity and negative predictive value. We also calculated the 95% confidence intervals for the AUC to be (0.871, 0.889) for both the ECG-only and hybrid classifier models. Table 1 presents the performance metrics of the foundational ECG-only and hybrid classification models.
Although the classifier was tuned for screening (sensitivity 0.92; NPV 0.98; Table 1), the PPV of 0.24 implies a substantial downstream burden of confirmatory testing. In the test cohort (TP=2,314; FN=189; FP=7,240; TN=13,182; N=22,925), the ECG-only classifier generated 9,554 positive screens (41.7%). Thus, in a clinical workflow in which a positive ECG screen prompts confirmatory TTE, 7,240/9,554 (75.8%) of confirmatory studies would be performed in patients without LVEF ≤40%, corresponding to ~3.1 additional confirmatory echocardiograms per true case identified (7,240 false positives per 2,314 true positives). Expressed per 1,000 screened at the observed prevalence (~10.9%), ~417 would be referred for echocardiography (≈101 true positives and ≈316 false positives). Because PPV is prevalence-dependent, targeting deployment to higher pre-test probability populations would be expected to improve PPV and reduce confirmatory-imaging burden.

## Discussion

Left ventricular ejection fraction is a fundamental clinical parameter used to guide diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis across a range of cardiovascular conditions. Traditionally, LVEF estimation relies on diagnostic imaging such as echocardiography and cMRI, but these methods are expensive, and not widely available. This study explores the use of inexpensive and readily available electrocardiographic data combined with deep learning techniques to estimate the LVEF. Our findings highlight several key insights, first, the early fusion configuration slightly outperformed the late fusion approach and was also more computationally efficient; second, incorporating structured features did not improve model performance, as the ECG-only and hybrid models demonstrated similar results; third, the model including both female and male data, outperformed the sex-specific models; fourth, Grad-CAM analysis revealed that the segments of the PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, and T-wave, from various leads, contributed significantly to the LVEF estimation; fifth, estimation of the prediction interval to quantify uncertainty of the LVEF estimate, indicates that most LVEF estimations are close to the ground-truth LVEF values, except at extreme LVEF values; sixth, the personalized model exhibited the lowest absolute error compared to the generalized model; seventh, the foundational model exhibited a good performance in an external validation cohort; eighth, the foundational ECG-only and hybrid classifier models exhibited very high sensitivity and negative predictive value in predicting left-ventricular systolic dysfunction.
Our study, utilizing a simple two-layer CNN architecture to estimate LVEF from ECG, achieved an MAE of 7.71% for the ECG-only model and 7.84% for the hybrid model, and exhibited similar performance as several state-of-the-art methods10,11,26. Other studies that have employed much more complex architectures, such as EfficientNet 10, achieved an overall MAE of 5.84% in internal validation (with LVEF ≤ 40% MAE of 6.69%, LVEF > 40% and ≤ 50% MAE of 8.08%, and LVEF > 50% MAE of 5.41%), and an external validation MAE of 6.14% using ECG input as an image; DenseNet-12111 achieved an MAE of 5.28% for balanced samples of LVEF > 50% and ≤ 50% in internal validation, with an MAE of 9.56% in external validation. Another study, using ECG12Net 26 obtained an MAE of 7.43%. Additionally, in this study, the foundational ECG-only and hybrid classifier models achieved an AUC of 0.88, comparable to prior work of achieving 0.94 10, 0.961 27 and 0.84 28.
To effectively screen for left ventricular systolic dysfunction, we chose metrics to optimize the model’s performance that minimize Type II (false negatives) errors 29, resulting in the classifier’s clinically significant, high sensitivity and negative predictive values. Unavoidably, the observed low positive predictive value may result in additional confirmatory TTE evaluations, and increased healthcare resource utilization.
With a simpler and more computationally-efficient architecture, our model performs comparably to more complex models, demonstrating the effectiveness of lightweight models for this regression task, and permitting deeper model introspection, transparency and explainability as shown in Figure S7. The addition of tabular features in our foundational hybrid model showed similar performance, consistent with findings from another study10. A likely explanation is that the raw ECG waveform already provides a high-dimensional representation of conduction timing and morphology (including information closely related to heart rate and interval-based features) and may implicitly encode demographic and clinical signatures, making many structured covariates redundant. Additionally, our hybrid model used a relatively simple early-fusion strategy (feature concatenation), which may not optimally capture cross-modal interactions.
Future work should evaluate more expressive multimodal fusion approaches (e.g., late-fusion, gated or attention-based fusion, multimodal transformers) and incorporate richer longitudinal EHR features to identify complementary information beyond the ECG.
While more complex architectures have shown minor improvements10-12,26,30, our results suggest that well-optimized simpler models can achieve comparable predictive power.
Furthermore, deploying and fine-tuning simpler models for real-world applications is more resource-efficient.
Prediction intervals are commonly used to quantify uncertainty associated with model estimations17, and are particularly valuable in clinical settings. By providing a probable range for LVEF, prediction intervals can enhance diagnostic confidence. Although the results for both the CNN and PNN architectures were similar, the primary advantage of the PNN model lies in its ability to provide prediction intervals that reflect the uncertainty of its estimates. The figures indicate that extreme LVEF values are often overestimated, and the model lacks confidence in these estimations, as reflected by the prediction intervals do not contain the actual LVEF values.
In contrast, the model demonstrates more reliable estimations for LVEF values within the range of 45-70%, where the intervals are narrower and the estimated LVEF values fall within the prediction intervals (as shown in Figures S4 and S6).
It is important to note that employing the SD to assess the uncertainty of point estimates13 limits the clinical interpretability, as it does not directly provide the probability that an individual outcome falls within a specific range. In contrast, our model outputs both a mean LVEF estimate and subject specific prediction intervals, which offer a probabilistic estimate of where the true LVEF is likely to fall. In practice, for example, a narrow prediction interval around an LVEF estimate may increase confidence in diagnosing heart failure with reduced LVEF, potentially prompting treatment initiation. Conversely, a wide interval especially near diagnostic thresholds (e.g., LVEF = 40%) may prompt additional testing, such as echocardiography, to reduce the risk of misclassification.
We have observed that the foundational ECG-only model identified lead aVR as one of the significant leads in the estimation of the LVEF. This finding aligns with existing literature, which highlights the significance of the aVR lead in identifying heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, defined as LVEF > 50% 31. Specifically, T-wave changes in lead aVR, which are strongly associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction 28, are consistently selected as significant features by GRAD-CAM.
The personalized model, estimated the LVEF with lower error compared to the generalized model, as shown in Figure 4, and with a progressively lower uncertainty and fewer outliers (as shown in Figure 4), with each additional ECG sample from the same subject, but its use presupposes longitudinal ECG availability and an updating workflow. In practice, personalization is most realistic in care settings where patients accumulate repeated ECGs as part of routine management (e.g., chronic heart failure/cardiomyopathy follow-up, recurrent emergency/inpatient encounters, or structured outpatient surveillance). By leveraging subject- specific data, the model adapted to individual ECG patterns through an iterative training process, where it continuously learned from each subject’s prior samples. This led to a consistent decrease of the relative error (Figures 4 and 6), demonstrating improved performance with more data per subject. Furthermore, the personalized model achieved significantly lower error across all LVEF ranges, confirming its robustness (Figures 5 and 7). These findings underscore the value of personalization in clinical tasks with high inter-subject variability at the small cost of model retraining as new data becomes available (approximately, per each new ECG, 2.99 sec in an Intel Core i9-9900 CPU @ 3.10 GHz and 1.30 sec in a NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU). For each new unseen sample, the model uses the most recent personalized weights to generate a prediction.
Personalized models are stored as lightweight parameter sets containing only the model weights, which are incrementally updated as new data becomes available. This approach minimizes both storage and computational demands. Personalization also introduces trade-offs, including added operational complexity (update scheduling, model governance/versioning, and quality control) and potential overfitting if updates are performed on sparse or noisy individual-level data; in our implementation, overfitting is mitigated through early stopping based on a relative error threshold of less than 1% and regularization. However, for patients with few or no prior ECGs, the generalized model remains the appropriate default and personalization is expected to confer limited incremental benefit. Future work should evaluate scalable approaches that reduce per- patient updating burden, such as parameter-efficient personalization (e.g., small patient-specific adapters/heads), meta-learning, or cohort-level adaptation, while quantifying how performance gains vary by the number and how recent are the available ECGs as well as by clinical subgroup, to better characterize who benefits most.
When traditional imaging modalities are unavailable or delayed, the model may provide an interim LVEF estimate to support triage decisions (e.g., prioritizing limited imaging capacity, escalation of monitoring, or earlier referral), while recognizing that this scenario demands careful attention to calibration and clinical thresholds and does not replace definitive imaging when it becomes available. Longitudinal monitoring represents a distinct application requiring prospective evaluation of within-patient stability and change-detection performance. It is conceivable, that given the high prognostic value of LVEF and the growing research and development in making ambulatory monitoring devices more “medical grade” 32-34, accurate, efficient, portable, convenient, interoperable35,36 and accessible37, LVEF could be measured in an out-of-office setting periodically, conveniently and comfortably, on an as needed basis, similarly with other vital sign signals38.
Although all the data were sourced from a single metropolitan area, the data were collected from many hospitals, attracting patients with very diverse demographics, which is representative to the demographics of the whole US. Another limitation is the reference- standard “noise” inherent to TTE-derived LVEF, which is known to exhibit substantial intra- and inter-observer variability 4. In this study, LVEF labels were obtained from routine TTE reports using a rule-based NLP extraction approach, which may reflect heterogeneous clinical readers and measurement practices across sites and over time. This variability likely imposes an effective lower bound on achievable regression error, such that the ECG-only MAE of 7.71% and personalized MAE of 5.98% should be interpreted in the context of measurement uncertainty in the ground truth. Future work should evaluate higher-fidelity supervision (e.g., standardized quantitative reads or core-lab adjudication) and methods that explicitly incorporate label uncertainty (e.g., repeated-measure modeling or noisy-label learning) to further improve calibration and reduce residual error.
In conclusion, our study demonstrates the ability to accurately estimate the LVEF using CNN and PNN models, leveraging the ECG and structured features, with TTE imaging as the ground truth. It also explores the uncertainty in LVEF estimations across the whole LVEF range.
The proposed personalized model and the PNN model for uncertainty estimation offer significant potential for improving diagnostic accuracy and optimizing clinical decision-making, at a lower cost, and in under-resourced communities. We envision that the proposed model could serve as an effective tool for determining LVEF and left-ventricular dysfunction, offering a cost-effective method for improving care and prevention strategies, in remote and under-resourced communities.

##### [AI based ECG data recovery and cardiovascular diseases classification (CEDRC-network)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3)

```
## Abstract

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are a significant and widespread cause of death in the world, continuing to increase mortality rates. Therefore, timely identification and diagnosis are essential for a patient’s optimized recovery and longevity. In this regard, ECG is an effective tool for detecting anomalous heart conditions. However, interfering factors like noise, transient changes, and missing data could affect the accurate diagnosis of CVDs. The Cardiovascular ECG Data Recovery and Classification Network (CEDRC-Net) sorts and collates noisy data while also recovering missing data caused by equipment malfunction or human error, using a multistage machine-learning and deep-learning model. Moreover, CEDRC-Net is incorporated into the Transformer-based Convolutional Denoising Autoencoder (TCDAE) model to methodically mitigate noise, subsequently the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) or Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) are systematically employed as an alternative to accurately reconstruct and forecast ECG signals. Following this, the system classified heart diseases, including atrial fibrillation, sinus bradycardia, and tachycardia, using several machine-learning algorithms, based on data from a dataset comprising 2426 patients.TFT showcased better performance than VAE in ECG signal reconstruction, achieving up to 98% accuracy with Gradient Boosting, compared to 96% by VAE. Furthermore, in downstream classification, signals enhanced by TFT led to superior model results, with SVM and XGBoost both reaching 98.4% accuracy and F1-scores. The TFT achieved substantially lower reconstruction errors (MAE = 0.015, MSE = 0.00045, RMSE = 0.0132) compared to the VAE (MAE = 0.075, MSE = 0.011, RMSE = 0.107). These results highlight TFT’s strong denoising capability for improving ECG diagnostic accuracy, while the suggested system ensures reliable measurements under noisy and non-ideal conditions. It is highly conducive for early and accurate diagnosis, better clinical decisions, and decreased patient load on the cardiologists. The research is performed on the MIMIC-IV-ECG 12-lead real-time dataset.

## Introduction

Electrocardiography (ECG) is a fundamental diagnostic approach in the identification and diagnosis of heart diseases. The 12-lead ECG is also called a gold standard diagnostic method that captures the electrical activity of the heart[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR1 "Yoo, H. et al. Restoration of missing or low-quality 12-lead ECG signals using ensemble deep-learning model with optimal combination. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 83, 104690 (2023)."). Moreover, the twelve electrodes provide a complete evaluation of the heart function and detect anomalies. It measures the heart’s electrical activity by positioning electrodes based on a set of predetermined guidelines[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR2 "McStay, S. Recording a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). Br. J. Nurs. (Lond. Engl.) 28, 756–760 (2019)."),[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR3 "Dohare, A. K., Kumar, V. & Kumar, R. Detection of myocardial infarction in 12 lead ECG using support vector machine. Appl. Soft Comput 64, 138–147 (2018)."). These signals are classified into bipolar leads (I, II, III), augmented unipolar leads (aVR, aVL, aVF), and precordial leads (V1 to V6), based on the voltage difference between electrodes. At the same time, bipolar leads and augmented unipolar leads record the cardiac activity on the frontal plane, while precordial leads record the cardiac activity in the horizontal plane through six electrodes around the heart[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR4 "Mc Loughlin, M. J., \"New electrocardiographic methods based on the standard 12-leads Ecg: Bipolar Precordial Leads,\" Available at SSRN 4250757, 2022."). In this regard, Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig1) shows a standard electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform P wave, QRS complex, T wave, PR interval, ST segment, and QT interval illustrating different phases of cardiac electrical activity[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR5 "Apostol, A. and Nutu, M. \"Arrhythmia classification from 12-lead ECG signals using convolutional and transformer-based deep learning models,\" arXiv preprint 
arXiv:2502.17887
, 2025.").

The ECG is always used in diagnosis, prognosis and prevention of cardiovascular disease, nonetheless, obstacles persist, including a growing unmet need for proficient cardiologists who can reliably read ECGs, technical anomalies, such as poor contacts between electrodes due to patient movement, obesity, muscular contraction artefacts and equipment malfunctions, such distortions can lead to misdiagnosis or a delay in treatment. To overcome this issue researchers are applying multiple ECG reconstruction and denoising techniques for accurate diagnosis[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR6 "Khalili, M., GholamHosseini, H., Lowe, A. & Kuo, M. M. Motion artifacts in capacitive ECG monitoring systems: A review of existing models and reduction techniques. Med. Biol. Eng. Comput 62, 3599–3622 (2024)."),[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR7 "Singh, A. K. & Krishnan, S. ECG signal feature extraction trends in methods and applications. Biomed. Eng. Online 22, 22 (2023)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR8 "Peng, H., Chang, X., Yao, Z., Shi, D. & Chen, Y. A deep learning framework for ECG denoising and classification. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 94, 106441 (2024).").

Traditional ECG reconstruction and denoising algorithms, which are based on signal-processing principles, such as linear filtering, adaptive filtering and transform-based approaches, play a vital role in maintaining optimal signal integrity. The purpose of these methods is to remove noise in ECG signals, and enhance the quality of the data during analysis[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR9 "Hamici, H., Kanan, A. & Al-hammuri, K. Optimized fir filter using genetic algorithms: A case study of ecg signals filter optimization. Advancements and applications of adaptive filters in signal processing. J. Européen des Systèmes Automatisés

Technol 38, 1–28 (2022)."),[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR13 "Malik, S. A., Parah, S. A., Aljuaid, H. & Malik, B. A. An iterative filtering based ECG denoising using lifting wavelet transform technique. Electronics (Basel) 12, 387 (2023)."),[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR14 "Hussein, A. F., Mohammed, W. R., Jaber, M. M. & Khalaf, O. I. Even though the desired performance is not always attained by conventional signal processing methods, especially where non-stationary, complex noises or low-amplitude signals are involved[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR15 "Chatterjee, S., Thakur, R. S., Yadav, R. N., Gupta, L. & Raghuvanshi, D. K. Review of noise removal techniques in ECG signals. IET Signal Process 14, 569–590 (2020)."). The trend among researchers is changing to overcome the weaknesses of the conventional methods. The AI models are trained with large data sets to detect complex and subtle patterns and thus, offer more adaptive, flexible and specific solutions to denoising, reconstruction, and classification[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR16 "Martínez-Suárez, F., Alvarado-Serrano, C. & Casas, O. Robust algorithm for the detection and classification of QRS complexes with different morphologies using the continuous spline wavelet transform with automatic scale detection. Biomed. Phys. Eng. Express 10, 025008 (2024).").

To address these limitations, the recent studies have shifted to the focus on data-driven and AI-based approaches. Specifically DL models have produced substantial improvements in Signal-To-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and retained the key clinical characteristics of P-waves, QRS complexes and T-waves hence making them clinically relevant and of great benefit[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR17 "Wang, H. et al. Fully-gated denoising auto-encoder for artifact reduction in ECG signals. Sensors 25, 801 (2025) ((Basel, Switzerland))."),[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR20 "Guo, Y., Tang, Q., Li, S. & Chen, Z. Deep learning-based models such as GANs, and hybrid network techniques offer end-to-end learning and are considered for robust on several ECG benchmarks[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR22 "Nademi, Y., Kalmady, S. In particular, CNNs, especially U-Net models, have been trained to complete missing segments of ECGs by taking advantage of the patterns obtained by analyzing known signal records and features of the waveforms[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR23 "Beco, S. C., Pinto, J. R. & Cardoso, J. S. Electrocardiogram lead conversion from single-lead blindly-segmented signals. BMC Med. Inform. Decis. Mak. 22, 314 (2022)."). Similarly GANs learn the distribution of natural ECG patterns, which allows them to be used to produce realistic replacements of absent data[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR24 "Joo, J., Joo, G., Kim, Y., Jin, M. N., Park, J., & Im, H., \"Twelve-lead ECG reconstruction from single-lead signals using generative adversarial networks,\" in International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention, 2023, pp. 184–194."). Likewise, VAEs have shown promise in reconstructing missing signals by modeling latent distributions[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR25 "Nishikimi, R., Nakano, M., Kashino, K. & Tsukada, S. Variational autoencoder–based neural electrocardiogram synthesis trained by FEM-based heart simulator. Cardiovasc. Digit. Health J. 5, 19–28 (2024).").VAEs provide a probabilistic generative model to impute missing ECG data[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR26 "Roskams-Hieter, B., Wells, J., & Wade, S., \"Leveraging variational autoencoders for multiple data imputation,\" in Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases, 2023, pp. 491–506."). Meanwhile, Transformer-based models utilize self-attention mechanisms to learn long-range dependencies in ECG signals[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR27 "Xu, M. et al. Pulseimpute: A novel benchmark task for pulsative physiological signal imputation. Adv. Neural. Inf. Process. Syst. 35, 26874–26888 (2022)."). Recent advancements, such as MuRe-LAT integrates convolutional feature extraction, lead-attention, and dual-scale transformer encoders to capture both local ECG morphology and long-term temporal dependencies for arrhythmia classification[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR28 "Niloy, M. et al. Lead-aware multi-resolution transformer with domain adaptation for beat-level ECG arrhythmia classification. IEEE Open J. Comput. Soc. 6, 1946–1957 (2025)."). Likewise, HCTG-Net hybrid CNN transformer combines waveform morphology and temporal dynamics by combining residual convolutional feature maps with transformer-based gated fusion modules[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR29 "Xiong, N., Wei, Z., Wang, X., Wang, Y. & Wang, Z. HCTG-Net: A hybrid CNN–transformer network with gated fusion for automatic ECG arrhythmia diagnosis. Bioengineering (Basel) 12, 1268 (2025)."). Other transformer-based ECG pipelines make use of attention-focused feature learning and optimized preprocessing pipelines to allow effective multi-class arrhythmia detection, and automated cardiac diagnostics[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR30 "Ikram, S. et al. Transformer-based ECG classification for early detection of cardiac arrhythmias. Front. Med. 12, 1600855 (2025)."). Alongside, TFTs use gating mechanisms and multi-horizon attention to generate accurate forecasting of the missing data segments[31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR31 "Lim, B., Arık, S. Ö., Loeff, N. & Pfister, T. Temporal fusion transformers for interpretable multi-horizon time series forecasting. Int. J. Forecast. 37, 1748–1764 (2021).").

The reviewed studies mainly focus on the developments in automated ECG-based detection and classification of cardiovascular diseases, including arrhythmia, heart failure and atrial fibrillation, by the use of the state-of-the-art deep learning architectures. Despite these advancements, there are still serious limitations, such as low interpretability, imbalanced classes, and low cross-dataset generalizability. Past literature also shows poor multimodal contextual information integration[32](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR32 "Atwa, A. E. M. et al. Interpretable deep learning models for arrhythmia classification based on ECG signals using PTB-XL dataset. Diagnostics 15, 1950 (2025).").Similarly excessive use of complicated preprocessing and poor long-range temporal modeling[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR33 "Qiu, C., Li, H., Qi, C., & Li, B., \"Enhancing ECG classification with continuous wavelet transform and multi-branch transformer,\" Heliyon, vol. 10, 2024."), poor inter-lead structural-dependency[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR34 "Andayeshgar, B., Abdali-Mohammadi, F., Sepahvand, M., Almasi, A. & Salari, N. Arrhythmia detection by the graph convolution network and a proposed structure for communication between cardiac leads. BMC Med. Res. Methodol. 24, 96 (2024)."), and significant computational cost that makes it difficult to use in practice[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR35 "Kraft, D. & Rumm, P. Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter detection using deep learning. Sensors 25, 4109 (2025).").

The proposed CEDRC-Net is a multi-stage framework designed for ECG denoising, missing data reconstruction, and cardiac disease classification, trained on the MIMIC-IV-ECG dataset comprising over 800,000 ECG recordings[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#ref-CR36 "Gow, B., Pollard, T., Nathanson, L. A., Johnson, A., Moody, B., Fernandes, C., et al., \"MIMIC-IV-ECG: diagnostic electrocardiogram matched subset,\" Type: dataset, vol. 6, pp. 13–14, 2023."). The model analyzes a variety of missing-data conditions and compares reconstructed signals to the original ones to assess predictive performance. Another goal is to increase diagnostic accuracy, decrease workload in clinicians and provide early intervention in cardiovascular disease (CVD).

## Results

Cardiovascular ECG Data Recovery and Classification Network (CEDRC-Net) is a multi-stage model dedicated to reconstructing and classifying the ECG signal efficiently. It performs better in restoring lost ECG signals through advanced architectures in improving the accuracy of CVDs diagnosis.

### Variational autoencoder

The performance of a VAE in reconstructing ECG signals with missing data is shown in Fig. [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig8). Each subplot compares the original ECG with the imputed ECG. The reconstruction quality drops slightly as the missing ratio increases; however, the model still captures waveform patterns, even with 50% data loss. The findings indicate that VAE is strong in imputing ECGs.

### Temporal fusion transformer

In the same manner, Fig. [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig9) also shows the results of the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) to reconstruct electrocardiogram (ECG) signals with missing data. Each plot compares the predicted ECG to the actual signal over time. At 10% of the missing data, the prediction closely matches the actual signal. As missing data increases to 30% and 50%, the prediction deviates slightly, with more amplitude discrepancies. Despite this, the TFT retains the underlying waveform structure, demonstrating its robustness in handling incomplete ECG data and generating reliable reconstructions.

### Evaluation metrics of VAE and TFT

The performance of the VAE and TFT models is evaluated using the Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root mean square Error (RMSE) and Loss.

All ECG signals are normalized to the [0, 1] range prior to training and evaluation to ensure consistent scale across samples. As shown in Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Tab3), the TFT achieved substantially lower reconstruction errors (MAE = 0.015, MSE = 0.00045, RMSE = 0.0132) compared to the VAE (MAE = 0.075, MSE = 0.011, RMSE = 0.107). Furthermore, the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) of 0.0167 indicates that the reconstruction error corresponds to approximately **1**.67% of the normalized ECG signal amplitude**,** demonstrating high reconstruction fidelity and improved clinical interpretability. This swift convergence indicates that the model effectively captures underlying data patterns early in the training process and achieves stable optimization during training.

### Model evaluation for classification

This study investigates the performance of two prominent deep-learning models, VAE and the TFT in the reconstruction of ECG signals and how they affect downstream classification tasks that are executed by standard machine-learning methods. The study has been performed under two different experimental conditions, (1) ECG measurements that do not contain missing values and (2) ECG measurements that have been rebuilt, with proportions of missing-segments of 10%, 30% and 50%.

#### Performance with clean ECG signals

ECG signals reconstructed using the TFT model consistently achieved higher classification performance than those reconstructed with the VAE as shown in Table [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Tab4). Even Precision and recall values remained tightly aligned across most classifiers, these results are highlighting the TFT’s superior feature reconstruction capability.

The bar chart, presented in Figs. [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig10) and [11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig11), shows the classification accuracy of various machine learning models trained on VAE- and TFT-based feature extraction of cleaned ECG signals. Each bar represents a specific ECG disease class across models such as Random Forest, SVM, and XGBoost. Notably, “Possible Ectopic” and “Sinus Rhythm” consistently show high classification accuracy. The heat map in Figs. [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig10) and [11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig11) provides a clear visual comparison of model performance across ECG conditions. The color intensity reflects the classification accuracy.

#### Performance with missing data and reconstructed signals

The models are tested under the second scenario where ECG segments are missed by10%, 30% and 50% of the data. The reconstruction was done through VAE and TFT. TFT again performed better than VAE in all the classifiers and in all levels of derivation of the signal degradation, TFT is capable of restoring more semantically significant temporal pattern.

From a metrics perspective, higher recall values under TFT reconstructions indicate that more true-positive cases (e.g., cardiac events) were correctly identified, a clinically desirable outcome. For example, Random Forest with TFT maintained 0.97 accuracy even at 10% data loss, indicating a high true-positive rate and a low false-negative rate. In contrast, VAE-based reconstructions showed a marginal decline in performance as missing data increased, indicating poorer generalization under incomplete signal conditions.

The analysis strongly supports the conclusion that TFT-based reconstruction is superior to VAE in both complete and incomplete ECG scenarios. TFT’s attention-based mechanism enables it to model long-range dependencies and temporal trends in ECG signals, which are critical for accurate signal recovery and subsequent classification. The improved performance across classifiers and evaluation metrics, especially precision and recall, confirms TFT’s potential as a robust preprocessing model for clinical ECG analysis pipelines. These findings contribute to the growing body of evidence favoring transformer-based architectures in biomedical signal processing tasks.

Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Tab5) is reporting the exact Accuracy ± Standard Deviation (SD) for all evaluated models. Evaluations is conducted using a strict patients wise hold-out test split (N = 485) to prevent data leakage. Bootstrapped resampling (1000 iterations) method is applied on these predictions to rigorously quantify variance.

VAE Model ECG Classification Accuracy with missing data (10%, 30% and 50%) by Class with Heat map Visualization is shown in Fig. [12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig12).

TFT Model ECG Classification Accuracy with missing data (10%, 30% and 50%) by Class with Heat map Visualization is shown in Fig. [13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Fig13).

### Statistical testing

Predictive performance was evaluated using a paired statistical comparison between VAE- and TFT-based models on identical test instances. McNemar’s test is employed to compare patient-wise classification correctness (correct vs. incorrect predictions) between paired classifiers, which is appropriate for evaluating differences in predictive accuracy on the same samples. The results Table [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-46232-3#Tab6) demonstrate statistically significant differences at α = 0.05 under 50% missing data across the evaluated classifiers, indicating that TFT-based reconstructions yield superior downstream predictive performance compared with VAE-based reconstructions. These findings confirm that the performance advantages of TFT become particularly pronounced under severe data degradation.

## Discussion

The cumulative findings of the examined literature indicate the growing importance of automated electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis in the accurate detection of cardiovascular abnormalities with a specific focus on arrhythmias. The Deep-learning models, such as Transformer models, Convolutional Neural Network-Transformer models, and self-attention autoencoders, have produced significant improvements in ECG classification and diagnostic performance. The modular ECG analysis framework that is presented in the current paper has several methodological strengths that are consistent with the modern trends in the field of artificial intelligence implementation in the processing of cardiac signals. Its staged structure, including denoising, reconstruction and classification, facilitates interpretability, systematic assessment, and reproducibility without depending on a single, monolithic end-to-end deep-learning structure. The application of ECG reconstruction as a medically relevant aspect instead of a technical addition is supported by clinical evidence in the support of ECG reconstruction. Additionally, the combination of Transformer-based temporal fusion enables the strict modelling of temporal relationships and missing data, and the use of autoencoder-based denoising makes it possible to implement in a computationally limited setting.

However, a number of constraints still exist. Reconstruction effectiveness depends on the composition of leads, sampling properties and the particular clinical environment, thus restricting its applicability outside the datasets studied. Deep-learning models also have interpretability limitations and cause minimal morphological distortions that may interfere with clinical reliability. The ECG signals are prone to inter-patient variability, different recording conditions and electrode locations; furthermore, noise artefacts and baseline drift also contributes to poor signal integrity. Inequality in datasets, evaluation procedures, and class imbalances also hinder cross-study comparison. Therefore, more recent research is looking into hybrid architectures, domain adaptation methods and advanced feature-extraction algorithms including wavelet transformations and multi-branch Transformer networks to enhance model robustness and maintain clinically significant ECG features.

## Conclusion

The major purpose of this study is to present a powerful multistage deep-learning and machine-learning model called CEDRC-Net that can not only restore ECG signals, but also classify heart diseases. The pipeline starts with a TCDAE to do first denoising, then there is a reconstruction block, either in the form of a VAE or a TFT. This sequential architecture deals with the issues of noise, missing data and diagnostic heterogeneity of real-world ECG recordings. The obtained results show that the TFT performs better than the VAE in both reconstruction accuracy, especially when the signal is highly degraded. These findings demonstrate the importance of attention-based processes including the TFT to capture complex temporal dynamics that are critical to accurate cardiovascular diagnostics.

CEDRC-Net is a new approach of automated ECG analysis that may help alleviate the load on clinical staff, improving the quality of the diagnosis. Its ability to recreate and analyze intricate ECG waves offers clinicians an effective tool for early and rightful identification of cardiac disease. This framework is scalable with high performance measures making it a desirable resource in the development of cardiovascular care and biomedical signal processing. To further extend the work and improve diagnostic accuracy and contextual awareness, the model will be integrated with multimodal signals. These enhancements should be validated through prospective clinical trials across diverse populations to ensure generalizability and clinical relevance.
