##### [Comparative evaluation of deep learning models for cardiovascular disease diagnosis and classification](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3)

```
## Abstract

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide, highlighting the need for accurate and computationally efficient diagnostic tools. Electrocardiography (ECG) is widely used for the diagnosis of CVD and is a noninvasive, cost-effective method. However, manual interpretation requires substantial time and can lead to human error. In this study, we propose and systematically compare low-complexity Artificial Intelligence (AI)–driven Deep Learning (DL) models for multi-class ECG-based CVD diagnosis and classification. Using the publicly available PTB Diagnostic ECG (PTB-ECG) dataset, which comprises multiple CVD categories, we evaluate CNN, LSTM, MLP, CNN-MLP, and ConvLSTM architectures, focusing on balancing diagnostic performance and computational complexity. Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)–based feature extraction and data-level imbalance handling are employed to enhance efficiency and robustness. Experimental results show that the LSTM model achieves the best overall performance, with an accuracy of 99.98%, an F1 score of 98%, and a precision of 100%, while maintaining low computational complexity, measured in Real Multiplications Per Symbol (RMpS). These findings demonstrate that high diagnostic accuracy can be achieved without high computational complexity, supporting the feasibility of real-time and resource-constrained clinical deployment.

## Introduction

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) arise from a complex interplay of medical conditions, including abnormal heart rhythms, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, and other metabolic disorders, as well as lifestyle-related risk factors such as smoking, unhealthy diet, and chronic stress[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR1 "Ahsan, M. M. & Siddique, Z. Machine learning-based heart disease diagnosis: A systematic literature review. Artif. Intell. Med. 128, 102289 (2022)."). Despite continuous progress in medical science, heart attacks, or myocardial infarctions, remain the primary cause of heart-related fatalities. CVDs are estimated to be responsible for around 17.9 million deaths annually worldwide, accounting for roughly 32% of all mortalities[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR2 "Alkayyali, Z. K., Idris, S. A. B. & Abu-Naser, S. S. A systematic literature review of deep and machine learning algorithms in cardiovascular diseases diagnosis. J. Theoretical Appl. Inform. Technol. 101 (4), 1353–1365 (2023)."). Of these, approximately 85% result from heart attacks. Early identification of CVDs could preserve countless lives, thereby underscoring the urgent need for prompt and accurate diagnosis. Ultimately, improving early AI-detection strategies holds the potential to reduce the global burden of CVDs[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR3 "Shafik, W. et al. A systematic literature review on transparency and interpretability of AI models in healthcare: taxonomies, tools, techniques, datasets, open research challenges, and future trends. Health Technol. 1–22. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s12553-025-01051-w
(2026)."). Traditionally, the diagnosis and assessment of CVD rely on clinical examinations supported by diagnostic tools such as electrocardiography (ECG), cardiac imaging modalities including Computed Tomography (CT) and Cardiac Magnetic Resonance imaging (CMR), Cardiac MRI, and laboratory tests[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR4 "Chizner, M. A. The diagnosis of heart disease by clinical assessment alone. Dis. Mon. 48 (1), 7–98 (2002)."), [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR5 "Swathy, M. & Saruladha, K. A comparative study of classification and prediction of Cardio-Vascular Diseases (CVD) using Machine Learning and Deep Learning techniques. ICT express. 8 (1), 109–116 (2022)."). Among these modalities, ECG is particularly prominent due to its noninvasive nature, low cost, wide availability, and ability to provide real-time insights into cardiac electrical activity. However, despite its clinical value, manual ECG interpretation is time-consuming, highly dependent on clinician expertise, and susceptible to inter-observer variability, especially in high-volume clinical environments and long-term monitoring scenarios, which increases the risk of error[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR6 "Lopes, R. R. et al. Improving electrocardiogram-based detection of rare genetic heart disease using transfer learning: An application to phospholamban p. Arg14del mutation carriers. Comput. Biol. Med. 131, 104262 (2021)."), [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR7 "Rath, A., Mishra, D., Panda, G. & Satapathy, S. C. Heart disease detection using deep learning methods from imbalanced ECG samples. Biomed. Signal Process. Control. 68, 102820 (2021)."). These limitations highlight the need for more efficient and reliable diagnostic support systems.

In parallel, the growing adoption of real-time health monitoring technologies has enabled continuous tracking of physiological signals, allowing clinicians to identify subtle abnormalities, such as arrhythmias or early hemodynamic changes, before they progress to critical events[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR8 "Baghdadi, N. A. et al. Advanced machine learning techniques for cardiovascular disease early detection and diagnosis. J. Big Data. 10 (1), 144 (2023)."), [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR9 "Iqbal, J. M. A novel deep learning approach for early detection of cardiovascular diseases from ECG signals. Med. Eng. Phys. 125, 104111 (2024)."), [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR10 "Mohanbabu, C. & Ambika, B. Real-time machine learning for big data approach to early identification of heart disease. Int. J. Adv. Res. Comput. Communication Eng. 12 (5), 667–669 (2023)."). Continuous data streams not only facilitate timely medical intervention but also promote patient engagement and collaborative care between patients and healthcare providers[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR11 "Baikuvekov, M., Tursynova, A. & Yespayev, G. A Deep Learning for Cardiovascular Diseases Detection on Wearable Devices Data. In 2024 IEEE 4th International Conference on Smart Information Systems and Technologies (SIST) (pp. 272–277). (IEEE, 2024)"), [12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR12 "Moshawrab, M., Adda, M., Bouzouane, A., Ibrahim, H. & Raad, A. Smart wearables for the detection of cardiovascular diseases: a systematic literature review. Sensors 23 (2), 828 (2023)."). However, the increasing volume and complexity of such data exceed the practical limits of manual analysis, further motivating the adoption of automated and intelligent diagnostic approaches. Recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) methods, has become a valuable complement to the diagnosis and classification of CVDs. By learning complex, non-linear patterns from large-scale ECG datasets, AI-driven models can uncover diagnostically relevant features that may not be readily discernible through traditional analysis[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR7 "Rath, A., Mishra, D., Panda, G. & Satapathy, S. C. Heart disease detection using deep learning methods from imbalanced ECG samples. Biomed. Signal Process. Control. 68, 102820 (2021)."), [13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR13 "Acharya, U. R. et al. Automated detection of coronary artery disease using different durations of ECG segments with convolutional neural network. Knowl. Based Syst. 132, 62–71 (2017)."), [14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR14 "Karthik, S., Santhosh, M., Kavitha, M. S. & Paul, A. C. Automated Deep Learning Based Cardiovascular Disease Diagnosis Using ECG Signals. Computer Syst. Sci. & Engineering, 42(1). 183-199 (2022)."). In recent years, many studies have used AI and DL frameworks that demonstrate impressive diagnostic accuracy. However, these often require substantial computational resources, limiting their use in real-time, embedded, and resource-limited clinical environments[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR15 "Saleh, R. A., Ghaleb, M., Shafik, W. & Ertunc, H. M. Efficient white blood cell identification with hybrid inception-xception network. J. Supercomputing. 80 (17), 25155–25187. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11227-024-06405-1
(2024)."). In practice, improvements in model accuracy often come at the cost of higher computational complexity, yet many studies overlook this critical trade-off.

To address this challenge, the present study focuses on the development and comparative evaluation of low-complexity AI-driven DL architectures for multi-class ECG-based CVD diagnosis and classification. Specifically, we investigate Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long-Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), and their combination (i.e., ConvLSTM and CNN-MLP) models, to diagnose and classify CVDs using the PTB Diagnostic ECG (PTB-ECG) dataset. The proposed framework aims to achieve high diagnostic accuracy while explicitly minimizing computational complexity, thereby enhancing feasibility for real-time and resource-limited clinical deployment.

### Highlights

- The study presents the design and evaluation of low-complexity AI-driven DL models tailored for efficient and accurate CVD detection and classification using ECG signals.
    
- A comprehensive performance comparison was conducted across CNN, MLP, LSTM, CNN-MLP, and ConvLSTM models using the PTB-ECG dataset, emphasizing both diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency.
    
- The research demonstrates the suitability of the PTB-ECG dataset for AI-driven DL models, reinforcing its potential for reliable and efficient CVD diagnosis.
    

The remainder of this research is structured as follows: Sect.  2 details the related literature. Section  3 presents materials and methodology, entailing the dataset’s characteristics and the deep learning architectures employed. Section  4 details the simulation results, including an accuracy-versus-complexity analysis and confusion matrix. Section  5 details the discussions. Section  6 provides the concluding remarks.

## Result

A comparative analysis of several DL algorithms for diagnosing and classifying CVDs was conducted. The study aims to develop DL models that achieve a balance between accuracy and computational complexity. We employed AI-driven DL techniques, specifically CNN, LSTM, MLP, and hybrid CNN-MLP and ConvLSTM models. We utilized Python (3.12.3) along with TensorFlow (2.17.0) and Keras (3.3.3) libraries to develop the proposed models. This study employed the PTB-ECG dataset[33](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR33 "Goldberger, A. L. et al. PhysioBank, PhysioToolkit, and PhysioNet: components of a new research resource for complex physiologic signals. Circulation 101 (23), e215–e220 (2000)."), a widely used dataset for CVD studies. We measured accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score metrics to assess the models’ performance. While also evaluating the computational complexity through Real Multiplications per Symbol (RMpS)[35](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR35 "Freire, P. J. et al. Performance versus complexity study of neural network equalizers in coherent optical systems. J. Lightwave Technol. 39 (19), 6085–6096 (2021).").

The preprocessing phase and certain modifications of the ECG signal are necessary. To improve data quality, several established techniques were applied, including handling missing values, applying a high-pass filter with a 0.5 Hz cutoff to eliminate low-frequency noise, and downsampling the ECG signals to 250 Hz. Then, feature extraction was performed using the DWT, specifically the db3 wavelet[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR15 "Saleh, R. A., Ghaleb, M., Shafik, W. & Ertunc, H. M. Efficient white blood cell identification with hybrid inception-xception network. J. Supercomputing. 80 (17), 25155–25187. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11227-024-06405-1
(2024)."), followed by min–max normalization to standardize the extracted features. Importantly, the extracted DWT features were integrated with the raw ECG signal representations, rather than being used independently. To address class imbalance, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied exclusively to the training set after the train–test split, thereby preventing data leakage and ensuring an unbiased evaluation of model performance.

This study performs multi-class classification across eight cardiovascular disease categories, as described in this paper. We also utilized the confusion matrix to demonstrate the model’s classification performance. After preprocessing, we randomly split the dataset into 80% for training and 20% for testing. To ensure data independence, all ECG records from each subject were assigned to either the training or the testing set, but not both. The input to all models consisted of ECG signals rather than images. To account for variability and ensure statistical robustness, we repeated this 80/20 split five times using different random seeds and report the mean and standard deviation of all performance metrics. We trained our models for 50 epochs, using early stopping to prevent overfitting and underfitting. Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#Tab1) demonstrates the various training parameters, including batch size, learning rate, and number of epochs.

### Accuracy-versus-complexity analysis

Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#Tab2) presents a comparative evaluation of the proposed DL models, with a primary emphasis on reducing computational complexity while preserving diagnostic performance. Unlike many existing studies that prioritize accuracy alone, the central objective of this work is to achieve reliable CVD diagnosis while explicitly minimizing computational complexity, a critical requirement for real-time and resource-constrained clinical systems. Accordingly, model performance is analyzed across a complexity range of approximately [, ] RMpS. To enable this reduction, DWT–based feature extraction using the db3 wavelet was applied in combination with signal preprocessing and dimensionality reduction. This strategy resulted in a three-order-of-magnitude decrease in computational complexity, from approximately to RMpS, without compromising classification effectiveness. This finding directly demonstrates that high-dimensional ECG representations are not required to achieve strong diagnostic performance.

Among the evaluated architectures, the LSTM model provides the most favorable balance between accuracy and computational complexity, achieving a computational complexity of approximately RMpS while maintaining an accuracy of 99.98%, an F1 score of 98%, and a precision of 100%. Importantly, these results indicate that near-optimal classification performance can be achieved at the lowest complexity level investigated, highlighting the efficiency of temporal modeling when combined with compact feature representations. While the CNN, MLP, CNN-MLP, and ConvLSTM models also demonstrate competitive accuracy, their performance gains are accompanied by higher computational demands, yielding F1 scores of 91%, 93%, 94%, and 96%, respectively. These results further reinforce that increasing architectural complexity does not necessarily translate into proportional performance improvements. Overall, the findings confirm that the proposed framework enables low-complexity multi-class ECG-based CVD diagnosis and classification, with the LSTM model emerging as the most suitable candidate for deployment in real-time, embedded, and wearable healthcare applications.

### Confusion matrix

Figure [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#Fig8) demonstrates the confusion matrix commonly utilized in our analysis. Here, samples are classified into three main categories: MI (A), Heart Failure (B), and Healthy (C). The terms “True Positive (TP)”, “False Positive (FP)”, “True Negative (TN)”, and “False Negative (FN)” pertain to the classification test’s accuracy. The confusion matrix allows for the calculation of precision and recall metrics. Precision measures the ratio of TP predictions among all positive predictions made by the model and is calculated as the ratio of TP to the total of TP and FP (). Recall denotes the proportion of true positive predictions compared to all actual positive cases, calculated as the ratio of TP to the total of TP and FN (). Accuracy, the simplest performance metric, indicates the proportion of observations that are correctly classified out of the total observations. It is best suited for scenarios where class distribution is balanced, and the consequences of false positives and false negatives are comparable. However, it may not be an effective measure in unbalanced datasets where positive and negative classes vary significantly in their instances. Therefore, alternative metrics are needed for performance assessment. An optimal classifier aspires to achieve equality between precision and recall, which suggests the absence of false positives and false negatives. Therefore, a metric that combines both precision and recall is essential. The F1 score incorporates these dimensions, defined as the harmonic mean of precision and recall . This measure provides a balanced evaluation of precision and recall, making it a more thorough metric for assessing classification models. Figure [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#Fig9) presents four confusion matrix created by (a) CNN, (b) LSTM, (c) MLP, (d) CNN-MLP, and (e) ConvLSTM models.

## Discussion

In this study, we developed and implemented advanced AI-driven DL models to classify CVDs into distinct conditions, each representing unique pathological effects on cardiac function. Through a comprehensive analysis, our approach demonstrated strong diagnostic capabilities, aligning with previous research that highlights the effectiveness of DL techniques in medical imaging and CVD diagnosis. These findings not only confirm the robustness of our models but also highlight the increasing role of AI-based systems in improving clinical decision-making and enhancing early detection and treatment strategies for cardiovascular disorders. The findings of our research support previous studies that demonstrate the value of ML and DL models in diagnosing CVD. Notably, in a reference study[36](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR36 "Hasan, N. I. & Bhattacharjee, A. Deep learning approach to cardiovascular disease classification employing modified ECG signal from empirical mode decomposition. Biomed. Signal Process. Control. 52, 128–140 (2019).")[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR37 "Hasan, N. I. & Bhattacharjee, A. Deep learning approach to cardiovascular disease classification employing modified ECG signal from empirical mode decomposition. Biomed. Signal Process. Control. 52, 128–140 (2019)."), the CNN model achieved an accuracy of 97.70% and an F1 score of 97%. A prior study reference[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-43543-3#ref-CR18 "Rath, A., Mishra, D., Panda, G., Satapathy, S. C. & Xia, K. Improved heart disease detection from ECG signal using deep learning based ensemble model. Sustainable Computing: Inf. Syst. 35, 100732 (2022)."), indicated that the SOM-AE model reached 98.2% accuracy and an F1 score of 97%. In contrast, our proposed model significantly outperforms these existing methods, achieving an accuracy of 99.98%, an F1 score of 98%, and a perfect precision rate of 100%, with a computational complexity of roughly RMpS. This remarkable performance highlights the effectiveness of our DL approach in diagnosing and classifying CVDs, providing enhanced diagnostic reliability. By improving both accuracy and F1 score, our model highlights its potential for practical clinical applications, where accurate and dependable classification is crucial for effective patient care. Furthermore, the results suggest that hybrid architectures, such as CNN-MLP, can achieve competitive diagnostic performance without the substantial computational complexity associated with deeper standalone models.

Several limitations should be noted. The PTB-ECG dataset suffers from class imbalance and limited samples for certain disease categories; although SMOTE was applied, synthetic data may not fully reflect real physiological variability, leading to unstable per-class metrics. Consequently, this study focuses on comparative model evaluation rather than disease-specific performance. In addition, misclassifications mainly occurred between clinically similar conditions, and real-time deployment may introduce further challenges related to noise and latency. However, the results presented here can guide future efforts to use these models to evaluate condition-specific metrics, such as AUROC, AUPRC, and calibration scores.

## Conclusion

This study evaluated multiple DL architectures for multi-class ECG-based CVD diagnosis and classification, with a primary focus on achieving high diagnostic performance while maintaining low computational complexity. The results demonstrate that accurate CVD classification can be achieved without reliance on computationally intensive models. Among the evaluated approaches, the LSTM model achieved the most favorable accuracy–complexity trade-off, attaining 99.98% accuracy, a 98% F1 score, and 100% precision while operating at a computational complexity on the order of RMpS. The consistent performance observed across all evaluated models highlights the effectiveness of combining DWT–based feature extraction with compact deep learning architectures. This strategy enabled a three-order-of-magnitude reduction in computational complexity while preserving clinically relevant diagnostic information, thereby supporting the suitability of the PTB-ECG dataset for efficiency-oriented AI-driven CVD diagnostics.

Future work will focus on validating the proposed framework on larger, more diverse datasets, exploring transformer-based temporal models, and further optimizing feature engineering to enhance robustness while maintaining low computational complexity. Overall, the proposed low-complexity DL framework provides a practical foundation for real-time ECG-based cardiovascular screening and decision support in resource-constrained clinical and wearable healthcare settings.

##### [Validation of AI-enhanced ECG image analysis for identifying extreme cardiac magnetic resonance metrics in a cross-ethnic UK biobank study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5)

```
## Abstract

Artificial intelligence enhanced electrocardiography (AI-ECG) has shown promise in detecting cardiac abnormalities, but validation against cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), the reference standard for cardiac structure and function, remains limited. We evaluated the diagnostic performance of six AI-ECG models in identifying CMR-defined cardiac abnormalities in a population-based cohort. This cohort study included 38,804 UK Biobank participants with paired 12-lead ECG and CMR data. AI-ECG models, originally developed using Korean hospital-based datasets, were externally validated in this sample. Cardiac abnormalities were defined as the top 1% of CMR-derived values. Outcomes were the performance of AI-ECG in detecting left and right ventricular dysfunction, based on ejection fraction (QCG-LVD and QCG-RVD) and strain (ECG-LVGLS and ECG-RVGLS), and structural abnormalities including left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and left atrial enlargement (LAE). Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with subgroup analyses by age, sex, and comorbidities. Among 38,804 participants (mean age 64.2 years; 48.2% male), AI-ECG models showed high accuracy for detecting left ventricular dysfunction (AUC 0.887 for QCG-LVD and 0.896 for ECG-LVGLS) and right ventricular dysfunction (AUC 0.778 for QCG-RVD and 0.825 for ECG-RVGLS). In a sub-cohort of 21,267 individuals, AUCs were 0.824 for detecting LVH and 0.883 for LAE. Subgroup analyses showed consistent performance, with higher accuracy among older individuals, males, and those with hypertension or ischemic heart disease. In this large multiethnic cohort, AI-ECG models demonstrated strong performance in detecting CMR-defined abnormalities, supporting their potential as a scalable, noninvasive screening tool for cardiovascular disease.

## Introduction

Electrocardiography (ECG) is a widely accessible, non-invasive, and cost-effective tool for evaluating cardiovascular health. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have significantly expanded its clinical utility[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR1 "Attia, Z. I. et al. Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram. Nat. Med. 25, 70–74. 
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0240-2
(2019)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR2 "Yao, X. et al. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiograms for identification of patients with low ejection fraction: a pragmatic, randomized clinical trial. Nat. Med. 27, 815–819. 
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-021-01335-4
(2021)."),[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR3 "Sau, A. et al. Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram for mortality and cardiovascular risk estimation: a model development and validation study. Lancet Digit. Health. 6, e791–e802. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/S2589-7500(24)00172-9
(2024)."). AI-enhanced ECG (AI-ECG) enables the prediction of structural and functional cardiac abnormalities that have typically required advanced imaging modalities such as echocardiography or cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR). By leveraging the ubiquity of ECG, AI-ECG offers a scalable strategy for early detection and screening of cardiovascular disease, potentially reducing dependence on resource-intensive imaging tools.

Our group has previously developed and validated deep learning based AI-ECG models that analyze ECG images to generate digital biomarkers for various cardiac conditions[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR4 "Choi, H. M. et al. AI derived ECG global longitudinal strain compared to echocardiographic measurements. Sci. Rep. 14, 26458. 
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-78268-8
(2024)."),[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR5 "Cho, Y. et al. Artificial intelligence-based electrocardiographic biomarker for outcome prediction in patients with acute heart failure: Prospective cohort study. J. Med. Internet Res. 26, e52139. 
https://doi.org/10.2196/52139
(2024)."),[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR6 "Park, J. et al. Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography analysis as a promising tool for predicting obstructive coronary artery disease in patients with stable angina. Eur. Heart J. Digit. Health. 5, 444–453. 
https://doi.org/10.1093/ehjdh/ztae038
(2024)."),[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR7 "Choi, J. et al. Artificial intelligence predicts undiagnosed atrial fibrillation in patients with embolic stroke of undetermined source using sinus rhythm electrocardiograms. Heart Rhythm. 21, 1647–1655. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hrthm.2024.03.029
(2024)."). These models rely on image-based ECG input rather than raw signal data, offering flexibility in clinical implementation and demonstrating high diagnostic performance. However, despite their promising performance, further validation is necessary to assess their generalizability in broader populations, particularly across different ethnicities and outside of hospital-based cohorts.

This study aims to validate previously developed AI-ECG models in a general population from the UK Biobank, comprising over 38,000 participants with paired ECG and CMR data.

## Results

### Baseline characteristics

Baseline characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Tab1). The mean age of participants was 64.2 ± 7.8 years, with 48.2% being male. Comorbidities included hypertension in 32.9%, diabetes mellitus in 5.9%, and dyslipidemia in 24.1%. The mean left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) measured by CMR was 59.5 ± 6.1%, and the mean right ventricular ejection fraction (RVEF) was 57.3 ± 6.2%.

## AI-ECG performance for detecting left and right ventricular dysfunction

Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Tab2) presents baseline characteristics stratified by the presence of left ventricular dysfunction (LVD) and right ventricular dysfunction (RVD). Participants with LVD or RVD were generally older and had a higher prevalence of comorbid conditions compared to those without dysfunction. In particular, hypertension was more prevalent in both LVD and RVD groups. Individuals with LVD had higher rates of diabetes mellitus and ischemic heart disease, while those with RVD more frequently had heart failure.

As expected, CMR-derived LVEF was significantly lower in the LVD group compared to those without LVD (36.9 ± 5.1% vs. 59.5 ± 6.1%; _p_ < 0.001), and RVEF was markedly reduced in the RVD group (35.2 ± 5.7% vs. 57.4 ± 5.9%; _p_ < 0.001). Corresponding AI-ECG scores were significantly higher among participants with ventricular dysfunction (all _p_ < 0.001), highlighting the clear separation in AI-ECG values between normal and abnormal groups (Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Fig1)).

AI-ECG models demonstrated excellent performance in detecting LVD, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.887 (95% CI 0.866–0.907) for Quantitative ECG (QCG™)-LVD and 0.896 (95% CI 0.876–0.916) for ECG-LV global longitudinal strain (LVGLS). For RVD, AUCs were 0.778 (95% CI 0.751–0.804) for QCG-RVD and 0.825 (95% CI 0.800–0.850) for ECG-RVGLS (Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Fig1)). Although performance for RVD detection was slightly lower than for LVD, the AI-ECG models still demonstrated substantial diagnostic value, particularly given the challenges of assessing RVD using ECG alone. In subgroup analyses, AI-ECG performance for LVD detection was particularly high in older individuals and males, suggesting potential demographic variations in model accuracy. Subgroup analyses revealed higher diagnostic accuracy for LVD in older individuals and males. For RVD, model performance remained consistent across subgroups stratified by body mass index (BMI) groups and individuals with and without comorbidities. Notably, the model exhibited slightly higher accuracy in subgroups with a higher prevalence of ventricular dysfunction, such as older individuals and those with ischemic heart disease. (Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Fig2)) Using bootstrap resampling (200 iterations), bias-corrected calibration and discrimination metrics were estimated (Supplementary Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#MOESM2), [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#MOESM3), and Supplementary Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#MOESM1)), which demonstrated reasonable calibration.

Additionally, in the sub-cohort with available CMR-derived LVGLS data, the ECG-LVGLS model demonstrated robust performance in identifying abnormal LVGLS, defined as the lowest 1% of CMR-LVGLS distribution, with an AUC of 0.829 (95% CI 0.794–0.865). The ECG-LVGLS was significantly lower in participants with abnormal CMR-LVGLS. (Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Fig3))

## AI-ECG performance for detecting structural abnormalities

Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Tab3) presents baseline characteristics stratified by the presence of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and left atrial enlargement (LAE), as defined by CMR. Participants with LVH had a higher BMI (27.7 ± 5.3 vs. 26.4 ± 4.3 kg/m²; _p_ < 0.001) and were more likely to have hypertension (55.4% vs. 31.0%; _p_ < 0.001), heart failure (2.3% vs. 0.5%; _p_ < 0.001), and ischemic heart disease (12.7% vs. 5.7%; _p_ < 0.001). Similarly, individuals with LAE were older (67.6 ± 7.4 vs. 62.8 ± 7.5 years; _p_ < 0.001), predominantly male (66.2% vs. 47.7%; _p_ < 0.001), and had higher rates of hypertension (61.0% vs. 30.9%; _p_ < 0.001) and ischemic heart disease (18.8% vs. 5.7%; _p_ < 0.001).

CMR-derived left ventricular mass index (LVMI) (76.6 ± 7.2 vs. 45.6 ± 7.9 g/m²; _p_ < 0.001) and LAVI (80.6 ± 13.9 vs. 38.6 ± 10.3 mm³/m²; _p_ < 0.001) were significantly elevated in LVH and LAE groups, respectively. AI-ECG scores were significantly elevated in participants with structural abnormalities. AI-ECG-LVH scores were markedly increased in participants with LVH (0.51 ± 0.21 vs. 0.22 ± 0.14; _p_ < 0.001), and AI-ECG-LAE scores were notably higher among those with LAE (0.53 ± 0.25 vs. 0.19 ± 0.13; _p_ < 0.001), demonstrating clear separation between groups.

AI-ECG demonstrated strong diagnostic accuracy for identifying structural abnormalities. AI-ECG-LVH achieved an AUC of 0.877 (95% CI 0.851–0.902) for detecting LVH, while AI-ECG-LAE exhibited AUC of 0.883 (95% CI 0.858–0.908) for detecting LAE (Fig. [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Fig4)). In subgroup analyses, predictive performance for LVH and LAE detection was robust across demographic categories, including age, sex, and BMI subgroups. The accuracy of AI-ECG was particularly strong in older individuals and males, reflecting trends similar to those observed in functional abnormality (ventricular dysfunction) analyses. Model performance was also enhanced in subgroups characterized by higher prevalence rates of cardiovascular comorbidities, notably hypertension and ischemic heart disease, highlighting the clinical relevance of AI-ECG as a potential non-invasive screening tool for structural cardiac abnormalities. (Fig. [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Fig5)) The AI-ECG-LVH and AI-ECG-LAE scores demonstrated superior diagnostic performance compared with conventional ECG criteria. (Supplementary Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#MOESM4)) Detailed diagnostic performance metrics—including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value—are summarized in Table [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#Tab4) for each AI-ECG model. Additional sensitivity analyses using broader percentile-based definitions (top/bottom 1%, 2%, and 5%) demonstrated that model performance remained acceptable across the various thresholds tested (Supplementary Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#MOESM1)).

## Discussion

In this study of 38,804 UK Biobank participants, we demonstrated that AI-ECG can accurately detect structural and functional cardiac abnormalities, as defined by CMR. Using the top 1% of extreme CMR-derived values to define abnormalities, AI-ECG models achieved high diagnostic performance across a range of conditions: left ventricular dysfunction (AUC 0.887–0.896), right ventricular dysfunction (AUC 0.778–0.825), left ventricular hypertrophy (AUC 0.824), and left atrial enlargement (AUC 0.883). These findings support the potential utility of AI-ECG as a scalable, non-invasive tool for population-level cardiovascular screening, extending its application beyond the hospital-based Korean cohorts in which the models were originally developed.

Previous research has shown that AI-ECG can effectively identify various cardiac conditions. Notably, a Mayo Clinic study demonstrated reliable detection of left ventricular dysfunction using AI applied to ECGs, validated against echocardiography-defined ejection fraction[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR8 "Kashou, A. H. et al. Artificial intelligence-augmented electrocardiogram detection of left ventricular systolic dysfunction in the general population. Mayo Clin. Proc. 96, 2576–2586. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mayocp.2021.02.029
(2021)."). Our group has similarly developed ECG image–based models that perform well in detecting structural and functional abnormalities[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR4 "Choi, H. M. et al. AI derived ECG global longitudinal strain compared to echocardiographic measurements. Sci. Rep. 14, 26458. 
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-78268-8
(2024)."),[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR5 "Cho, Y. et al. Artificial intelligence-based electrocardiographic biomarker for outcome prediction in patients with acute heart failure: Prospective cohort study. J. Med. Internet Res. 26, e52139. 
https://doi.org/10.2196/52139
(2024)."). However, prior studies have primarily focused on hospital-based or ethnically homogeneous populations. The present study uniquely validates these models in a multiethnic, community-based cohort from the UK Biobank, enhancing their generalizability and external validity. Despite differences in ethnicity and healthcare settings, our AI-ECG algorithms maintained high accuracy, suggesting the robust nature of ECG image-based analysis and generalizable convolutional neural network-based AI methodologies. This multiethnic validation significantly strengthens the external validity and potential clinical utility of AI-ECG for broad population-level screening.

CMR is widely regarded as the gold standard for evaluating cardiac structure and function due to its reproducibility and accuracy, particularly for parameters such as ventricular volumes and myocardial mass. Compared with echocardiography, CMR avoids geometric assumptions and operator dependency, resulting in more reliable assessments[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR9 "Alfakih, K., Reid, S., Jones, T. & Sivananthan, M. Assessment of ventricular function and mass by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Eur. Radiol. 14, 1813–1822. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s00330-004-2387-0
(2004)."). Consequently, significant discrepancies between echocardiography and CMR-derived parameters have been consistently reported, with one study noting up to 60% discordance in patients with reduced LV ejection fraction (≤ 45%)[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR10 "Clark, J. et al. Interchangeability in left ventricular ejection fraction measured by echocardiography and cardiovascular magnetic resonance: Not a perfect match in the real world. Curr. Probl. Cardiol. 48, 101721. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpcardiol.2023.101721
(2023)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR11 "Marcos-Garces, V. et al. Ejection fraction by echocardiography for a selective use of magnetic resonance after infarction. Circ. Cardiovasc. Imaging. 13, e011491. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCIMAGING.120.011491
(2020)."),[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR12 "Marwick, T. H., Neubauer, S. & Petersen, S. E. Use of cardiac magnetic resonance and echocardiography in population-based studies: Why, where, and when? Circ. Cardiovasc. Imaging. 6, 590–596. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCIMAGING.113.000498
(2013)."). This is especially important for right ventricular function, which is often difficult to evaluate via echocardiography due to its complex geometry and limited acoustic windows, making CMR a more reliable reference standard[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41824-5#ref-CR13 "Bowen, D. J. et al. Comparison of advanced echocardiographic right ventricular functional parameters with cardiovascular magnetic resonance in adult congenital heart disease. Eur. Heart J. Imaging Methods Pract. 1, qyad033. 
https://doi.org/10.1093/ehjimp/qyad033
(2023)."). Given these inherent methodological differences and the population-based nature of the UK Biobank cohort, we defined cardiac structural and functional abnormalities using the top 1% CMR-measured values rather than applying traditional echocardiographic thresholds. This approach enabled identification of individuals with marked deviations from normal cardiac function and provided a rigorous reference standard for AI-ECG validation in a general population setting.

Beyond confirming strong overall performance, our subgroup analyses offered additional insights into its performance across various demographic and clinical subgroups. Notably, diagnostic accuracy for both LVD and RVD was significantly higher among older participants and males compared to younger individuals and females. The presence of hypertension significantly enhanced the diagnostic accuracy of AI-ECG for both LVD and RVD, while diabetes and dyslipidemia tended to improve RVD detection. Regarding structural abnormalities, the diagnostic accuracy of AI-ECG for LVH was greater in participants with diabetes, whereas the predictive performance for LAE was enhanced among older individuals and those with higher BMI. These trends likely reflect the greater degree of cardiac remodeling in individuals with established cardiovascular risk factors, resulting in more pronounced ECG changes and improved model discrimination. Although performance was broadly consistent across subgroups, these findings suggest that AI-ECG may have particularly high clinical value in high-risk populations. Results of sensitivity analyses supported the interpretation that the models detect extreme CMR measurements across varying degrees of stringency. Notably, while the strict 1% definition yielded very high NPV, expanding the definition to 2% and 5% resulted in progressive improvements in PPV. This pattern suggests that the models capture a spectrum of extreme CMR measurements and may have potential utility as a rule-out–oriented screening tool for identifying individuals unlikely to harbor marked structural or functional deviations, rather than as a definitive diagnostic test.

The robust diagnostic performance and high accessibility of AI-ECG demonstrated in this study suggest substantial implications for clinical practice. In real-world healthcare settings, AI-ECG could serve as a scalable, non-invasive initial screening tool, efficiently identifying individuals at higher cardiovascular risk who may benefit from more detailed diagnostic assessments or preventive interventions. For instance, AI-ECG could be integrated into routine primary care visits or community-based screening programs, promptly flagging patients with subtle but clinically meaningful abnormalities such as early-stage heart failure, asymptomatic left ventricular hypertrophy, or atrial remodeling indicative of increased atrial fibrillation risk. This early identification could facilitate timely intervention, potentially reducing morbidity and mortality associated with undetected cardiac conditions. Furthermore, because our AI-ECG algorithms operate on standard printed ECG images, their implementation requires minimal infrastructural changes, allowing rapid integration into diverse healthcare environments, including resource-limited settings where access to advanced cardiac imaging modalities remains challenging. Ultimately, our results highlight the practical and clinical value of incorporating AI-ECG into broader cardiovascular disease prevention and management strategies, emphasizing its potential to improve patient outcomes on a population scale.

This study has several limitations. While the UK Biobank dataset expands research from Korean populations to a predominantly European cohort, this represents a cross-ethnic validation between the development and validation cohorts. However, its primarily White demographic composition may still limit the generalizability within the validation population, highlighting the need for validation in more ethnically diverse cohorts. The top 1% CMR values offers reasonable and practical cut-off value for defining the functional and structural abnormalities in general population, but may not align with previously established thresholds, potentially limiting its application in routine clinical workflows where fixed cut-offs are standard. Moreover, good calibration in a retrospective cohort does not automatically translate to prospective performance. The healthy volunteer effect in the UK Biobank may introduce spectrum bias, potentially impacting model performance compared to more diverse or high-acuity clinical populations. Furthermore, identifying extreme percentile metrics focuses on population-based structural deviations rather than clinical disease, a distinction that is essential for interpreting the model’s diagnostic accuracy. The black-box nature of AI-ECG models may pose challenges for clinical adoption, underscoring the need for further efforts to improve interpretability. Lastly, while our AI-ECG algorithms demonstrated robust diagnostic performance, this study was limited by the lack of longitudinal follow-up data. Future prospective studies are required to evaluate the prognostic utility of these AI-ECG scores and to confirm whether their application can meaningfully enhance cardiovascular outcomes.

In conclusion, the newly developed AI-ECG scores are highly effective in detecting functional and structural cardiac abnormalities within a general population. These findings highlight AI-ECG’s potential as a cost-effective and accessible screening tool, addressing limitations in availability and diagnostic accuracy associated with current imaging modalities, such as echocardiography and CMR.
```
##### [Reliable ECG classification using parallel hybrid models with limited resources](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0)

```
## Abstract

Accuracy in classification of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is vital in healthcare for diagnosing arrhythmias and other cardiovascular disorders. There exist reliability and computational efficiency limitations while using deep learning models particularly in resource constrained environments. This study introduces the Parallel Hybrid Model (PHM), an innovative ensemble approach that combines three lightweight classifiers, EfficientNet, SequentialNet, and LeNet-5 enhancing reliability and accuracy of ECG classification. The PHM employs a novel weighted soft voting approach to aggregate predictions, minimizing misclassification errors while integrating a unique interpretable confidence framework via reliability zones. These zones include the Correct Decision Zone (with a correct probability P(C) = 0.9645), the Misclassification Zone (with an error probability P(E) = 0.0076), and the False Decision Zone (with a false decision probability P(F) = 0.0279), offering a clear measure of confidence. The proposed PHM model is evaluated on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, achieving an accuracy of 98.46%, outperforming individual models (LeNet-5: 98.13%, EfficientNet: 97.92%, SequentialNet: 98.08%), with an error rate of 1.54%. This study’s primary aim is to provide a computationally efficient and reliable system for resource-constrained environments. This reliability focused approach ensures robustness in performance in resource-limited devices such as wearable ECGs, offering clinicians dependable and interpretable outcomes for improved diagnostics.

## Introduction

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) represent a major global health challenge, accounting for approximately 19.8 million deaths globally in 2022, as reported by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2023[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR1 "World Health Organization. World Health Statistics 2023: Monitoring Health for the SDGs (World Health Organization, 2023)."). This figure has remained significant and demands an urgent need for effective diagnostic tools. Among CVD complications, arrhythmias irregular heart rhythms is a serious threat. This abnormality potentially leads to severe outcomes such as strokes, heart failure, or sudden cardiac arrest if not diagnosed early. Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, which record the heart’s electrical activity, are essential for identifying these arrhythmia and other abnormalities promptly. Thus, ECG is considered as a primary low-cost diagnostic method in clinical practice. However, conventional approaches to ECG classification, such as rule-based systems or checking features manually, are slow and prone errors, limiting their effectiveness[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR2 "Zhang, J., Liu, A., Chen, X. & Zhang, X. Interpatient ECG heartbeat classification with an adversarial convolutional neural network. J. Healthcare Eng. 2021, 9946596. 
https://doi.org/10.1155/2021/9946596
(2021)."). There is a dire need for accurate, reliable and fast methods to meet these critical demands.

Deep learning methods, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have emerged as a promising solution for classification of ECG patterns. CNNs can analyze raw ECG data to detect features without requiring extensive manual inputs[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR3 "Gan, Y., Shi, J.-C., He, W.-M. & Sun, F. Parallel classification model of arrhythmia based on DenseNet-BiLSTM. Biocybern. Biomed. Eng. 41(1), 1548–1560. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbe.2021.09.001
(2021)."). Research has shown that CNNs can sometimes outperform cardiologists in arrhythmia detection[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR4 "Rajpurkar, P., Hannun, A. Y., Haghpanahi, M., Bourn, C. & Ng, A. Y. Cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection with convolutional neural networks. Nat. Med. 23(1), 65–69. 
https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.4045
(2017)."). However, these models have also significant drawbacks as they demand substantial computational resources. Thus, making them impractical for low-power devices like wearable ECG monitors or rural clinics. Moreover, the misclassification by CNNs introduces serious risks in healthcare system, as such errors can have life-threatening consequences[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR5 "Mondéjar-Guerra, V., Novo, J., Rouco, J., Quiñones, M. & Ortega, M. Heartbeat classification fusing temporal and morphological information of ECGs via ensemble of classifiers. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 47, 41–48. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bspc.2018.08.007
(2019)."). Such challenges of high resource requirements and unreliable outcomes highlight a gap that must be addressed.

Recent advancements in ECG classification have further highlighted this efficiency gap. For instance, hybrid transformer models for arrhythmia detection achieve high accuracy but require intensive computational resources, limiting their deployability in low-resource settings[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR6 "Liu, K., Zhang, W. & Li, Z. Hybrid transformer model for arrhythmia detection in ECG signals. IET Signal Process. 18(2), 145–156. 
https://doi.org/10.1049/spr2.12145
(2024)."). Similarly, advances in AI for ECG diagnostics emphasize the growing need for interpretability, which existing high-performance models often overlook in favor of pure accuracy[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR7 "Rodriguez, M. & Kumar, S. Advances in artificial intelligence for ECG diagnostics: A review. MDPI Bioeng. 12(3), 234. 
https://doi.org/10.3390/bioengineering12030234
(2025)."). The MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database remains the primary benchmark in ECG research, allowing for direct performance comparisons and validation of arrhythmia detection against established baselines[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR8 "Gupta, A., Thompson, P. & Wilson, R. Benchmarking ECG classification models: The enduring role of MIT-BIH database. Springer Biomed. Eng. Lett. 15(1), 45–58. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s13534-024-00345-8
(2025).").

This paper proposes a novel Parallel Hybrid Model (PHM) to work and address these issues directly. The PHM combines three low complexity classifiers EfficientNet, SequentialNet, and LeNet-5 designed to operate efficiently on low resource hardware, such as wearable devices or rural remote hospital systems. By using a weighted soft voting mechanism, the proposed PHM reduces errors and integrates a confidence score for each diagnostic prediction. This approach not only achieves improved accuracy but also ensures reliable and practical ECG classification. This is particularly helpful for machines with limited resources, potentially transforming patient care into remote or low resource environments[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR9 "Kiranyaz, S., Ince, T. & Gabbouj, M. Real-time patient-specific ECG classification by 1D convolutional neural networks. IEEE Trans. Biomed. Eng. 63(3), 664–675. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/TBME.2015.2468589
(2016).").

## Problem statement

Accurate classification of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals for heart abnormalities remains a significant challenge in healthcare system. Existing models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNN), demonstrate good performance in identifying cardiac abnormalities, however, their extensive application is hindered by substantial computational resource requirements and inconsistent reliability of results. These classification models often demand high performance hardware, making them impractical for resource limited environments, such as wearable ECG devices or low resource computing systems in remote areas health facilities. Furthermore, the concern of misclassification poses critical risks in medical diagnostics where precision is vital. Although hybrid approaches have been explored to address these limitations[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR15 "Chen, T. et al. A hybrid model for ECG classification based on CNN and RNN. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 57, 101788. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bspc.2019.101788
(2020)."), they often introduce complexity without reliability. The primary aim of this study is to develop the Parallel Hybrid Model (PHM) as an efficient and reliable ECG classification system for resource-constrained environments, integrating lightweight CNNs with weighted voting and reliability zones to achieve high accuracy while providing confidence measures for clinical support. This study seeks to develop an ECG classification model that is both highly reliable and computationally efficient while minimizing errors and providing a confidence measure to support clinical decision making. The MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database is utilized as the benchmark dataset for this study, as it remains the foundational standard used in many arrhythmia studies, ensuring comparable results without introducing variability from less standardized datasets[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR27 "Thompson, M. & White, S. The MIT-BIH arrhythmia database: Benchmarking and validation in contemporary ECG research. BioMed. Eng. OnLine 24(1), 67. 
https://doi.org/10.1186/s12938-025-01234-8
(2025).").

## Experimental results

This section elaborates a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed Parallel Hybrid Model (PHM) for ECG classification, on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. Simulation is performed to assess the performance of PHM in terms of accuracy, error rates, reliability zones, and classification metrics. The results demonstrate the PHM’s superiority over individual classifiers ie EfficientNet, SequentialNet, and LeNet-5 while confirming its suitability for resource-constrained environments. All results were obtained on a hold-out test set (11,889 samples), as described in Section “[LeNet-5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec10)”, ensuring robust evaluation. While statistical significance testing is commonly used for clinical trials, our deterministic evaluation on the standardized MIT-BIH benchmark demonstrates clinically meaningful improvements through: (1) absolute accuracy gains (> 0.3% over all baselines), (2) reliability zone probabilities, and (3) consistent performance across all arrhythmia classes (Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab5)). These metrics provide stronger evidence for ECG classification systems than p-values when using established benchmarks.

### Accuracy and error progression

The performance of the PHM was evaluated by over 20 training epochs, with metrics recorded to track accuracy and error progression.

As depicted in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Fig2), the accuracy of the ensemble PHM model consistently surpasses that of the individual classifiers, stabilizing at 98.46% by the 20th epoch. This improvement is attributable to the weighted soft voting mechanism, which integrates predictions from EfficientNet (97.92%), SequentialNet (98.08%), and LeNet-5 (98.13%) based on their final validation accuracies, as described in Section “[Mathematical analysis](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec15)”. The PHM’s accuracy demonstrates minimal fluctuations after the 10th epoch, that indicates robust convergence.

Figure [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Fig2) also presents the epoch wise accuracies and errors for all individual models and the PHM ensemble. For instance, when LeNet-5 achieves a maximum accuracy of 98.13%, EfficientNet reaches 97.92%, and SequentialNet attains 98.08% by the 20th epoch, however, the PHM achieves 98.46%. Correspondingly, the error rates calculated as 1 minus accuracy show the PHM with the lowest error of 1.54%, as compared to 1.87% for LeNet-5, 2.08% for EfficientNet, and 1.92% for SequentialNet. Figure [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Fig3) illustrates the error progression that highlights the PHM’s consistent reduction in errors, showing its reliability in minimizing misclassifications.

### Reliability zones

The reliability zones ie Correct Decision Zone (P(C)), Misclassification Zone (P(E)), and False Decision Zone (P(F)) provides a transparent measure of the PHM’s decision making process, as depicted in Sect. 4.2.2.

Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab3) summarizes the zone probabilities computed at the end of each epoch. After 20 epochs, the PHM exhibits a dominant P(C) of 0.9645, indicating a 96.45% probability that all classifiers agree on the correct class, reflecting high confidence. The P(E) is very low at 0.0076 (0.76%), signifying minimal unanimous misclassifications, while P(F) stands at 0.0279 (2.79%), representing instances of disagreement resolved by weighted voting.

These probabilities align with the mathematical analysis in Section "[Reliability zones](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec20)", where P(C) exceeds the theoretical product of individual correct probabilities due to the weighted voting’s enhancement, prioritizing higher-accuracy classifiers like LeNet-5. The low P(E) and P(F) values confirm the PHM’s robustness, ensuring reliable classifications even in resource limited settings, such as wearable ECG devices, where computational efficiency is utmost important.

### Confusion matrices

The classification performance of the individual models and the PHM is further highlighted through confusion matrices, presented in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Fig4). These matrices quantify correct classifications and misclassifications across five classes (normal sinus rhythm and four arrhythmia types) from the MIT-BIH ECG dataset. The PHM’s confusion matrix demonstrates superior performance, correctly classifying 14,446 samples as normal (class 0), compared to 14,463 by LeNet-5, 14,408 by EfficientNet and 14,381 by sequentialNet, with only 115 misclassifications for the PHM versus 145 for LeNet-5, 175 for EfficientNet and 94 for SequentialNet.

This reduction in misclassifications, particularly for critical arrhythmia classes, highlights the PHM’s enhanced reliability, driven by the weighted voting mechanism that mitigates errors in the False Decision Zone. The ensemble’s ability to outperform individual models underscores its practical utility in clinical settings, where minimizing false negatives is essential for patient diagnostics.

### Classification reports

Detailed classification reports of all models, provided in Tables [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab4), [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab5), [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab6), and [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab7), offer precision, recall, and F1-score metrics across the five classes. We have updated all classification tables to include both sensitivity (recall) and specificity metrics to provide a more comprehensive clinical evaluation. The proposed PHM classification report, as shown in Table [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab7), achieves the highest F1-score of 0.99 for the majority class (normal, class 0), with improved performance for minority classes (e.g., arrhythmia) compared to individual models. For instance, the PHM records an F1-score of 0.82 for class 1, 0.96 for class 2, 0.78 for class 3, and 0.99 for class 4, outperforming LeNet-5 (Table [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab4): 0.83, 0.95, 0.70, 0.98), EfficientNet (Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab5): 0.72, 0.96, 0.81, 0.98), and SequentialNet (Table [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab6): 0.80, 0.95, 0.77, 0.98).

The lower recall rates for Class 1 (0.72) and Class 3 (0.70) are primarily due to their rarity in the dataset (~ 2.5% and ~ 0.7% respectively) and morphological similarity to normal beats. While class-weighted loss mitigated this imbalance, the limited number of training examples for these minority classes remains challenging. Future work will explore advanced data augmentation techniques to further improve performance on these critical arrhythmia categories.

The PHM superior performance on minority classes addresses a common challenge in ECG classification imbalanced datasets and reinforces its reliability for clinical applications. The macro-averaged F1-score of 0.91 for the PHM (Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab5)) further validates its balanced accuracy across classes, achieving an overall accuracy of 98.46% and confirming its efficacy in resource constrained environments. As illustrated in Table [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab8) (F1-score comparison across models), the PHM consistently achieves higher F1-scores for minority arrhythmia classes (e.g., PVC: 0.82, APB: 0.78) compared to individual models, while maintaining near-perfect performance on normal rhythms (0.99). This demonstrates its robustness in handling class imbalance, a critical requirement for clinical ECG analysis where missed arrhythmia carry severe consequences.

### Comparison with State-of-the-art methods

Table [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Tab9) provides a comprehensive comparative analysis between the proposed PHM and recent state-of-the-art ECG classification methods. The PHM achieves competitive accuracy (98.46%) while maintaining significantly lower computational complexity (~ 200 k parameters) compared to hybrid CNN-BiLSTM models[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR26 "Martinez, L., Garcia, P. & Anderson, T. Hybrid CNN-BiLSTM model for ECG arrhythmia classification. Nat. Sci. Rep. 15(2), 3456. 
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-57890-4
(2025).") (98.5% accuracy, ~ 1.2 M parameters) and transformer-based approaches[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR6 "Liu, K., Zhang, W. & Li, Z. Hybrid transformer model for arrhythmia detection in ECG signals. IET Signal Process. 18(2), 145–156. 
https://doi.org/10.1049/spr2.12145
(2024).") (97.8% accuracy, ~ 2.5 M parameters). This demonstrates PHM’s unique advantage in balancing performance with efficiency, making it particularly suitable for resource-constrained deployment scenarios.

### Implications for resource-limited settings

The PHM’s low computational complexity confirms from the lightweight architectures of EfficientNet (~ 10,738 parameters), SequentialNet (~ 94,117 parameters), and LeNet-5 (~ 93,801 parameters), enabling efficient operation on medium range computing systems, as demonstrated in Section “[Dataset and preprocessing](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec5)”. The ensemble’s inference time, averaging 0.01 s per sample in the simulation, supports real-time ECG analysis in wearable devices or remote healthcare settings with less resources. Preliminary deployment testing on Raspberry Pi 4 demonstrated inference times of ~ 0.005 s per sample with energy consumption of ~ 0.1 mJ/sample, confirming feasibility for wearable applications and aligning with established resource-efficient models like AFibNet[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR30 "Pandey, S. et al. AFibNet: A lightweight convolutional neural network for atrial fibrillation detection in resource-constrained devices. BMC Med. Inform. Decis. Mak. 21(1), 345. 
https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-021-01689-2
(2021)."). Coupled with its high accuracy (98.46%) and reliability (P(C) = 0.9645), the PHM offers a practical solution for deploying advanced ECG classification in environments with limited resources, enhancing clinical decision making and patient outcome with confidence.

## Key contributions

This work introduces several significant contributions to the field of ECG classification, particularly for resource constrained environments, through the development and evaluation of the Proposed Parallel Hybrid Model (PHM). First, the PHM represents a novel ensemble approach integrating three lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures[31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR31 "Zhang, J. et al. ECG heartbeat classification using convolutional neural networks. IEEE Access 8, 8614–8624. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2020.2964030
(2020).") EfficientNet, SequentialNet, and LeNet-5 and utilizing a weighted soft voting mechanism to enhance classification accuracy and reliability. This methodology achieves an impressive accuracy of 98.46% on the MIT-BIH ECG Arrhythmia Database, surpassing the performance of individual models (EfficientNet: 97.92%, SequentialNet: 98.08%, LeNet-5: 98.13%), as demonstrated in Section “[Conclusion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec26)”.

Second, the introduction of reliability zones, namely the Correct Decision Zone (P(C) = 0.9645), Misclassification Zone (P(E) = 0.0076), and False Decision Zone (P(F) = 0.0279) provides a transparent and verifiable framework for assessing the PHM’s decision making process. This innovation, detailed in Sect. 4.2.2, enables healthcare professionals to evaluate the confidence and robustness of each classification, addressing a critical need for interpretability in medical applications.

Third, the weighted voting mechanism, applied in the False Decision Zone, constitutes an important advancement by assigning greater influence on higher-accuracy classifiers (e.g., weights of approximately 0.3267 for EfficientNet, 0.3277 for SequentialNet, and 0.3456 for LeNet-5, as calculated in Section “[Accuracy and error progression](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec19)”). This approach minimizes misclassification errors, enhancing the PHM’s reliability and aligning with its observed error rate of 1.54%, as reported in Section “[Conclusion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec26)”.

Fourth, the PHM’s computational efficiency, facilitated by the modest parameter counts of its constituent models (approximately 10,738 for EfficientNet, 94,117 for SequentialNet, and 93,801 for LeNet-5), ensures its practicality for deployment on medium-range computing systems, such as wearable ECG devices or remote healthcare setups, as discussed in “[Dataset and preprocessing](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec5)” and “[Conclusion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#Sec26)” sections. The PHM’s feasibility for wearable deployment is further validated by preliminary testing on Raspberry Pi 4, showing inference times of ~ 0.005 s per sample and energy consumption of ~ 0.1 mJ/sample, meeting the criteria for resource-constrained platforms (< 500 k parameters, < 1 GFLOPs, < 5 MB memory, < 0.05 s inference time) aligned with wearable standards[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-41370-0#ref-CR30 "Pandey, S. et al. AFibNet: A lightweight convolutional neural network for atrial fibrillation detection in resource-constrained devices. BMC Med. Inform. Decis. Mak. 21(1), 345. 
https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-021-01689-2
(2021).").

Finally, the PHM demonstrates superior performance in classifying minority classes (e.g., arrhythmias), achieving balanced F1-scores (e.g., 0.82 for class 1, 0.96 for class 2) and addressing the challenge of imbalanced datasets, thereby, advancing the state of the art in ECG classification for clinical reliability and accessibility.

Importantly, while some models report marginally higher accuracy, this work prioritizes reliability and clinical interpretability over marginal accuracy gains. The PHM provides a transparent, confidence-aware framework essential for trustworthy clinical decision-support, especially in resource-constrained settings where understanding model certainty is as critical as raw performance.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates the reliability of the Proposed Parallel Hybrid Model (PHM) in advancing ECG classification, particularly for resource-constrained environments. By integrating EfficientNet, SequentialNet, and LeNet-5 through a weighted soft voting mechanism, the PHM achieves an accuracy of 98.46% on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia ECG Dataset, outperforming individual models and maintaining a low error rate of 1.54%.

It is important to emphasize that the primary contribution of this work lies not merely in surpassing accuracy benchmarks, but in providing a reliability-aware classification framework a feature often absent in higher-accuracy black-box models. Through the introduction of reliability zones the Correct Decision Zone (P(C) = 0.9645), Misclassification Zone (P(E) = 0.0076), and False Decision Zone (P(F) = 0.0279) the PHM offers clinicians a transparent and interpretable measure of prediction confidence. This approach ensures that the system not only classifies accurately but also signals when predictions are uncertain, thereby enhancing trust and safety in real-world diagnostic settings.

The PHM framework is coupled with the PHM’s computational efficiency (enabled by lightweight architectures with approximately 10,738, 94,117, and 93,801 parameters, respectively), demonstrating its suitability for practical deployment in resource-constrained settings, such as wearable ECG devices and remote healthcare systems.

The PHM also shows superior performance in minority classes (e.g., arrhythmias) addresses the challenge of imbalanced datasets, offering significant potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes performance. Improved detection of minority classes, such as ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmia, enhances early diagnosis of critical conditions, reducing risks of stroke, heart failure, or sudden cardiac arrest, thereby improving patient outcomes in clinical settings**. **Future research will focus on extending the PHM to other physiological signal classifications, such as EEG and EMG, and optimizing its deployment for edge computing environments to further enhance its accessibility and utility in resource-limited settings.

## Limitations and future scope

This study has certain limitations that provide directions for future research. The current work focuses exclusively on the MIT-BIH dataset for benchmarking purposes, which, while being the standard in the field, may limit generalizability to other ECG databases with different recording conditions and patient populations. Additionally, while computational efficiency metrics and preliminary Raspberry Pi testing demonstrate feasibility for wearable deployment, comprehensive implementation on various resource-constrained platforms (such as FPGAs or dedicated ASICs) and extensive energy consumption analysis remain for future work. The lower recall rates for rare arrhythmia classes (Class 1 and Class 3) suggest the need for advanced data augmentation techniques or few-shot learning approaches in future iterations. Future scope includes multi-dataset validation, hardware-software co-design for optimized edge deployment, integration with cloud-based systems for continuous learning, and exploration of the PHM framework for other biomedical signal processing applications beyond ECG classification.

Future research directions include:

- _Multi-dataset validation_ using publicly available repositories such as PTB-XL, CPSC, and INCART to evaluate cross-dataset robustness and clinical generalizability.
    
- _Hardware-software co-design_ for optimized deployment on embedded systems, including quantization, pruning, and compiler-level optimizations to further reduce latency and energy footprint.
    
- _Integration with cloud-edge frameworks_ to enable continuous learning and model updating without compromising data privacy or requiring extensive local resources.
    
- _Extension of the reliability zone framework_ to other biosignal classification tasks, such as EEG, EMG, or PPG analysis, to assess its broader applicability in medical AI interpretability.
    
- _Clinical usability studies_ to evaluate the PHM’s reliability zones and confidence scores in real-world diagnostic workflows, assessing their impact on clinician trust and decision-making.
    

By addressing these limitations, future work can enhance the PHM’s applicability, reliability, and adoption in diverse clinical and resource-constrained environments.
```
##### [MEETI: A Multimodal ECG Dataset from MIMIC-IV-ECG with Signals, Images, Features and Interpretations](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1)

```
## Abstract

Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are essential for diagnosing arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and conduction disorders. While machine learning has achieved expert-level performance in ECG interpretation, the development of clinically deployable multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems is limited by the lack of public datasets that integrate raw signals, diagnostic images, and interpretation text. Most existing ECG datasets are single-modality or include, at most, signal-text pairs, restricting real-world applicability. To address this gap, we present MEETI (MIMIC-IV-Ext ECG-Text-Image), the first large-scale dataset that synchronizes raw ECG waveforms, high-resolution plotted images, and detailed textual interpretations generated by large language models. MEETI also includes beat-level quantitative parameters extracted from each lead, enabling fine-grained analysis and improving model interpretability. Built on the MIMIC-IV-ECG database of about 800,000 recordings, MEETI aligns each record across four components using unique identifiers: (1) raw signals, (2) plotted images, (3) per-beat parameters, and (4) interpretation text. This structure enables multimodal transformer learning and supports explainable, integrated analysis. MEETI provides a robust foundation and benchmark for next-generation cardiovascular AI research.

## Background & Summary

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of mortality worldwide[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR1 "Martin, S. S. et al. 2025 heart disease and stroke statistics: a report of us and global data from the american heart association. Circulation 151, e41–e660 (2025)."), contributing to over 17 million deaths each year. The electrocardiogram (ECG) remains the primary non-invasive modality to assess cardiac electrophysiology[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR2 "Tan, J. et al. A pediatric ecg database with disease diagnosis covering 11643 children. Scientific Data 12, 867 (2025)."). It provides temporal waveform information that is critical for diagnosing arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and conduction abnormalities[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR3 "Yagi, R., Mori, Y., Goto, S., Iwami, T. & Inoue, K. Routine electrocardiogram screening and cardiovascular disease events in adults. JAMA Internal Medicine 184, 1035–1044 (2024)."),[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR4 "Zheng, J., Fu, G., Anderson, K., Chu, H. & Rakovski, C. A 12-lead ecg database to identify origins of idiopathic ventricular arrhythmia containing 334 patients. Scientific data 7, 98 (2020)."). However, manually interpreting large volumes of ECG recordings is time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. Recently, machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) approaches have emerged as powerful tools for ECG analysis[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR5 "Hong, S., Zhou, Y., Shang, J., Xiao, C. & Sun, J. Opportunities and challenges of deep learning methods for electrocardiogram data: A systematic review. Computers in biology and medicine 122, 103801 (2020)."),[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR6 "Lan, X., Ng, D., Hong, S. & Feng, M. Intra-inter subject self-supervised learning for multivariate cardiac signals. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 36, 4532–4540 (2022)."),[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR7 "Lan, X., Yan, H., Hong, S. & Feng, M. Towards enhancing time series contrastive learning: A dynamic bad pair mining approach. In The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations. arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.03357 (2024)."),[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR8 "Li, J. et al. An electrocardiogram foundation model built on over 10 million recordings. NEJM AI 2, AIoa2401033 (2025)."). They can achieve expert-level performance in waveform analysis, arrhythmia detection, and risk stratification. These advances underscore the urgent need for comprehensive, multimodal ECG datasets. Such datasets are essential to ensure reproducible research and to accelerate clinical translation. Over the past few years, multimodal large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in interpreting complex medical imaging data[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR9 "Liu, F. et al. A medical multimodal large language model for future pandemics. NPJ Digital Medicine 6, 226 (2023)."). They can seamlessly integrate radiographic, histopathological, and clinical text inputs to support diagnostic and prognostic workflows[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR10 "Sandmann, S. et al. Benchmark evaluation of deepseek large language models in clinical decisionmaking. Nature Medicine pp. 1–1 (2025)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR11 "Zhou, S. et al.
