Large language models for disease diagnosis: A scoping review. npj Artificial Intelligence 1, 9 (2025)."). These advanced architectures use transformer-based encoders to fuse pixel-level features with semantic context. As a result, tasks such as lesion detection, disease classification, and report generation can be performed with near-human precision[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR12 "Hong, Q. et al. Evaluating the performance of large language & visual-language models in cervical cytology screening. NPJ Precision Oncology 9, 153 (2025)."). Despite these successes, current LLMs remain incapable of directly processing and understanding electrocardiographic waveforms. Cardiac signals have unique temporal dynamics and amplitude variations that differ fundamentally from spatial image patterns. Bridging this gap requires specialized datasets and model designs that jointly represent ECG signals alongside complementary textual and visual information.

```
Most existing ECG datasets provide only single-modality data (e.g., raw waveform signals) or, at most, dual modalities such as image–text pairs, as commonly seen in clinical reports. However, contemporary AI research increasingly requires multimodal representations to model the complex nature of ECG data, which inherently combine temporal waveforms, visual patterns, and diagnostic text[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR13 "Wagner, P. et al. Ptb-xl, a large publicly available electrocardiography dataset. Scientific data 7, 1–15 (2020)."),[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR14 "Gow, B. et al. Mimic-iv-ecg: Diagnostic electrocardiogram matched subset. Type: dataset 6, 13–14 (2023)."),[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR15 "Kansal, A., Chen, E., Jin, B. T., Rajpurkar, P. & Kim, D. A. Mc-med, multimodal clinical monitoring in the emergency department. Scientific Data 12, 1094 (2025)."). This mismatch between available data formats and modeling needs has hindered progress in developing explainable and generalizable ECG-based AI systems. Models trained on digitized time series cannot easily leverage the many image‐based clinical interpretations available online[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR16 "Al-Zaiti, S. S. et al. Machine learning for ecg diagnosis and risk stratification of occlusion myocardial infarction. Nature Medicine 29, 1804–1813 (2023)."),[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR17 "Chen, J. et al. Congenital heart disease detection by pediatric electrocardiogram based deep learning integrated with human concepts. Nature Communications 15, 976 (2024)."). Traditional analysis pipelines rely on handcrafted parameter extraction (e.g., QRS complex duration, ST segment deviations) to support diagnostic decisions[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR18 "Fan, S. et al. On-device Computation of Single-lead ECG Parameters for Real-time Remote Cardiac Health Assessment: A Real-world Validation Study. arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.17499 (2025)."). In contrast, deep learning models act as opaque black boxes without explicit feature semantics[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR19 "SAHiN, E., Arslan, N. N. & Özdemir, D. Unlocking the black box: an in-depth review on interpretability, explainability, and reliability in deep learning. Neural Computing and Applications 37, 859–965 (2025)."). These two limitations highlight that ECG data naturally combine visual, temporal, and textual information. As a result, we need a unified multimodal approach. Training multimodal language models to understand ECG data requires genuine ECG multimodal examples—paired waveform images, raw signals, and textual annotations[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR20 "Li, J., Liu, C., Cheng, S., Arcucci, R. & Hong, S. Frozen language model helps ecg zero-shot learning. In Medical Imaging with Deep Learning. PMLR pp. 402–415 (2024)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR21 "Lai, Y. et al. Diffusets: 12-lead ecg generation conditioned on clinical text reports and patient-specific information. Patterns (2025)."). However, existing public ECG datasets only include signal–text pairs and leave out image data[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR22 "Tsutsui, K. et al. Shdb-af: a japanese holter ecg database of atrial fibrillation. Scientific Data 12, 454 (2025)."),[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR23 "Zheng, J. et al. A 12-lead electrocardiogram database for arrhythmia research covering more than 10,000 patients. Scientific data 7, 48 (2020)."). This gap prevents a systematic study of how to combine visual and temporal cardiac representations in transformer-based models. The lack of integrated datasets is therefore a bottleneck for ECG multimodal research. It motivates the creation of resources that encode images, signals, and semantics together for end-to-end model training.

To address these limitations, we introduce MEETI[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR24 "Zhang, D. et al. Mimic- iv-ecg-ext-text-image (meeti): Diagnostic texts and images for mimic-iv-ecg. Zenodo. 
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15893351
(2025).") (MIMIC-IV-Ext ECG-Text-Image, Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#Fig1)), a multimodal ECG dataset that enables LLMs to process and interpret ECG data more effectively. MEETI is built on the MIMIC-IV-ECG dataset[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR14 "Gow, B. et al. Mimic-iv-ecg: Diagnostic electrocardiogram matched subset. Type: dataset 6, 13–14 (2023)."),[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-06796-1#ref-CR25 "Johnson, A. et al. Mimic-iv. PhysioNet. Available online at: 
https://physionet.org/content/mimiciv/1.0/
(accessed August 23, 2021) pp. 49–55 (2020)."), one of the largest and most representative public 12-lead clinical ECG collections available. It covers a wide range of cardiac conditions and signal qualities that reflect real-world clinical settings. MEETI is the first multimodal ECG dataset to provide synchronized access to four key components: raw ECG signals, plotted waveform images, extracted quantitative parameters, and detailed interpretation texts. By aligning these modalities, MEETI establishes a unified framework that integrates signal, visual, and language representations. This framework standardizes input formats for training LLMs and promotes explainable AI by enabling clinically interpretable reasoning, rather than replying on traditional black-box classification approaches. The integration of visual, temporal, and semantic modalities facilitates cross-modal alignment and supports the development of models capable of performing ECG analysis from multiple perspectives. Moreover, MEETI encourages a paradigm shift from conventional end-to-end diagnostic pipelines toward inference-based reasoning. Ultimately, this resource enhances the ability of multimodal LLMs to generate meaningful, context-aware interpretations of cardiac health.
```
##### [Multicenter validation of AI-enabled ECG for pediatric biological sex prediction](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9)

```
## Abstract

Biological sex is closely linked to patterns embedded within the electrocardiogram (ECG) with essential health and disease implications. We report multicenter verification of an AI-enabled ECG model to predict biological sex across pediatric development. A previously published Mayo Clinic model confirmed puberty-linked AUROC gradient during external validation at Texas Children’s Hospital (pre-puberty AUROC 0.64, peri-puberty AUROC 0.84, post-puberty AUROC 0.94). This phenomenon was replicated at Boston Children’s Hospital. Saliency mapping revealed established sex-related electrophysiologic patterns.

## Main text

The biological sex of an individual is closely linked to physiological and pathological characteristics embedded within the electrocardiogram (ECG). In a large, diverse cohort of healthy children, ECG intervals and amplitudes varied by biological sex[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR1 "Saarel, E. V. et al. Electrocardiograms in healthy North American children in the digital age. Circ. Arrhythm. Electrophysiol. 11, e005808 (2018)."), with shorter normal QTc intervals for males than females[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR2 "Giudicessi, J. R., Noseworthy, P. A. & Ackerman, M. J. The QT interval: an emerging vital sign for the precision medicine era? Circulation 139, 2711–2713 (2019)."). Biological sex is a major determinant of clinical manifestations in long QT syndrome and of arrhythmogenic risk when exposed to QTc prolonging medications[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR3 "Conrath, C. Gender differences in the long QT syndrome: effects of β-adrenoceptor blockade. Cardiovasc. Res. 53, 770–776 (2002)."). Biological sex-specific criteria have also been established for ECG-based diagnosis of left ventricular hypertrophy[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR4 "Peguero, J. G. et al. Electrocardiographic criteria for the diagnosis of left ventricular hypertrophy. J. Am. Coll. Cardiol. 69, 1694–1703 (2017)."). It is therefore of great interest to better understand the influence of biological sex on healthy and pathologic ECG patterns in order to improve pediatric ECG interpretation, and the electrophysiological manifestations of cardiovascular disease.

In the general adult population, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled ECG sex estimation is highly accurate and correlates with circulating sex hormones, supporting the notion that physiological signals are embedded in the waveform[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR5 "Attia, Z. I. et al. Age and sex estimation using artificial intelligence from standard 12-lead ECGs. Circ. Arrhythm. Electrophysiol. 12, e007284 (2019)."),[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR6 "Naser, J. A. et al. Artificial intelligence-augmented electrocardiogram in determining sex. Mayo Clin. Proc. 98, 541–548 (2023)."). More recently, Mayo Clinic assessed whether AI-ECG can similarly predict biological sex in children using: (1) a de novo model trained on pediatric data; and (2) a prior adult-derived AI-ECG model. Interestingly, they observed that both AI-ECG models performed poorly in pre-pubertal (0–7 year old) children, with performance improving in peri-pubertal children (8–14 year old) and excellent performance in post-pubertal (15–18 year old) children[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR7 "O’Sullivan, D. et al. Pediatric sex estimation using AI-enabled ECG analysis: influence of pubertal development. NPJ Digit. Med. 7, 176 (2024)."). These results are fascinating and hold important clinical and basic science implications.

In this study, we therefore aimed to provide multicenter verification of AI-ECG to predict biological sex across pediatric development. First, we externally validated Mayo Clinic’s AI-ECG models at Texas Children’s Hospital (TCH). The cohort included at TCH comprised of 118,003 ECGs (53,355 pre-pubertal, 39,764 peri-pubertal, 24,884 post-pubertal) from 67,578 patients (on average, 1.7 ECGs per patient). The TCH cohort was 52.7% male with median ECG age of 9.0 [2.0–14.0] years. There were on average 1.75 ECGs per patient and among patients with ≥2 ECGs, the mean interval between sequential ECGs was 0.3 years. Race (patient-level) was documented as White in 67.7%, Black or African American in 17.7%, Asian in 3.9%, American Indian and Alaska Native in 0.4%, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander 0.1%, other in 0.1% and unable to obtain in 10.2%. Ethnicity (patient-level) was recorded as Hispanic/Latino in 40.8%, not Hispanic/not Latino in 50.5%, and Unknown/Unable to Obtain in 8.7%. Similar to findings at Mayo Clinic, biological sex discrimination improved with age at TCH when using both the de novo pediatric AI-ECG model and the adult-derived AI-ECG model (Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#Tab1)). Threshold-dependent metrics followed the same pubertal gradient (Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#Tab1)).

To further evaluate generalizability of this relationship for normal and pathologic ECGs, Boston Children’s Hospital (BCH) developed and validated its own AI-ECG model using a model architecture and training approach that has been previously described for pediatric ECG tasks[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR8 "Mayourian, J. et al. Pediatric ECG-based deep learning to predict left ventricular dysfunction and remodeling. Circulation 149, 917–931 (2024)."). The training cohort comprised of 437,350 ECGs from 151,215 patients (49% male, median age at ECG 11.6 [IQR, 3.1-16.9] years, 44% normal ECGs), and the test cohort comprised of 145,784 ECGs from 50,405 patients (49% male, median age at ECG 12.0 [IQR, 3.3-17.0] years). On average, there were 2.9 ECGs per patient in the training and test set, with 0.8 years between ECGs. Race/ethnicity in the BCH cohort was documented as White in 51.8%, Unknown in 17.2%, Hispanic/Latino in 11.6%, Other in 8.4%, Black or African American in 7.5%, and Asian in 3.5%. To evaluate model performance, only one ECG per patient was used, ensuring that each test ECG corresponds to a unique patient not included in the training cohort. As shown in Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#Fig1), a similar pubertal gradient is noted, with poorest performance in pre-pubertal ECGs, highest performance in post-pubertal ECGs, and intermediate performance for peri-pubertal ECGs. This effect was seen regardless of using the first available, last available, or a random ECG per patient. This trend persisted in a subgroup analysis across a range of common and clinically pertinent pediatric ECG diagnoses (i.e., any ECG abnormality, prolonged QTc, left ventricular hypertrophy, right bundle branch block, or Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) (Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#Tab2)). Several other observations were noted: (1) overall performance is lower for abnormal versus normal ECGs; (2) performance remains excellent (AUROC >0.9) for post-pubertal ECGs, even in the setting of abnormalities such as prolonged QTc or left ventricular hypertrophy; (3) biological sex prediction is most sensitive to right bundle branch block.

To explore which ECG features the convolutional neural network relied upon for sex classification, we performed model explainability analysis (Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#Fig2)). Saliency maps highlighted the QRS complex and T waves as key features of the ECG, particularly in the precordial leads. Median waveform analysis illustrates that ECGs with highest probability of being male sex had a wider QRS complex, taller lateral precordial R waves, and taller T waves, whereas ECGs predicted to be female a longer QTc interval and flatter T waves.

Altogether, our study provides multicenter confirmation of the puberty-linked AUROC gradient for predicting biological sex. In addition to noting that AI-ECG prediction of biological sex is dependent on pubertal status, we also note that this effect is independent of institution, model architecture, which ECG is used, as well as the presence or absence of commonly observed ECG abnormalities.

These findings align with established sex-linked differences in ECG patterns that emerge after puberty and with sex-steroid regulation of repolarizing ion channels[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR1 "Saarel, E. V. et al. Electrocardiograms in healthy North American children in the digital age. Circ. Arrhythm. Electrophysiol. 11, e005808 (2018)."),[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR9 "Dickinson, D. F. The normal ECG in childhood and adolescence. Heart 91, 1626–1630 (2005)."),[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR10 "Kurokawa, J., Kodama, M., Clancy, C. E. & Furukawa, T. Sex hormonal regulation of cardiac ion channels in drug-induced QT syndromes. Pharmacol. Ther. 168, 23–28 (2016)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR11 "Locati, E. H. et al. Age- and sex-related differences in clinical manifestations in patients with congenital long-QT syndrome: findings from the international LQTS registry. Circulation 97, 2237–2244 (1998)."),[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR12 "Di Diego, J. M. et al. Ionic and cellular basis for the predominance of the Brugada syndrome phenotype in males. Circulation 106, 2004–2011 (2002)."),[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR13 "Stramba-Badiale, M., Spagnolo, D., Bosi, G. & Schwartz, P. J. Are gender differences in QTc present at birth? MISNES Investigators. Multicenter Italian Study on Neonatal Electrocardiography and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome. Am. J. Cardiol. 75, 1277–1278 (1995)."). In adults, AI-ECG probabilities of biological sex correlate with testosterone and estradiol, and discordance between predictions and reported biological sex aligns with measured hormone levels, supporting the hypothesis that AI-ECG captures a hormone-linked electrophysiologic profile[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR10 "Kurokawa, J., Kodama, M., Clancy, C. E. & Furukawa, T. Sex hormonal regulation of cardiac ion channels in drug-induced QT syndromes. Pharmacol. Ther. 168, 23–28 (2016)."). The pediatric results localize the rise of this profile during puberty, with steep gains from 7 to 14 years. AI-ECG sex probability may therefore serve as a noninvasive biomarker of maturational stage in contexts where pubertal timing modulates risk (e.g., congenital long-QT syndrome and drug-induced QT prolongation)[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR1 "Saarel, E. V. et al. Electrocardiograms in healthy North American children in the digital age. Circ. Arrhythm. Electrophysiol. 11, e005808 (2018)."),[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR2 "Giudicessi, J. R., Noseworthy, P. A. & Ackerman, M. J. The QT interval: an emerging vital sign for the precision medicine era? Circulation 139, 2711–2713 (2019)."),[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02416-9#ref-CR3 "Conrath, C. Gender differences in the long QT syndrome: effects of β-adrenoceptor blockade. Cardiovasc. Res. 53, 770–776 (2002).").

Limitations include the absence of clinical pubertal staging or hormone assays, and reliance on binary sex labels in the electronic health record. In addition, race/ethnicity data were not uniformly available and future work should examine the influence of demographics on performance. Finally, while performance was similar on ~8 s and 10 s 12-lead ECG recordings, future work includes systematically exploring whether there is a relationship between temporal window length and model performance.
```
##### [Time series electrocardiography (ECG) data for early prediction of cardiac arrest](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9)
```
## Abstract

Artificial intelligence is revolutionizing modern healthcare by enabling more precise and predictive diagnostics. In cardiology, AI is playing a vital role by assisting medical practitioners in analyzing complex electrocardiography (ECG) patterns with greater accuracy. As cardiovascular diseases continue to be a leading cause of mortality globally, the early prediction of sudden cardiac arrest remains a significant clinical challenge. This study explores the application of both machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques of time series ECG data for the early prediction of life-threatening cardiac events. The analysis confirms that deep learning models excel at detecting intricate patterns by automatically learning features directly from raw data, though they often demand large datasets and substantial computational resources. In contrast, traditional machine learning approaches are more computationally efficient and interpretable, making them a practical choice for resource-constrained environments. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of deep learning models, with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) achieving an accuracy of 99.89%. Among machine learning models, the Random Forest classifier performed best, achieving an accuracy of 99.06% and highlighting the reliability of ensemble learning methods. These findings demonstrate the significant potential of AI-based ECG analysis to improve early diagnosis and clinical decision making.

## Introduction

The cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) represent one of the most prevalent and severe global health challenges. The heart, essential for sustaining life, performs the critical functions of circulating oxygenated blood throughout the body and facilitating hormonal regulation to maintain optimal blood pressure[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR1 "World Health Organization Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) (2021)."). When cardiac function becomes compromised, it may present as CVDs, a comprehensive category encompassing disorders affecting both the heart and vascular system. Cardiovascular disease CVD is the most life threatening disease in humans, and it includes a wide spectrum of disorders that affect the heart and blood vessels, such as hypertension, coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and stroke[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR2 "Xiong, W. et al. Multichannel feature fusion network-based technique for heart sound signal classification and recognition. Expert Syst. Appl. 273, 126839 (2025)."). These conditions include congenital anomalies, pulmonary embolisms, cerebrovascular disorders, arrhythmias, peripheral arterial diseases, coronary artery disease (CAD), rheumatic heart[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR3 "Zhu, Y.et al. Identification of necroptosis and immune infiltration in heart failure through bioinformatics analysis. J. Inflamm. Res. 18, 2465–2481 (2025)."). The incorporation of time series electrocardiography (ECG) data has revolutionized the field of cardiac disease prediction and diagnosis, particularly for conditions leading to sudden cardiac arrest or myocardial infarction[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR1 "World Health Organization Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) (2021)."). By systematically analyzing the cardiac electrical activity patterns over time, medical practitioner can identify rhythm abnormalities and ECG irregularities that may indicate emerging life threatening conditions[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR4 "Amini, M., Zayeri, F. & Salehi, M. Trend analysis of cardiovascular disease mortality, incidence, and mortality-to-incidence ratio: Results from global burden of disease study 2017. BMC Public Health 21(1), 401 (2021)."). For instance, the abnormalities in ST segment elevation or depression and T wave inversions often signify myocardial ischemia or infarction, while QT interval variations may indicate medication toxicity or underlying genetic cardiac channelopathies. The diagram of the standard cardiac intervals and amplitude of the ECG is shown in Fig. [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#Fig1).

AI (Artificial Intelligence) algorithms combined with advanced analytics techniques provides medical practitioner to extract critical insights from time series ECG data, facilitating timely intervention to prevent adverse cardiac events. Kennedy _et al._[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR6 "Kennedy, C. E., Aoki, N., Mariscalco, M. & Turley, J. P. Using time series analysis to predict cardiac arrest in a PICU. Pediatr. Crit. Care Med. 16(9), e332–e339 (2015).") demonstrated the effectiveness of these approaches in their pioneering research, which significantly improved cardiac arrest prediction accuracy in paediatric intensive care units through advanced time series analysis. Their study highlights the transformative capacity of advanced modeling techniques in critical care environments where swift predictions significantly influences the impact patient outcomes. This paper explores the application of time series ECG data for cardiac arrest and myocardial infarction prediction, addressing both the strengths and limitations of these methodologies. Electrocardiography serves as a fundamental diagnostic and prognostic tool that captures hearst’s electrophysiological activity, providing medical practitioner with comprehensive insights into patients’ cardiovascular health. The combination of AI technologies with ECG monitoring enables real time analysis of cardiac signals, allowing healthcare professionals to identify patterns indicating imminent cardiac arrest and intervene accordingly[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR7 "Al Hinai, G., Jammoul, S., Vajihi, Z. & Afilalo, J. Deep learning analysis of resting electrocardiograms for the detection of myocardial dysfunction, hypertrophy, and ischaemia: A systematic review. Eur. Heart J. Digit. Health 2(3), 416–423 (2021)."). Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) algorithms provides distinct advantages for ECG interpretation[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR8 "Sengupta, J. Investigation of Deep Learning Models for Analysis of Heart Disorders in Smart Health Care based IoT Environment. J. Smat Internet Things (JSIoT) 2024(01), 01–16 (2024)."). Conventional machine learning approaches including classification, regression, random forest, support vector machine, and K-nearest neighbors algorithms leverage domain knowledge during training to generate clinically valuable insights[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR9 "Chang, A., Cadaret, L. & Liu, K. Machine learning in electrocardiography and echocardiography: Technological advances in clinical cardiology. Curr. Cardiol. Rep. 22(12), 168 (2020)."). DL, a specific ML subset, employs multilayered neural networks that mimic human biological neural processes to handle more complex data processing tasks with superior accuracy, particularly in high demand scenarios requiring human like pattern recognition. The subsequent sections of the paper are organized as follows: Section II offers a comprehensive background on cardiovascular diseases, their identification methodologies, and a comparative analysis of ML versus DL approaches. Section III provides practical applications of these AI approaches, with particular emphasis on CNN, LSTM, RNN, Transformers and hybrid implementations for CVD prediction. Section IV offers a comparative analysis evaluating the efficiency accuracy trade offs in resource constrained environments and explores future directions, such as implementation of explainable AI for enhanced clinical reliability and practical application.

## Background

### Identification of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) leading to cardiac arrest

In the initial phase of this study, we identified the cardiovascular conditions that commonly lead to cardiac arrest:

- Arrhythmias: These conditions involve irregular heart rhythms either excessively rapid or slow that can lead to cardiac arrest. Atrial fibrillation (AF) and ventricular tachycardia (VT) represent two particularly significant risk factors for sudden cardiac arrest[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR10 "Zhou, F.-Y., Jin, L.-P. & Dong, J. Premature ventricular contraction detection combining deep neural networks and rules inference. Artif. Intell. Med. 79, 42–51 (2017)."). AF causes irregular and accelerated heart rates, substantially increasing stroke and heart failure risk. Artificial intelligence systems analyzing ECG data can detect AF through identification of absent P waves and irregular RR intervals[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR11 "Jangra, M., Dhull, S., Singh, K., Singh, A. & Cheng, X. O-Wcnn: An optimized integration of spatial and spectral feature map for arrhythmia classification. Complex Intell. Syst. 9, 2685–2698 (2021)."). Similarly, ventricular tachycardia, which may deteriorate into ventricular fibrillation (VF), presents with characteristic wide QRS complexes on electrocardiograms. AI driven analytical approaches significantly enhance early detection capabilities, enabling timely clinical interventions[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR12 "Sakli, N. et al. ResNet-50 for 12-lead electrocardiogram automated diagnosis. Comput. Intell. Neurosci. 2022, 7617551 (2022).").
    
- Myocardial Infarction (Heart Attack): This condition occurs when blood flow to cardiac tissue is obstructed, resulting in myocardial damage or necrosis[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR13 "Haleem, M. et al. Time adaptive ECG driven cardiovascular disease detector. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 70, 102968 (2021).") . Diagnostic indicators include specific ECG changes such as ST segment elevation or depression and T wave inversion, which indicate acute ischemic events[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR14 "Zhang, X. et al. Automated detection of cardiovascular disease by electrocardiogram signal analysis: A deep learning system. Cardiovasc. Diagn. Ther. 10(2), 227–235 (2020).") . Advanced AI models, particularly deep learning architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showed efficiency in real time detection of these abnormalities, offering more immediate diagnostic capabilities compared to conventional manual ECG interpretation. The identification of hyperacute T waves or pathological Q waves is particularly enhanced through AI algorithms trained on comprehensive datasets[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR13 "Haleem, M. et al. Time adaptive ECG driven cardiovascular disease detector. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 70, 102968 (2021)."),[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR14 "Zhang, X. et al. Automated detection of cardiovascular disease by electrocardiogram signal analysis: A deep learning system. Cardiovasc. Diagn. Ther. 10(2), 227–235 (2020)."),[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR15 "Xiao, H. et al. Big data, extracting insights, comprehension, and analytics in cardiology: an overview. J. Healthc. Eng. 2021(1), 6635463 (2021).").
    
- Conduction Disorder: These conditions are characterized by unsual propagation of electrical impulses through cardiac tissue, resulting in irregular heartbeats. Bundle branch blocks (BBB) represent significant disruptions in the heart’s electrical conduction system and are typically identified through delayed or widened QRS complexes on electrocardiograms[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR9 "Chang, A., Cadaret, L. & Liu, K. Machine learning in electrocardiography and echocardiography: Technological advances in clinical cardiology. Curr. Cardiol. Rep. 22(12), 168 (2020)."). AI approaches can differentiate between Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB) characterized by QRS complexes exceeding 120 ms with distinctive bunny ear patterns in lead V1 and Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB), identified by broad, notched R waves in lateral leads.Therefore, AI based ECG analysis enhances early detection and treatment for patients with these conduction abnormalities[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR16 "Li, C. et al. DeepECG, Image-based electrocardiogram interpretation with deep convolutional neural networks. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 69, 102824 (2021).").
    
- Coronary Artery Disease (CAD): This condition involves narrowing and stiffening of coronary arteries that supply blood to the heart[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR17 "Lih, O. et al. Comprehensive electrocardiographic diagnosis based on deep learning. Artif. Intell. Med. 103, 101789 (2020)."). The resulting arterial constriction significantly reduces blood flow to cardiac tissue, compromising heart function[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR18 "Jahmunah, V., Ng, E., San, T. & Acharya, U. Automated detection of coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction and congestive heart failure using GaborCNN model with ECG signals. Comput. Biol. Med. 134, 104457 (2021).").
    
- Cardiomyopathies: These conditions involve irregularities in the size, shape, and structure of heart muscles, resulting in impaired cardiac pumping efficiency and reduced circulatory function[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR19 "Shen, Y. et al. Risk prediction for cardiovascular disease using ECG data in the China Kadoorie Biobank. Proc. Annu. Int. Conf. IEEE Eng. Med. Biol. Soc., pp. 2419–2422, (2016)."),[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR20 "Smigiel, S. ECG classification using orthogonal matching pursuit and machine learning. Sensors 22(13), 4960 (2022)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR21 "Wang, D., Meng, Q., Chen, D., Zhang, H. & Xu, L. Automatic detection of arrhythmia based on multi-resolution representation of ECG signal. Sensors 20(6), 1579 (2020).").
    

### Machine learning vs deep learning approaches

During our research of time series ECG data analysis for cardiovascular disease prediction, we observed a notable transformation in analytical methodologies. There is a increasing preference for end to end machine learning approaches, with particular focus on deep learning models that directly process raw ECG data[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR22 "Sangamesh, H., Cheripelli, R. & Nijaguna, G. S. Reconceiving the edge intelligence based IoT devices for an effective classification of ECG systems. J. Smat Internet Things (JSIoT) 2024(02), 79–92 (2024)."). These advanced techniques effectively overcome the traditional feature engineering processes that previously necessitated converting raw ECG signals into statistical or clinically derived features. In this field, the deep learning algorithms have become more prevalent than conventional machine learning approaches. The primary deep learning architectures include Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Long Short Term Memory Networks (LSTM), hybrid CNN-LSTM models, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), and combined CNN-RNN frameworks. What distinguishes deep learning models is their capability to process raw ECG signals across multiple informational dimensions, including both temporal and frequency domains. This multidimensional processing offers a more comprehensive analytical framework. The key advantage of these models include their ability to identify complex data representations and extract previously inaccessible hidden information within the signal data. As demonstrated by Yildirim et al.[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR23 "Yildirim, O., Plawiak, P., Tan, R. & Acharya, U. Arrhythmia detection using deep convolutional neural network with long-duration ECG signals. Comput. Biol. Med. 102, 411–420 (2018)."), this capability significantly enhances the potential of deep learning models to perform more detailed and thorough analysis of raw ECG signals, ultimately improving diagnostic and predictive accuracy. Though deep learning models excel in many ECG analysis applications, conventional machine learning algorithms maintain distinct advantages in specific contexts. These simpler machine learning approaches highlights the several practical benefits that make them preferable in certain clinical and research environments[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR24 "Saboor, A. et al. A method for improving prediction of human heart disease using machine learning algorithms. Mobile Inf. Syst. 2022(1), 1410169 (2022)."). This is because the machine learning models require significantly smaller training datasets compared to the deep learning approaches. This decreased reliance on data dependency allows machine learning models to be effectively developed and validated with limited samples. Moreover, the machine learning algorithms operate with significantly lower computational requirements, making them suitable for integration into predictive frameworks deployed on resource constrained platforms such as low power embedded systems. Model interpretability is another key factor that supports the conventional machine learning approaches.

Deep learning techniques often function as black boxes, obscuring their decision making processes, while machine learning algorithms offer greater transparency. Although certain machine learning methods including ensemble trees and Support Vector Machines (SVM) lack interpretability, they generally offer more accessible insight into their analytical processes through examination of feature importance and decision boundaries. This benefit of interpretability becomes significant in clinical environments where understanding the reason behind diagnostic recommendations is essential for physician acceptance and adherence to regulations. Additionally, deep learning frameworks such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) demonstrate vulnerability to slight changes in input data, potentially compromising their reliability even when these disruptions are minimal. This further highlights the practical significance of simpler machine learning algorithms in environments where model robustness, transparency, data limitations, and computational efficiency are critical factors. Existing research de,onstrated that the approaches involving artificial intelligence both ML and DL have been implemented in cardiology for either diagnostic or prognostic tasks. Diagnostic applications aims to assists medical practitioner in identifying specific cardiac conditions such as atrial fibrillation and various arrhythmias. In contrast, prognostic studies focus on predicting future cardiac events like myocardial infarction or stroke that are not clinically evident. Our literature review on the time series ECG analysis for CVD prediction highlights that both machine learning and deep learning approaches can be used in distinctively different ways. Conventional machine learning techniques typically process features extracted from ECG signals, while deep learning approaches analyze raw ECG data directly. Therefore, the literature examining various cardiovascular conditions can be categorized as follows:

- Arrhythmias: Two research papers specifically addressed arrhythmia disorders[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR10 "Zhou, F.-Y., Jin, L.-P. & Dong, J. Premature ventricular contraction detection combining deep neural networks and rules inference. Artif. Intell. Med. 79, 42–51 (2017)."),[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR11 "Jangra, M., Dhull, S., Singh, K., Singh, A. & Cheng, X. O-Wcnn: An optimized integration of spatial and spectral feature map for arrhythmia classification. Complex Intell. Syst. 9, 2685–2698 (2021)."),[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR12 "Sakli, N. et al. ResNet-50 for 12-lead electrocardiogram automated diagnosis. Comput. Intell. Neurosci. 2022, 7617551 (2022).")
    
- Myocardial infarction: Five studies addressed this condition[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR13 "Haleem, M. et al. Time adaptive ECG driven cardiovascular disease detector. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 70, 102968 (2021)."),[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR14 "Zhang, X. et al. Automated detection of cardiovascular disease by electrocardiogram signal analysis: A deep learning system. Cardiovasc. Diagn. Ther. 10(2), 227–235 (2020)."),[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR20 "Smigiel, S. ECG classification using orthogonal matching pursuit and machine learning. Sensors 22(13), 4960 (2022)."),[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR25 "Deng, Y. et al. ST-Net: Synthetic ECG tracings for diagnosing various cardiovascular diseases. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 61, 101997 (2020)."),[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR26 "Karthik, S., Santhosh, M., Kavitha, M. & Paul, A. Automated deep learning based cardiovascular disease diagnosis using ECG signals. Comput. Syst. Sci. Eng. 42(1), 183–199 (2022).")
    
- Conduction disorder: Primarily examined in two key studies[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR9 "Chang, A., Cadaret, L. & Liu, K. Machine learning in electrocardiography and echocardiography: Technological advances in clinical cardiology. Curr. Cardiol. Rep. 22(12), 168 (2020)."),[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR16 "Li, C. et al. DeepECG, Image-based electrocardiogram interpretation with deep convolutional neural networks. Biomed. Signal Process. Control 69, 102824 (2021).")
    
- Coronary Artery Disease (CAD): Focused in two studies[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR17 "Lih, O. et al. Comprehensive electrocardiographic diagnosis based on deep learning. Artif. Intell. Med. 103, 101789 (2020)."),[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR18 "Jahmunah, V., Ng, E., San, T. & Acharya, U. Automated detection of coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction and congestive heart failure using GaborCNN model with ECG signals. Comput. Biol. Med. 134, 104457 (2021).")
    
- Cardiomyopathies: Examined across three research studies[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR19 "Shen, Y. et al. Risk prediction for cardiovascular disease using ECG data in the China Kadoorie Biobank. Proc. Annu. Int. Conf. IEEE Eng. Med. Biol. Soc., pp. 2419–2422, (2016)."),[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR20 "Smigiel, S. ECG classification using orthogonal matching pursuit and machine learning. Sensors 22(13), 4960 (2022)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR21 "Wang, D., Meng, Q., Chen, D., Zhang, H. & Xu, L. Automatic detection of arrhythmia based on multi-resolution representation of ECG signal. Sensors 20(6), 1579 (2020).")
  
## Discussion

The results of the machine learning and deep learning highlights the effectiveness of both the approaches for ECG Classification. Both approaches successfully handled the class imbalance though they exhibit some of the false negatives for abnormal class as seen in the confusion matrices. However, the machine learning relys on the signal features offer computational efficiency, less training time and robust performance while the deep learning approach capture critical pattern from the raw data itself but requires more training time and resources.However, the recent techniques of the XAI for cardiac prediction have demonstrated that we can significantly enhance both accuracy and trustworthiness. Adopting similar frameworks, such as the DeepXplainer model proposed by Wani et al[41](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR41 "Wani, N. A., Kumar, R. & Bedi, J. DeepXplainer: An interpretable deep learning based approach for lung cancer detection using explainable artificial intelligence. Comput. Methods Progr. Biomed. 243, 107879 (2024)."),[42](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#ref-CR42 "Wani, N. A. et al. Synergizing fusion modeling for accurate cardiac prediction through explainable artificial intelligence. IEEE Trans. Consum. Electron. 71(1), 1504–1512 (2025).") for medical imaging, could bridge the gap between the high performance of our deep learning approach and the clinical need for interpretability.Future work could address the data imbalance of both the classes and validate these models on diverse datasets to enhance its application in the medical field.

### Model interpretability and clinical trust

A critical limitation of many cardiovascular AI systems is the lack of interpretability, which hinders clinical adoption. To address this, we employed SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) for machine learning models and Grad CAM (Gradient weighted Class Activation Mapping) for deep learning architectures. SHAP analysis revealed that heart rate variability features, QRS complex morphology, and ST segment characteristics were the most influential predictors for cardiac arrest classification. Grad CAM visualizations highlighted the specific ECG regions (particularly R-peaks and ST segments) that contributed most strongly to the CNN’s predictions, providing clinical validation that the model focuses on physiologically relevant patterns rather than spurious correlations. This interpretability framework enables medical practitioners to verify model reasoning, builds trust in automated predictions, and facilitates regulatory approval for clinical deployment. Future work should integrate these interpretability tools into real time clinical decision support interfaces. Figure [14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-35788-9#Fig14) shows the Grad CAM results for the Normal ECG signal classification. The areas of high activation demonstrate that the model is correctly focusing on clinically relevant features, such as the QRS complex, to make its predictions.

### Generalization and external validation

While our models achieved high performance on MIT-BIH and PTB-DB datasets, a key limitation is the lack of external validation on independent clinical cohorts. The MIT-BIH database contains primarily Caucasian patients from a single institution in the 1970s-1980s, which may not represent current diverse patient populations with different comorbidities, medications, and ECG characteristics. To assess generalization capability, we employed rigorous 5 fold cross validation and reported 95% confidence intervals for all metrics, demonstrating statistical stability. However, true clinical utility requires prospective validation on contemporary datasets from multiple hospitals, different demographics (age, sex, ethnicity), varied cardiac conditions (post-MI, heart failure, cardiomyopathy), and real-world scenarios with electrode noise and patient movement artifacts. We acknowledge this limitation and recommend future studies validate our models on recent databases such as MIMIC-IV ECG, PTB-XL, and institution-specific datasets before clinical implementation.

### Contribution

Our work advances the field beyond existing literature in several key aspects. First, we provide a comprehensive comparative analysis of traditional machine learning versus deep learning approaches using identical datasets and evaluation protocols, addressing the gap identified by recent systematic reviews. Second, unlike prior studies that report only accuracy metrics, we incorporate clinical relevance measures including false negative analysis (critical for cardiac arrest prediction), computational cost quantification (essential for edge device deployment), and statistical significance testing (McNemar’s test with Bonferroni correction) to ensure robust performance claims. Third, we integrate explainable AI techniques (SHAP and Grad CAM) into both approaches, directly responding to calls for interpretable cardiovascular AI systems. Fourth, our enhanced pseudocode and open source implementation provide reproducible benchmarks for the research community. While studies have demonstrated feature engineering and ensemble methods, our contribution lies in the systematic integration of interpretability, statistical analysis, and computational efficiency analysis within a unified framework. These contributions position our work as a practical bridge between research prototypes and clinically deployable cardiac monitoring systems.

## Conclusion

The integration of artifical intellegnce into ECG data analysis represents a significant advancement for forecasting and detecting cardiac disorders. This research highlights how machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms can enhance the precision and accuracy of cardiac event prediction. While challenges like complexity and interpretability associated with these models exist, ongoing advancements in AI will over these issues, ensuring more effective solutions for patients globally. Future research should focus on the performance and applicability balance in refining AI models by ensuring seamless integration with healthcare systems worldwide.
```

##### [A practical ECG-based model for early identification of acute heart failure following acute myocardial infarction](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9)

```
## Abstract

Ischemic infarction of the acute myocardium (AMI) is a major cause of acute heart failure (AHF), which markedly increases mortality and readmission rates. One purpose of this study was to establish an ECG-based model for the early prediction of AHF risk in AMI patients. In a retrospective analysis, 301 patients admitted to the hospital (October 2022–March 2025) for AMI met the study criteria. With LASSO, we identified six predictors—prolonged QTc interval, abnormal Q wave, heart rate > 100 bpm, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) from routine echocardiography, male sex, and age 60–75 years—and entered them into a logistic regression nomogram. The model showed good discrimination (AUC = 0.84; internal validation AUC = 0.823) and was validated internally with 2000 bootstrapping iterations; external multicenter validation is planned to confirm its generalizability. The QTc interval and heart rate were positively correlated with Killip grade, and age and QRS duration were negatively correlated. However, P-wave duration and dispersion were negatively correlated with Killip grade. This ECG-based nomogram offers a simple, low-cost and practical AHF early identification tool for patients with a history of AMI, especially those in primary healthcare settings and those who live away from cities.

## Introduction

Acute myocardial infarction (AMI), otherwise known as heart attack, continues to be the leading cause of mortality worldwide. The development of acute heart failure(AHF)in the context of AMI has substantial implications for patient survival and the likelihood of rehospitalization, although mortality specifically due to myocardial infarction following medical interventions and pharmaceutical treatments is decreasing. Statistics indicate that approximately one-fifth to one-third of all individuals admitted to a hospital for myocardial infarction also experience AHF, which considerably prolongs the duration of hospitalization and increases the risk of readmission and death, especially in primary care facilities[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR1 "Allescher, J. et al. QRS fragmentation does not predict mortality in survivors of acute myocardial infarction. Clin. Cardiol. 47, e24218 (2024).").

As a routine examination method, electrocardiogram (ECG) plays an important role in reflecting the severity of myocardial injury and predicting late adverse outcomes. Recent studies have shown that certain ECG parameters are positively associated with the occurrence of AHF. For example, a prolonged QTc interval not only reflects electrical conduction disorders but also significantly increases[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR2 "Welten, S. et al. Prolongation of the QTc interval is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases: The Hoorn study. J. Electrocardiol. 80, 133–138 (2023).") the risk of heart failure after myocardial infarction. Fragmented QRS complex (fQRS) has shown good predictive efficacy[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR3 "Xu, Y. et al. Predicting efficacy of combined assessment with fragmented QRS and severely depressed heart rate variability on outcome of patients with acute myocardial infarction. Heart Vessels. 37, 239–249 (2022).") in myocardial infarction patients both with and without ST-segment elevation, and these results[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR4 "Türkmen, S., Bozkurt, M., Hoşoğlu, Y. & Göl, M. Significance of fragmented QRS and predictors of outcome in ST-elevation myocardial infarction. J. Res. Med. Sci. 29, 23 (2024).") have been confirmed by other scholars. In addition, QRS-T angle enlargement is often predictive of myocardial structural remodeling and instability of electrical activity, which often cause heartfailure or death[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR5 "Han, X. et al. Prognostic significance of QRS distortion and frontal QRS-T angle in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Int. J. Cardiol. 345, 1–6 (2021)."). Zorluet al.[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR6 "Zorlu, Ç., Açıkel, B., Ömür, S. E. & Frontal Plane QRS - T angle is a predictor of ventricular arrhythmia in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Ann. Noninvasive Electrocardiol. 30, e70062 (2025).") reported that the QRS-T angle is closely related to rehospitalization for chronic heart failure. Turkmen[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR4 "Türkmen, S., Bozkurt, M., Hoşoğlu, Y. & Göl, M. Significance of fragmented QRS and predictors of outcome in ST-elevation myocardial infarction. J. Res. Med. Sci. 29, 23 (2024).") also confirmed the important role of ECG parameters in predicting arrhythmia and left ventricular remodeling after myocardial infarction by analyzing QT dispersion and the Tp-e interval. Although Martínez-Sellés[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR7 "Martínez-Sellés, M. & Marina-Breysse, M. Current and future use of artificial intelligence in electrocardiography. J. Cardiovasc. Dev. Disease. 10  (4), 175 (2023).")et al. attempted to use artificial intelligence models to integrate multiple ECG features for risk prediction, several problems, such as computing platform dependence, dataset resources, and technical thresholds, must be solved before the clinical application of such models.

Therefore, multiple traditional 12-lead ECG parameters (e.g., the QTc interval, fQRS, QRS-T angle and Tp-e interval) were combined according to practical clinical requirements, and common biomarkers (e.g., general clinical data and the left ventricular ejection fraction) were selected via LASSO regression. A simple and clear structural nomogram model was then constructed to both achieve early identification of AHF. and quantify the risk of AHF in patients with myocardial infarction. The purpose of this study was to provide a set of practical and feasible risk assessment tools for primary hospitals and to promote the accurate hierarchical management of cardiovascular diseases.

## Results

### Comparison of baseline characteristics

Table [1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Tab1) displays the clinical and electrocardiographic data of 301 registered individuals with AMI grouped according to the presence or absence of AHF. Among the 301 registered individuals, 185 (61.5%) were in the AHF group, and 116 (38.5%) were in the non-acute heart failure (NAHF) group. A chi-square test or Mann‒Whitney U test was used to compare variables between the 2 groups according to the type of variable. The results revealed notable variations in a variety of clinical and ECG parameters. There were significantly more women in the AHF group (26.9%) than in the NAHF group (11.3%). Atrial fibrillation (14.6%) and fQRS (17.2%) were much more common in the AHF group than in the NAHF group. Moreover, abnormal Q waves, a history of smoking, low-voltage QRS and a prolonged QTc interval (> 460 ms) were more common in the AHF group than in the NAHF group (all _P_ < 0.05) and were closely related to AHF. Critically, the median LVEF in the AHF group, which was 47.0% [38.5, 51.7], was considerably lower than that in the NAHF group, which was 58.5% [56.2, 63.0] (_P_ = 0.05).

### Feature variable selection by LASSO regression analysis

The results of the LASSO regression analysis of all the clinical and ECG variables are shown in Fig. [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig2) and ten-fold cross-validation was used to determine the optimal regularization parameter λ for screening the variables with predictive value for AHF. In the figure, panel A shows the LASSO regression paths, with each curve representing the change trend of the regression coefficient of a variable at different λ values. As λ gradually increases, the penalty imposed by the model on the variables is strengthened, and the coefficients of most variables gradually approach 0, indicating that their contribution to the model is small. Panel B shows the average binomial deviation corresponding to different λ values obtained via cross-validation, with red dots representing the mean and gray error bars representing the standard error (min. = −3.9), as well as the simplest model parameter within a standard error range (λ.1 se = −3.3). Finally, the model corresponding to λ.1 se was selected to achieve the best generalizability and model simplification. At this λ value, there were 8 variables with nonzero coefficients, namely, sex, abnormal Q wave, left ventricular ejection fraction, heart rate, QTc interval, 60–75 years of age, fQRS and NT-proBNP, which were ultimately included in the subsequent multivariate regression model. These variables were considered key factors in predicting the occurrence of AHF.

### Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses

Univariate logistic regression revealed that a variety of clinical and ECG parameters were strongly related to AHF (Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Tab2)). Individuals with atrial fibrillation (OR = 4.710; 95% CI 1.780–16.270; _P_ = 0.005) had a significantly increased risk of AHF, which was related to the presence of a fragmented QRS complex (fQRS; OR = 3.210; 95% CI 1.440–8.150; _P_ = 0.007), an abnormal Q wave (OR = 2.910; 95% CI 1.800–4.730; _P_ < 0.001), and a low-voltage QRS complex (OR = 3.250; 95% CI 1.620–7.120; _P_ = 0.002). Moreover, a heart rate exceeding 100 beats per minute (OR = 6.210, 95% CI 2.390–21.240; _P_ = 0.001) substantially increased the risk of AHF. Conversely, the risk of AHF was significantly lower in females (OR = 0.350; 95% CI 0.170–0.650; _P_ = 0.002) as well as in those who consumed alcohol (OR = 0.410; 95% CI 0.230–0.710; _P_ = 0.002). The left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was a constant variable, and each unit increase in the LVEF was related to a significantly lower risk of AHF (OR = 0.860, 95% CI 0.820–0.890; _P_ < 0.001).

The aforementioned statistically significant variables were subsequently included in the multivariate logistic regression model for additional verification. The outcomes revealed that female sex (OR = 0.342; 95% CI 0.141–0.789; _P_ = 0.014) was still associated with a lower risk of AHF. An abnormal Q wave (OR = 2.390; 95% CI 1.316–4.402; _P_ = 0.004), a prolonged QTc interval (OR = 2.252; 95% CI 1.092–4.756; _P_ = 0.030), a heart rate exceeding 100 beats per minute (OR = 4.004; 95% CI 1.235–16.350; _P_ = 0.032), and age between 60 and 75 years (OR = 2.607; 95% CI 1.393–5.001; _P_ = 0.003) were independent risk factors for AHF. The LVEF remained significant in the multivariate model (OR = 0.864; 95% CI 0.819–0.906; _P_ < 0.001), indicating that it had a stable protective effect against AHF.

### Construction and interpretation of the nomogram model

The results of the multivariate logistic regression model constructed to predict the risk of AHF in patients with AMI are shown in Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig3). Five categorical variables (male sex, an abnormal Q wave, heart rate > 100 beats/min, a prolonged QTc interval, and age between 60 and 75 years) and one continuous variable (left ventricular ejection fraction, LVEF) were included in the model. In the nomogram, each variable corresponds to a scoring axis, and different risk scores are assigned according to its clinical situation. By adding the score for each variable to obtain the total score, the probability of AHF can be predicted according to the total number of points. As shown in the figure, the LVEF has the greatest weight in the model, and the range of the LVEF score is wide, indicating that it contributes the most to the prediction of AHF risk; this is followed by the QTc interval and heart rate, sex, Q wave abnormality, and age range. The probability range of the nomogram is 0.1–0.9, which indicates good risk stratification. Thus, the nomogram could help clinicians quickly evaluate the risk of AHF in individuals and aid early identification and precise treatment of AHF.

### Model discrimination ability and calibration performance evaluation

The discrimination ability and degree of calibration of the established model are shown in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig4). As shown in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig4)A, the area under the ROC curve (AUC) of the combined model was 0.8404, which was greater than that of any single indicator, including the fQRS (AUC = 0.5525), QTc interval (AUC = 0.7403), QT dispersion (QTd, AUC = 0.5715) and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF, AUC = 0.7712), indicating that this multivariate model had better discrimination power in identifying AHF. The red curve shows the LOWESS smooth fitting results, the blue points and error bars represent the actual incidence and 95% confidence intervals after grouping, and the gray dashed line represents the ideal calibration reference line. The results showed that the predicted probability of the model was highly consistent with the actual incidence, indicating good calibration of the model in effectively predicting the probability of disease in an individual and its strong potential for clinical application.

### Internal validation results of the model

The validation of the constructed prognostic paradigm, which performed well in terms of both discrimination and calibration, is shown in Fig. [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig5). As in Fig. [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig5)A, the AUC was equal to 0.823, with 95% confidence interval between 0.776 and 0.871, which implies that the model was likely to identify AHF. The blue shaded region denotes the 95% confidence interval, and the blue line drawn on the horizontal denotes the standard error of the sensitivity at the changing limits with most of the range being characterized by a high sensitivity in the model. Panel B gives the calibration curve of the model produced using the bootstrap method (bootstrapping iterations, B = 2000). The green line is the fitting outcome of the projected risk getting rid of the observed rate, the red dotted line is the obtained results, and the yellow dotted line is the perfect calibration curve. Overall, the calibration curve was very close to the ideal curve, indicating that the prognostic outcomes of the model were in good agreement with the real outcomes and that the model demonstrated high calibration accuracy.

### Clinical utility of the line chart according to decision curve analysis

In order to further confirm the practical usefulness of the developed model in clinical decision-making,we also conducted a decision curve analysis, which is shown in Fig. [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig6). The net benefit is illustrated in the vertical axis and the predicted risk threshold in the horizontal axis. The findings showed that, the model (orange curve) offered a higher net benefit as compared to the all intervention (blue curve) and no intervention (black baseline) under the range between around 0.13 and 0.65 threshold probability, showing that the model has good clinical use in this probability range. In particular, at the common decision-making risk range of 0.1–0.5, the model has always been more effective than the traditional treatment strategy, which suggests its applicability as an auxiliary tool to base clinical judgment on and contribute to reaching a more reasonable stratification and management of patients.

Figure [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig7) Violin plots showing the correlations of the Killip grade of AHF with electrocardiogram parameters.

### Correlation analysis of the Killip grade and electrocardiogram parameters in patients with AMI complicated with AHF

Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Tab3) shows the correlations between the Killip grade and six key clinical and computerized ECG parameters. Spearman correlation analysis revealed that the QTc interval (ρ = 0.392; _P_ = 0.001), heart rate (ρ = 0.391; _P_ = 0.001) and age (ρ = 0.265; _P_ = 0.003) were significantly positively correlated with the Killip grade, whereas the P-wave duration (ρ = −0.257; _P_ = 0.004), P-wave dispersion (ρ = −0.226; _P_ = 0.012) and QRS duration were weakly but still significantly correlated (ρ = 0.184; _P_ = 0.043). The distribution of each parameter in patients with diseases of different Killip grades is shown in violin plots in Fig. [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#Fig7). The results indicate that (A and B) the QTc interval and heart rate increased with increasing Killip grade, (C) age increased slightly at high Killip grades, and (D and E) the P-wave duration and P-wave dispersion decreased, but (F) the QRS duration slightly differed but tended to increase with increasing Killip grade. The above results suggest that some ECG parameters have potential reference value in determining the severity of heart failure.

## Discussion

With this study, we proposed a practical prediction model for heart failure in AMI patients, which is based mainly on ECG parameters that the physician can use every day. The model served to distinguish patients with HF better than other forms (AUC = 0.84) and was well calibrated, demonstrating that ECG-based functional assessment requires even less math than print-out from one bank machine. In addition, compared with the laboratory testing- and image-intensive factors that must be found in GRACE, TIMI, MAGGIC, or GWTG-HF, all the ECG-based models require rapid physical examination (cycles can last for less than 15 min at the bedside); therefore, this is another example of a simple and objective tool suitable for use by either one physician or a rural hospital. Although LVEF was retained as a core variable, the model remains primarily ECG-based to ensure practicality and rapid bedside applicability in primary and primary care settings. The model would handle this kind of low-technology medical task perfectly, although it might not be generalizable to other practices. The validity of the model is supported by its stable discrimination and calibration in internal validation, while its simple structure may facilitate application in settings where only routine ECG and echocardiographic data are available.

### Interpretation and comparison of the main findings

QTc interval prolongation is considered the most prominent cardiac risk indicator on electrocardiography. The QTc interval reflects the full duration of ventricular repolarization. If the QTc interval is prolonged, the conduction velocity of the myocardial action potential is uneven, which is an important cause of heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Weltenet al.[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR2 "Welten, S. et al. Prolongation of the QTc interval is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases: The Hoorn study. J. Electrocardiol. 80, 133–138 (2023).") reported that in patients with AMI, a QTc interval longer than 460 ms was significantly associated with left ventricular dysfunction and that the risk of heart failure increased by approximately 11% for every 10 ms of QTc interval prolongation. In contrast, in the present study, a clear cutoff value was not set, but the QTc interval was identified as a key variable via the LASSO method to better predict clinical risk. Abnormal Q waves usually indicate a large area of extensive myocardial necrosis, which is closely related to both ventricular dyskinesis and cardiac remodeling. Houdmont[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR12 "Houdmont, M. et al. Pathological Q waves at presentation of anterior ST segment elevation myocardial infarction predict heart failure: A Southeast Asian perspective. Coron. Artery Dis. 36, 378–383 (2025).") reported that in patients with AMI in the anterior wall, the depth of the Q wave was positively correlated with the left ventricular end-diastolic volume, which independently predicted the likelihood of heart failure during the waiting period. The results of this study are consistent with these findings and suggest that Q-wave characteristics can also be used to roughly assess risk in primary care settings. The increase in heart rate during AMI may result from sympathetic tension or from compensatory mechanisms of cardiac output, and tachycardia may induce heart failure. Chan[13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR13 "Chan, J. S. K. et al. Fragmented QRS is independently predictive of Long-Term adverse clinical outcomes in Asian patients hospitalized for heart failure: A retrospective cohort study. Front. Cardiovasc. Med. 8, 738417 (2021).") reported that decreased heart rate variability and elevated heart rate were strongly associated with in-hospital heart failure. In this study, the resting heart rate was used as a variable to show that the heart rate itself is a valuable indicator, even when heart rate variability monitoring devices are not used. Reduced left ventricular systolic function is directly related to heart failure, especially in patients experiencing AMI for the first time. Park[14](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR14 "Park, C. S. et al. Left ventricular ejection fraction 1 year after acute myocardial infarction identifies the benefits of the Long-Term use of β-Blockers: Analysis of data from the KAMIR-NIH registry. Circ. Cardiovasc. Interv. 14, e010159 (2021).") confirmed that an LVEF < 45% is the strongest predictor of major adverse cardiac events within a year. This study further highlights the irreplaceable role of cardiac ultrasound in predicting heart failure. Taken together, these findings emphasize that ECG findings predict heart failure risk following AMI; its low and slow approach differs from that of conventional medicine models that depend on biochemical or imaging data. Therefore, with its rapid low-cost features, ECG is very suitable for primary care setters inside the human body. Internal validation revealed that ECG was robust; external multicenter validation is planned to further assess its applicability.

### Interesting findings regarding other parameters

The given research uncovered a number of valuable observations, especially when it comes to defining how cardiac electrophysiological characteristics interplay with individual factors, including sex and age. To begin with, a fragmented QRS (fQRS), which is an indicator of myocardial scarring and changes in electrical conduction, is more effective predictor of AHF in the aftermath of AMI than other variables and it is more prevalent in men than in women, implying that it can detect sex-specific differences[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR15 "Luo, G. et al. The predictive value of fragmented QRS for cardiovascular events in acute myocardial infarction: A systematic review and Meta-Analysis. Front. Physiol. 11, 1027 (2020)."),[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR16 "Terho, H. K. et al. Prevalence and prognostic significance of fragmented QRS complex in middle-aged subjects with and without clinical or electrocardiographic evidence of cardiac disease. Am. J. Cardiol. 114, 141–147 (2014).") in structural remodelling. Additionally, extended Tp-e interval and QT dispersion are signs of higher heterogeneity in ventricular repolarization and repolarization measures are more predictive in women patients indicating that there is a sex difference between the electrophysiologic responses[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR17 "Iwahashi, N. et al. Global strain measured by Three-Dimensional speckle tracking echocardiography is a useful predictor for 10-Year prognosis after a first ST-Elevation acute myocardial infarction. Circ. J. 85, 1735–1743 (2021)."). Moreover, the predictive value of the electrophysiological parameters enhanced with the age, particularly in older patients, which implies that not only does the age contribute to the risk factor, but also it may modify the mode of risk assessment[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR18 "Hempel, P. et al. Explainable AI associates ECG aging effects with increased cardiovascular risk in a longitudinal population study. NPJ Digit. Med. 8, 25 (2025).") by influencing the expression of the electrophysiological parameters. Interestingly, a combination of multiple ECG parameters was better than any and one variable in predicting heart failure and that reinforce the possibility of multidimensional analysis of electrical signals. Nonetheless, certain conventional clinical variables (like atrial fibrillation or mere heart rate) do not predict as well which again demonstrates the benefits[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR19 "Lee, M. S. et al. Artificial intelligence applied to electrocardiogram to rule out acute myocardial infarction: The ROMIAE multicentre study. Eur. Heart J. 46, 1917–1929 (2025).") of electrophysiological variables in personalized risk evaluation. The reason why the risk in the 60–75 years group was apparently higher than in the 75 years group could be due to cohort-specific sampling and this pattern needs to be verified in larger and externally validated populations.

The study did not directly investigate the issue of P-wave dispersion in patients; however, the related literature indicates that it might have a predictive value. Yang[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR20 "Yang, N. et al. The role of P-Wave variables in enhancing prediction of New-Onset atrial fibrillation in patients with acute myocardial infarction. Ann. Noninvasive Electrocardiol. 30, e70041 (2025).") stated that dispersion of P-wave exceeded 40 ms can predict heart failure following AMI, which might be associated with heart failure induced by atrial fibrillation. The implication of these findings is that variations in the dispersion of P-wave may be added to future models in order to enhance sensitivity. The parameters were not included in this study, regarding ST-segment changes, although Kazemi[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR21 "Kazemi, E. et al. The prognostic effect of ST-elevation in lead aVR on coronary artery disease, and outcome in acute coronary syndrome patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur. J. Med. Res. 27, 302 (2022).") found out that an ST shift in aVR lead could be used to predict left ventricular dysfunction in multivescular disease patients. According to Siren et al.[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR22 "Sirén, M. et al. The prognostic significance of single-lead ST-segment resolution in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction patients treated with primary PCI - A substudy of the randomized TOTAL trial. Am. Heart J. 269, 149–157 (2024)."), the rate of new or progressive heart failure after incomplete ST-segment resolution after PCI was higher in the study by Siren et al., which indicates that ST resolution is a useful predictor of postinfarction outcomes, and continuous ECG monitoring can aid in improving early risk identification. This study did not determine the Tp-e interval, although Ozbek[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR23 "Özbek, S. C. & Sökmen, E. Usefulness of Tp-Te interval and Tp-Te/QT ratio in the prediction of ventricular arrhythmias and mortality in acute STEMI patients undergoing fibrinolytic therapy. J. Electrocardiol. 56, 100–105 (2019).") reported that the increase in the Tp-e interval indicates dysregulation of the compensatory mechanisms and is a significant predictor of ACS after AMI. Gallowayet al.[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR24 "Galloway, C. D. et al. Development and validation of a Deep-Learning model to screen for hyperkalemia from the electrocardiogram. JAMA Cardiol. 4, 428–436 (2019).") developed a T-wave alternation algorithm on the basis of the images of electrocardiogram (ECG) and deep learning models and proposed that T-wave change could be used to indicate heart failure even in cases where there are no severe structural alterations.

The present study also revealed that the Killip grade was significantly correlated with ECG parameters such as the QTc interval, heart rate, and P-wave characteristics, indicating its potential value in the assessment of AHF. With increasing Killip grade, the QTc interval also increased, which is consistent with the findings of El Amrawy et al.[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR25 "El Amrawy, A. M. et al. QTc interval prolongation impact on in-hospital mortality in acute coronary syndromes patients using artificial intelligence and machine learning. Egypt. Heart J. 76, 149 (2024)."). reported that prolongation of the QTc interval significantly predicts a higher Killip grade and a higher risk of in-hospital mortality in STEMI patients. Killip grade was also positively related to heart rate and Jensenet al.[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR26 "Jensen, M. T. et al. Heart rate at admission is a predictor of in-hospital mortality in patients with acute coronary syndromes: Results from 58 European hospitals: The European hospital benchmarking by outcomes in acute coronary syndrome processes study. Eur. Heart J. Acute Cardiovasc. Care. 7, 149–157 (2018).") affirmed that higher heart rate is an independent predictor of higher Killip grade and poor outcomes. Also, the duration of P-wave shortened, and the conductivity declined with gradual Killip grade, which could indicate atrioventricular conduction remodeling. These findings are indirectly supported by the suggestion of Bulluck et al.[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR27 "Bulluck, H. et al. Independent predictors of cardiac mortality and hospitalization for heart failure in a Multi-Ethnic Asian ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction population treated by primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Sci. Rep. 9, 10072 (2019).") that electrophysiological and imaging parameters combined can enhance the prediction power of the Killip grade. The Killip grade and QRS duration were poorly correlated in this study, but Gabaldon-Perezi et al.[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-40600-9#ref-CR28 "Gabaldón-Pérez, A. et al. Prognostic value of cardiac magnetic resonance early after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction in older patients. Age Ageing. 51(11), afac248 (2022).") have found that flow disturbances in patients with Killip grade I-II disease can also have severe complications pointing to the fact that electrocardiographic abnormalities also can predict patients with low Killip grades.
```
