```
(2006)."),[48](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR48 "Wannamethee, S. G., Shaper, A. G. & Ebrahim, S. Respiratory function and risk of stroke. Stroke 26(11), 2004–2010. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.26.11.2004
(1995)."), Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19)[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR34 "Elkind, M. S. V., Boehme, A. K., Smith, C. J., Meisel, A. & Buckwalter, M. S. Infection as a stroke risk factor and determinant of outcome after stroke. Stroke 51(10), 3156–3168. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/STROKEAHA.120.030429
(2020)."), and atrial fibrillation[49](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR49 "Wolf, P. A., Abbott, R. D. & Kannel, W. B. Atrial fibrillation as an independent risk factor for stroke: the framingham study. Stroke 22(8), 983–988. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.22.8.983
(1991)."). These respiratory complications have all been proven to be risk factors of stroke[37](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR37 "Hart, C. L., Hole, D. J. & Smith, G. D. Comparison of risk factors for stroke incidence and stroke mortality in 20 years of follow-up in men and women in the renfrew/paisley study in scotland. Stroke 31(8), 1893–1896. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.31.8.1893
(2000)."),[42](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR42 "O’Leary, D. H. et al. Carotid-artery intima and media thickness as a risk factor for myocardial infarction and stroke in older adults. N. Engl. J. Med. 340(1), 14–22. 
https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199901073400103
(1999)."). This paves the way for using respiratory features as predictors of stroke-risk.

It remains unknown which signal or feature contributes the most in stroke-risk prediction, as AI models do not provide an in-depth analysis of how the model reached its output decision. Therefore, recent studies applied eXplainable AI (XAI) to provide interpretable results so humans can produce more explainable models[51](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR51 "Dwivedi, R. et al. Explainable ai (xai): Core ideas, techniques, and solutions. ACM Comput. Surv. 55(9), 194. 
https://doi.org/10.1145/3561048
(2023)."), bridging the gap between an AI model’s decision-making process and human comprehension[52](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR52 "Das, A., & Rad, P. Opportunities and challenges in explainable artificial intelligence (xai): A survey (2020) 
https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2006.11371
."). This is especially important in the healthcare field where accurate real-time diagnosis and user trust are both important[53](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR53 "Mehdiyev, N., Majlatow, M. & Fettke, P. Interpretable and explainable machine learning methods for predictive process monitoring: a systematic literature review. Artif. Intell. Rev. 58(12), 378. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11399-0
(2025)."). Some of the prominent XAI techniques are SHAP[54](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR54 "Lundberg, S., & Lee, S.-I. A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions (2017). 
https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1705.07874
."), LIME[55](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR55 "Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S. & Guestrin, C. Why Should I Trust You? Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier. Assoc. Comput. Mach. 
https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939778
(2016)."), and Anchors[56](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR56 "Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S., & Guestrin, C. Anchors: High-precision model-agnostic explanations. In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 32(1) (2018) 
https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v32i1.11491
."). XAI was only applied to stroke-risk prediction models trained on individual signals[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR20 "Islam, S., Hussain, I., Rahman, M., Park, S. J. & Hossain, M. Explainable artificial intelligence model for stroke prediction using eeg signal. Sensors 22, 9859. 
https://doi.org/10.3390/s22249859
(2022)."),[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR21 "Hussain, I. & Jany, R. Interpreting stroke-impaired electromyography patterns through explainable artificial intelligence. Sensors 24, 1392. 
https://doi.org/10.3390/s24051392
(2024)."), failing to determine which signal plays the most critical role when several signals are used simultaneously.

SHAP, LIME, and Anchors are all post-hoc explainers, which means that they are used after the model is trained, and thus do not faithfully represent the true internal mechanisms of the model. However, they offer understandable insights into the model’s decisions for human users. Additionally, they are simple to implement and do not compromise model accuracy or performance, which is crucial in this field. In contrast, intrinsically interpretable models generate more faithful representations of a model’s internal mechanisms but are constrained by practical restrictions such as linearity, monotonicity, additivity, and sparsity. Current intrinsically interpretable models are typically simple and thus lack the flexibility to capture complex relationships that naturally occur in real-world applications[53](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR53 "Mehdiyev, N., Majlatow, M. & Fettke, P. Interpretable and explainable machine learning methods for predictive process monitoring: a systematic literature review. Artif. Intell. Rev. 58(12), 378. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11399-0
(2025)."),[57](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR57 "Kruschel, S. et al. Challenging the performance-interpretability trade-off: An evaluation of interpretable machine learning models. Bus. Inf. Syst. Eng. 1, 1. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s12599-024-00922-2
(2025)."). Post-hoc explainers also have the advantage of being model-agnostic, allowing them to be used even when the model becomes more complex, for example, with the availability of additional data.

The variability in outputs across different XAI models have raised the question of which model’s interpretations are the most reliable, demonstrating the need for a standardized XAI evaluation metric that is objective and can be experimentally validated[58](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR58 "Kadir, M.A., Mosavi, A., & Sonntag, D. Evaluation metrics for xai: A review, taxonomy, and practical applications. In 2023 IEEE 27th International Conference on Intelligent Engineering Systems (INES), pp. 000111–000124. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/INES59282.2023.10297629
."). Elgezawy et al. proposed an XAI evaluation metric for classification: the Model Explanation Metric Consensus (MEMC)[59](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR59 "El-gezawy, A., Abd elkader, H. & Ali, A. A new xai evaluation metric for classification. IJCI. Int. J. Comput. Inf. 10, 58–62. 
https://doi.org/10.21608/ijci.2023.236156.1132
(2023)."). The XAI technique with the highest MEMC value is the most reliable. While this metric has not been applied widely, it acts as a fair evaluation metric that can be used.

In this study, we aim to address the research gaps in this field by offering the following contributions:

1. 1.
    
    We integrated respiratory signals for the first time into a multi-modal stroke-risk prediction model alongside ECG, EMG, and blood pressure (BP) and discovered their importance in stroke-risk prediction, guiding future research into exploring the role of respiratory signals on stroke-risk and other cardiovascular diseases.
    
2. 2.
    
    We applied three state-of-the-art XAI techniques namely LIME, SHAP, and Anchors to interpret the model’s decisions and identify the most influential features in stroke-risk prediction and found that CO-derived features are key factors in stroke-risk prediction, guiding clinicians and medical experts to study the physiology of these signals further, and study the physiological aspect of these features.
    
3. 3.
    
    We evaluated the reliability of these XAI techniques using the MEMC to determine which explainer offers the most trustworthy results, making this the first study to evaluate the use of XAI in this field.
    

The paper is structured as follows: “[Methods](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Sec2)” describes the data that was used in this study and the steps taken to conduct the experiment to allow for reproducibility. The results of the experiment are analysed in “[Results](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Sec16)” and discusses them in Sect. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Sec25), alongside the limitations and future work. Finally, “[Conclusion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Sec26)” contains the conclusion which outlines the clinical significance of this work.

## Results

### Data analysis

Subjects with missing signals or incomplete tests were excluded from this study, leaving 64 subjects, 37 of which suffered a stroke. From the 10 minutes of data collected, the signals were trimmed to 9.5 minutes, as some subjects had missing data in the last 30 seconds. ECG and EMG were down-sampled to 500 Hz to match the other signals so that the extracted features can be fairly fused together. Demographic information regarding the remaining subjects is seen in Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab2). To determine whether the two groups come from the same population, independent _t_-tests were conducted using the IBM SPSS Statistics software on Age, BMI, Height, and Mass, with = 0.05. The resulting _p_-values are in Table [2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab2). Since all the _p_-values are greater than , there is no significant difference between the two groups.

### Optimal window size and overlap percentage

The performance of the proposed model when tested with different window sizes and overlap values is in Fig. [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig3). The worst performance was achieved when a window size of 1 second was used, where the resulting accuracies are less than 66% for all overlap values. Increasing the window size increased accuracy generally, and this was seen in all overlap values. However, the highest accuracy of 79.87% was achieved when using a window size of 14 seconds and an overlap of 75%. The window size of 14 seconds was also found to be the most effective in classifying breathing disorders[63](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR63 "Fekr, A. R., Janidarmian, M., Radecka, K. & Zilic, Z. Respiration disorders classification with informative features for m-health applications. IEEE J. Biomed. Health Inform. 20(3), 733–747. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/jbhi.2015.2458965
(2016)."), yet was achieved when overlap was set to 90%. Therefore, a window size of 14 seconds and an overlap of 75% were used for this study.

### Model evaluation

Using the optimal window size and overlap values found above, we performed a grid search to find the optimal hyperparameter values for the model. It was found that increasing the number of layers degraded our model’s performance. Therefore, a single-layer perceptron was used. The highest accuracy of 84.91% was obtained when Adam optimizer was used and the model was trained for 700 epochs, with a learning rate of 0.03 and a batch size of 128. The model was tested with and without respiratory signals to assess their significance. The mean accuracy of the proposed model was 84.91% ± 5.48% with respiratory signals and 59.36% ± 12.15% without them, as shown in Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig4). We conducted a _t_-test at = 0.05 and found the _p_-value to be 0.0061, which is less than . Therefore, there is significant difference between the two cases.

To validate the model’s performance, we compared our proposed model with recent ML and DL models. We reproduced each study’s method as closely as possible while using the same dataset discussed in “[Dataset](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Sec3)”[60](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR60 "Goldberger, A. L. et al. Physiobank, physiotoolkit, and physionet: components of a new research resource for complex physiologic signals. Circulation 101(23), 215–20. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/01.cir.101.23.e215
(2000)."). For techniques relying on time-series data[12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR12 "Choi, Y.A., Park, S.J., Jun, J.A., Pyo, C.S., Cho, K.H., Lee, H.S., & Yu, J.H. Deep learning-based stroke disease prediction system using real-time bio signals. Sensors (Basel) 21(13). 
https://doi.org/10.3390/s21134269
(2021)."),[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR15 "Yu, J. et al. Ai-based stroke disease prediction system using real-time electromyography signals. Appl. Sci. 10(19), 6791. 
https://doi.org/10.3390/app10196791
(2020)."),[16](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR16 "Yu, J., Park, S., Kwon, S. H., Cho, K. H. & Lee, H. Ai-based stroke disease prediction system using ecg and ppg bio-signals. IEEE Access 10, 43623–43638. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2022.3169284
(2022)."), we used the raw signals. For other studies using features[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR19 "Bouazizi, S. & Ltifi, H. Enhancing accuracy and interpretability in eeg-based medical decision making using an explainable ensemble learning framework application for stroke prediction. Decis. Support Syst. 178, 114126. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dss.2023.114126
(2024)."),[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR26 "Islam, R., Debnath, S., & Palash, T.I. Predictive analysis for risk of stroke using machine learning techniques. In 2021 International Conference on Computer, Communication, Chemical, Materials and Electronic Engineering (IC4ME2), pp. 1–4. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/IC4ME253898.2021.9768524
.") and ML methods, we extracted the features in “[Feature extraction](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Sec7)”. The results of each model’s performance on the unseen test set are in Fig. [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig5), where our proposed model achieved the highest accuracy of 88.29% with respiratory signals. Incorporating respiratory signals generally improved performance, highlighting their value in stroke-risk prediction. Only a few models, namely BiLSTM, E-ESN, and XGBoost, performed better without respiratory signals, though the differences were small and the performance remained poor. On the other hand, adding respiratory signals improved accuracy by over 10% for the Voting Classifier[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR26 "Islam, R., Debnath, S., & Palash, T.I. Predictive analysis for risk of stroke using machine learning techniques. In 2021 International Conference on Computer, Communication, Chemical, Materials and Electronic Engineering (IC4ME2), pp. 1–4. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/IC4ME253898.2021.9768524
."), Logistic Regression, KNN, and our model.

### XAI

#### SHAP

The SHAP global summary plot showing the 12 most important features, 8 of which are derived from respiratory signals (CO and flow rate), is in Fig. [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig6). According to SHAP, the most important feature is the CO mean which changed the model’s predicted probability by 0.15 on average. The CO variance and BP mean (abp_mean) were also key predictors and changed the model’s output by approximately 0.14, on average.

The SHAP summary plot in Fig. [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig7) shows: (1) the direction in which these features influenced the model’s prediction (stroke or non-stroke), and (2) which values of these features (low or high) caused the model to move in that direction. A high CO mean increased the probability of predicting stroke by up to 0.75, and a low value decreased this probability by up to 0.75. Additionally, a high abp_mean and a low CO variance were influential factors in predicting stroke.

Local SHAP plots for a stroke and a non-stroke subject are seen in Fig. [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig8). The plots start at _E_[_f_(_X_)] which represents the model’s baseline output for all subjects and is calculated using Eq. ([27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Equ27)). Each feature’s SHAP value is then added to _E_[_f_(_X_)] to achieve the final prediction for that subject, as in Eq. ([26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Equ26)). Since _E_[_f_(_X_)] is larger than 0.5, the model’s baseline prediction is a stroke, this bias may have occurred as there are more stroke subjects in the training dataset than control.

For the non-stroke subject in Fig. [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig8), the least important features referred to as “124 other features” when combined decreased the predicted probability of stroke by 0.41. The largest contribution towards predicting non-stroke was caused by the CO mean value of -1.128, which reduced the model’s probability of predicting a stroke by 0.45. This is consistent with the global SHAP findings in Fig. [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig7). The second most influential feature was the ECG2 skewness with a value of -2.327 which increased the prediction of a stroke by 0.32. However, after adding all SHAP values to the base value, _E_[_f_(_X_)], the final predicted probability is 0.118, resulting in a non-stroke prediction. For the stroke subject, the low values of 0.281 and -1.422 for the BP mean and CO variance, respectively, were the most influential in causing the model to predict the stroke class, with SHAP values of 0.21 and 0.2, respectively. Finally, the SHAP values combined for this subject resulted in a final probability of 0.833, leading to a stroke prediction.

#### LIME

The LIME global plot was created by aggregating the absolute LIME weights of each feature across all test instances[55](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR55 "Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S. & Guestrin, C. Why Should I Trust You? Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier. Assoc. Comput. Mach. 
https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939778
(2016)."). The 12 most important features according to LIME, are in Fig. [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig9), where the three most important features are the amount of zero crossings from CO (co2_zero_crossings), the mean flow rate, and the CO variance.

The LIME explanations for a stroke and a non-stroke subject are in Fig. [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig10). For the non-stroke subject, the amount of zero crossings by BP (abp_zero_crossings) being less than or equal to -0.03 contributed the most to predicting a non-stroke with an assigned weight of 0.198. The three next most contributing features towards correctly predicting non-stroke were the ECG1 mean energy, CO zero crossings, and the ECG1 FFT energy. For the stroke subject, the ECG1 high frequency power being greater than 0.08 had the largest positive weight, i.e. contributed the most towards the prediction of stroke. The other influential features in correctly predicting stroke for this subject were the means of the ECG2, ECG1, and EMG1.

#### Anchors

To create a global plot from Anchors, we counted how often each feature appears in a rule for all predictions (Fig. [11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig11)). This was done following SHAP’s and LIME’s method of computing global importance, which is to aggregate the feature importance of each feature[54](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR54 "Lundberg, S., & Lee, S.-I. A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions (2017). 
https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1705.07874
."),[55](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR55 "Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S. & Guestrin, C. Why Should I Trust You? Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier. Assoc. Comput. Mach. 
https://doi.org/10.1145/2939672.2939778
(2016)."). The CO mean was the most influential feature according to Anchors, appearing 61 times as part of an Anchor. The second and third most important features were the EMG2 median and ECG2 mean, respectively.

The anchors for a non-stroke and a stroke subject are seen in Fig. [12](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig12). For the non-stroke prediction, the anchor identified three rules that when satisfied, were sufficient for the model to classify the subject as non-stroke: a flow rate skewness greater than 1.09, an ECG2 kurtosis greater than 0.42, and a flow rate variance greater than 1.28. The corresponding feature values for this subject were 1.44, 0.69, and 2.02, respectively. On the other hand, the set of rules for predicting stroke for the stroke subject was a low EMG2 median and BP 3rd moment.

#### XAI evaluation

The three most influential features according to each XAI model are in Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab3). SHAP and Anchors agreed that the CO mean was the most important feature. SHAP and LIME also agreed on CO variance as one of the most important feature, although the order differs. Each XAI model identified at least one feature derived from respiratory signals as important. The top three most important features according to LIME are all derived from respiratory signals. Only Anchors identified ECG and EMG features as some of the most important.

As seen in Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab3), the three XAI models produced different results, thus creating doubts regarding which results to follow. To address this, we find the most reliable model by selecting the one with the highest MEMC value. To calculate the MEMC of each XAI model, the 3 most important features according to each model must be removed in order, and the new metrics must be computed each time a feature is removed, as in Eq. ([31](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Equ31)). In Tables [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab4), [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab5) and [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab6), the metrics after removing the most important features are observed for SHAP, LIME, and Anchors, respectively. Removing the three most important features according to each XAI model noticeably degraded performance. Removing the CO mean, which is the most important feature according to SHAP and Anchors, decreased the accuracy by 1.88% (Tables [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab4) and [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab6)). On the other hand, removing the CO zero crossings which is the most important feature according to LIME, reduced the accuracy by only 0.63% (Table [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab5)). Removing the two most important features according to the three XAI models decreased the accuracy by 2.71% for SHAP, 1.88% for LIME, and 2.13% for Anchors. Lastly, removing the three most important features decreased the accuracy by 3.19% for SHAP, 1.88% for LIME, and 2.03% for Anchors.

The MEMC for each XAI model is seen in Fig. [13](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig13). The results show that SHAP is the most reliable XAI model as observed by the highest MEMC value. Therefore, the three most important features in our model are the same ones identified by SHAP, which are the CO mean, CO variance, and the BP mean.

## Discussion

The first step was to find the optimal window size along with the overlap percentage, which we found to be 14 seconds and 75% overlap. Physiological signals such as ECG, blood pressure, EMG, and respiration are quasi-periodic and inherently noisy. Very short windows are highly sensitive to noise, leading to unstable time- and frequency-domain feature estimates. When only a single cycle of a biological signal is captured, extracted features may be dominated by local irregularities rather than representative signal behavior. On the other hand, longer windows may introduce redundant information and reduce temporal sensitivity and dilute transient but informative patterns relevant to the classification task. With a window size of 14 seconds, at least 3 breathing cycles were captured, and the model could relate these cycles with the other signals. This also means that the model prioritised capturing the respiratory signals’ cycles, also proving that they are important in this task. Even when enough cycles of ECG, EMG, and BP were captured, the model still performed the best when a few breathing cycles were captured. A recent study has also demonstrated that 14-second windows are effective for respiratory disorder diagnosis[63](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR63 "Fekr, A. R., Janidarmian, M., Radecka, K. & Zilic, Z. Respiration disorders classification with informative features for m-health applications. IEEE J. Biomed. Health Inform. 20(3), 733–747. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/jbhi.2015.2458965
(2016)."). Capturing multiple cycles reduces the influence of noisy individual breaths and yields more stable physiological representations. Additionally, the optimal window size depends on the classification task. Longer windows have been shown to be preferable for tasks such as apnea detection[83](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR83 "Castillo-Escario, Y., Werthen-Brabants, L., Groenendaal, W., Deschrijver, D., & Jane, R. Convolutional neural networks for apnea detection from smartphone audio signals: Effect of window size. In 2022 44th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC), pp. 666– 669 ( 2022). 
https://doi.org/10.1109/EMBC48229.2022.9871396
.") or certain ECG analyses[84](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR84 "Lee, S., Lee, S., Yun, S., Ryu, S. & Jeong, I. C. Toward real-world ecg-based human activity recognition: Optimal window size and subject-independent 1-d cnn approach. IEEE Sens. J. 25(16), 31754–31768. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/JSEN.2025.3581211
(2025)."), where prolonged temporal context is required. For our task, it was found that shorter window sizes are optimal, but not too short, such as less than 5 seconds. While smaller window sizes could be used for blood pressure, ECG, and EMG, they cannot capture a whole breathing cycle, which is why our model performed poorly at smaller window sizes. The use of a 75% overlap further improves robustness by reducing the step size between windows, smoothing transitions, mitigating the impact of noise, and increasing the effective number of training samples without altering the underlying physiological content.

All models were tested with and without the incorporation of respiratory signals, and including these signals almost always increased the accuracy of the model (Fig. [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig5)). Further validation with the _t_-test solidified the significance of adding respiratory signals on the model’s accuracy (Fig. [4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig4)). Another key observation is that the single perceptron model, using signal features as input, outperformed state-of-the-art ML and DL models (Fig. [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig5)). This may be due to the small data set, where deeper models (LSTM variants) tended to overfit and performed poorly, while shallow models (decision tree) underfit by failing to capture the non-linear feature relationships of the dataset. As a result, our proposed model struck a good balance between the two and outperformed the other models. Table [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab7) shows the advantages and limitations of the proposed model against state-of-the-art methods, as well as the use of XAI.

The model used in this study is a single-layer perceptron with 126 input features and no hidden layers, resulting in minimal computational overhead. Each forward-backward pass per sample requires roughly 254 operations. With a batch size of 128, 1908 samples (after windowing), and 700 training epochs, the total number of operations is approximately . The time complexity of our model is therefore O(), scaling linearly with the number of samples (), epochs (), and features (), demonstrating the model’s efficiency.

After windowing, we extracted eighteen statistical and frequency-domain features as shown in “[Feature extraction](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Sec7)”, from each of the seven signals. These features, such as mean, variance, higher-order moments, and spectral descriptors, capture the temporal and spectral properties of each signal while remaining robust to noise and local variability. Using the same feature set across signals provides computational efficiency, simplifies the pipeline, and allows consistent comparison and fusion of multimodal data. Statistical and frequency-domain features have been effective in identifying abnormal physiological patterns without requiring explicit waveform segmentation or signal-specific morphological analysis[72](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR72 "Rekanos, I. T. & Hadjileontiadis, L. J. An iterative kurtosis-based technique for the detection of nonstationary bioacoustic signals. Signal Process. 86(12), 3787–3795. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sigpro.2006.03.020.
(2006) (Special Section: Multimodal Human-Computer Interfaces)."),[73](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR73 "Chua, K. C., Chandran, V., Acharya, U. R. & Lim, C. M. Application of higher order statistics/spectra in biomedical signals-a review. Med. Eng. Phys. 32(7), 679–689. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.medengphy.2010.04.009
(2010)."),[74](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR74 "Phinyomark, A., Phukpattaranont, P. & Limsakul, C. Feature reduction and selection for emg signal classification. Expert Syst. Appl. 39(8), 7420–7431. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2012.01.102
(2012)."),[85](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR85 "Ghorbani Afkhami, R., Azarnia, G. & Tinati, M. A. Cardiac arrhythmia classification using statistical and mixture modeling features of ecg signals. Pattern Recogn. Lett. 70, 45–51. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patrec.2015.11.018
(2016)."),[86](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR86 "Alotaiby, T. N., Alrshoud, S. R., Alshebeili, S. A. & Aljafar, L. M. Ecg-based subject identification using statistical features and random forest. J. Sensors 2019(1), 6751932. 
https://doi.org/10.1155/2019/6751932
(2019) 
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1155/2019/6751932
."),[87](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR87 "Kaya, Y., Pehlivan, H. & Tenekeci, M. Effective ecg beat classification using higher order statistic features and genetic feature selection. Biomed. Res. India 28, 7594–7603 (2017).").

Using a larger feature set also helped the model in predicting more accurately. In the SHAP waterfall plot for the non-stroke subject (Fig. [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig8)), several features with high SHAP values increased the probability of a stroke prediction by at least 0.10. Nevertheless, the 124 least important features decreased the probability of stroke by 0.41 when combined. This shows how using a larger feature set helped the model reach the correct prediction (non-stroke). The inclusion of frequency-domain features also helped in improving the model’s accuracy for the stroke subject (Fig. [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig8)), where the ECG2 spectral entropy increased the model’s confidence in predicting the true class. This was also seen for the non-stroke subject in the LIME local plot (Fig. [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig10)), where the ECG1 FFT energy contributed to the model reaching the correct decision.

The results of the XAI models are in Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab3). The mean feature was the most common extracted feature, appearing five times in Table [3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Tab3). The three most important features according to each XAI model are all statistical features showing them as better differentiators of the two classes compared to frequency-domain features. The results also highlight how all three XAI models identified respiratory signals’ contribution towards stroke-risk prediction compared to the rest of the signals used, specifically CO, where five of the most important features according to all XAI models are derived from it. This shows that CO was an important signal in predicting stroke-risk. One study[88](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR88 "Jiang, D. et al. Normal variations in brain oxygen extraction fraction are partly attributed to differences in end-tidal co2. J. Cereb. Blood Flow Metab. 40(7), 1492–1500. 
https://doi.org/10.1177/0271678x19867154
(2020).") discovered that CO is closely related to cerebral oxygen extraction fraction, which is an important physiological index of the brain’s oxygen consumption and supply, and thus a potential biomarker for stroke. SHAP, which was identified as the most reliable XAI model by the MEMC, determined that the CO mean, CO variance, and BP mean were the most important features. In other words, the mean values of BP and CO, and the dispersion of CO values from their average are key determinants in predicting whether the subject is at risk of stroke. Moreover, only Anchors identified ECG or EMG features as key predictors. The ECG carries extensive information about cardiovascular health, which likely explains why the mean was considered important[89](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR89 "Kamaruddin, N.H., Murugappan, M., & Omar, M.I. Early prediction of cardiovascular diseases using ecg signal: Review. In 2012 IEEE Student Conference on Research and Development (SCOReD), pp. 48– 53 ( 2012). 
https://doi.org/10.1109/SCOReD.2012.6518609
."). For EMG, the median was highlighted as a significant feature. While similar to the mean, the median is more robust to outliers and less sensitive to extreme values[90](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR90 "Rousseeuw, P. J. & Hubert, M. Robust statistics for outlier detection. WIREs Data Min. Knowl. Discov. 1(1), 73–79. 
https://doi.org/10.1002/widm.2
(2011) 
https://wires.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/widm.2
."), which is relevant given the inherently noisy nature of EMG signals. This feature’s importance is also consistent with the clinical role of EMG in assessing muscle pain[91](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR91 "Mian Qaisar, S., Nisar, H. & Subasi, A. Advances in Non-Invasive Biomedical Signal Sensing and Processing with Machine Learning. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-23239-8
(2023)."), a condition commonly observed in stroke patients[92](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR92 "Lin, C.-H. et al. Muscle pain intensity and pressure pain threshold changes in different periods of stroke patients. Am. J. Phys. Med. Rehab. 93(4), 299–309. 
https://doi.org/10.1097/phm.0000000000000003
(2014).").

According to the SHAP plot with feature effects (Fig. [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#Fig7)), a high CO mean is a key predictor of stroke-risk. This finding is backed by a study which found that an increased level of carbon dioxide, known as hypercarbia, is a stroke-risk factor[93](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR93 "Vlisides, P. E. et al. Carbon dioxide, blood pressure, and perioperative stroke: A retrospective case-control study. Anesthesiology 137(4), 434–445. 
https://doi.org/10.1097/aln.0000000000004354
(2022)."). Additionally, the SHAP plot found that a high BP mean is a key predictor for stroke-risk. This is also supported by literature as high BP, or hypertension, is a major risk factor of stroke[94](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR94 "Alloubani, A., Saleh, A. & Abdelhafiz, I. Hypertension and diabetes mellitus as a predictive risk factors for stroke. Diabetes Metab. Syndr. 12(4), 577–584. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsx.2018.03.009
(2018)."),[95](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR95 "Alter, M., Friday, G., Lai, S. M., O’Connell, J. & Sobel, E. Hypertension and risk of stroke recurrence. Stroke 25(8), 1605–1610. 
https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.25.8.1605
(1994)."). The SHAP plot also found that a low CO variance, or CO signals with little dispersion from the average are a major predictor of stroke-risk. So, a steadier CO signal with less aggressive movement is linked to stroke-risk. This is probably because subjects at risk of stroke had more decrements in respiratory capacity and control than subjects not at risk of stroke[38](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR38 "Hawari, F. I. et al. Respiratory health and quality of life in young exclusive, habitual smokers - a comparison of waterpipe smokers, cigarette smokers and non-smokers. Int. J. Chronic Obstruct. Pulm. Dis. 14, 1813–1824. 
https://doi.org/10.2147/COPD.S205050
(2019)."), which explains why stroke subjects have fewer fluctuations in their CO signals. On the other hand, non-stroke subjects who are still able to use their respiratory capacity to their full capacity are able to attain larger, more rapid changes in their CO signals, leading to a higher CO variance. Nevertheless, these results should be further studied by medical experts to gain deeper insights.

_Limitations_: One limitation of this study is the lack of publicly available stroke datasets, which restrict the ability to validate the proposed model on external data. Another limitation is the use of a post-hoc explainer, which remains controversial as some researchers argue that explanations should be derived intrinsically rather than after the model is trained[96](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR96 "Swamy, V., Frej, J., & Käser, T. The Future of Human-centric eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) Is Not Post-hoc Explanations. 
https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2307.00364
(2023)."). Additionally, while LIME and Anchors are local explainers, they were applied globally by aggregating their explanations across all test cases. Although this was feasible due to the small test sample size, it may become impractical for larger datasets where such aggregation could be time-consuming.

_Future Work_: Future work can build upon the findings of this study. Notably, the models developed and used in other studies did not perform similarly on this dataset, despite achieving high accuracy on their datasets (>98%). This emphasizes the need to develop models with better generalizability that can reproduce strong performance across different datasets. This is a common challenge in this field. Chen et al. conducted a systematic review of 41 studies that used ML algorithms to build prognostic prediction models for ischemic stroke and 88% of these studies did not validate their models on external datasets[97](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR97 "Chen, M. et al. Systematic review of machine learning applied to the secondary prevention of ischemic stroke. J. Med. Syst. 48(1), 8. 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10916-023-02020-4
(2024)."). Different and novel validation methods must be used, such as the A-test proposed by Gharehbaghi[98](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR98 "Gharehbaghi, A. Deep Learning in Time Series Analysis, 1st edn., p. 208. CRC Press, Boca Raton (2023). 
https://doi.org/10.1201/9780429321252
."), and the proposed model should also be validated using an external dataset. Furthermore, computation of the 95% confidence interval of accuracies, and the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and area under curve (AUC) values must be performed in future work to obtain a more robust evaluation of the proposed model against other models[99](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR99 "Altan, G. Deepoct: An explainable deep learning architecture to analyze macular edema on oct images. Eng. Sci. Technol. Int. J. 34, 101091. 
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jestch.2021.101091
(2022)."),[100](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-37777-4#ref-CR100 "Altan, G., Kutlu, Y. & Allahverdi, N. Deep learning on computerized analysis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. IEEE J. Biomed. Health Inform. 24(5), 1344–1350. 
https://doi.org/10.1109/JBHI.2019.2931395
(2020)."). Our results show that respiratory signals are important for stroke-risk prediction, and future work should explore whether they can be used on their own without other bio-signals. These results also show that more focus should be placed on CO’s role in stroke-risk prediction.

## Conclusion

In this study, we developed a multi-modal stroke-risk prediction model integrating respiratory signals (CO and respiration flow) alongside ECG, EMG, and BP, highlighting the clinical value of underexplored physiological signals. Our results show that respiratory signals, particularly CO-derived features, provide unique and critical information for identifying individuals at risk of stroke, complementing traditional cardiovascular indicators, and suggest that future research and clinical investigation of these signals could reveal new predictive biomarkers for stroke and other cardiovascular diseases. This is the first study to demonstrate the predictive importance of CO features in stroke-risk assessment, suggesting their potential as actionable biomarkers. Clinically, incorporating respiratory signals into routine monitoring could enable earlier identification of high-risk patients, support timely interventions, and guide personalized management. Future studies with larger patient cohorts are required to validate these findings and facilitate broader clinical implementation.
```

##### [SBTM: epileptic seizure prediction from EEG signal using deep learning in blockchain-enabled smart healthcare monitoring with IoT networking](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1)

```
## Abstract

Epileptic Seizure prediction is highly significant for the identification and reduction of high risks related to serious brain injuries, strokes, and brain tumors. Early and accurate diagnosis is vital for providing intervention measures for enhancing the quality of life of the affected individuals. Numerous techniques have been developed based on Machine vision techniques to predict epileptic seizures. Nonetheless, the acquisition of precise epileptic seizure detection with low false positive rates is challenging. Moreover, the emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) revolutionized healthcare monitoring with technological improvements, aiming to handle the concerns related to data interoperability, scalability, as well as privacy issues. Hence, this research proposes the Smart Healthcare Monitoring Framework, namely Spizella Optimization-based Bidirectional Short Term Memory Network (SBTM), for determining the seizure states, thereby allowing the provision of remote care. Specifically, the proposed model exploits the Bi-LSTM architecture that captures the temporal dependencies and nonlinear dynamics of EEG signals, making the model highly efficient for predicting the seizure patterns. Besides, the Spizella Optimization is applied for fine-tuning the hyperparameters of the classifier, thereby leading to accurate prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SBTM model accomplishes superior results by achieving high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity equivalent to 97.52%, 97.51% and 98.51% with 90% training, outperforming the state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the presented approach significantly improves the remote monitoring, guaranteeing on-time medical care, ensuring data security, and enhancing the overall performance of applications in tech-aided healthcare systems.

Blockchain-enabled healthcare system for detection of diabetes. J. Information Secur. Appl. 58, 102771 (2021)."). To deal with the concerns in the existing techniques, the presented research presents the IoT-assisted Epileptic seizure prediction using the SBTM model that attempts to apply blockchain and IoT technologies in smart healthcare systems to suggest on-time diagnosis for patients with better accuracy when compared with manual diagnosis, which consumes time and suffers from inaccuracy issues. Moreover, the monitoring of the registered physicians is enabled department-wise, and recognized under the genuine user category for accessing the patient data of their own department for diagnosing the disease. Thus, the focus on authenticated data access and patient health monitoring supports the disease detection accuracy.

Due to the authenticated data communication and storage in smart healthcare systems, Blockchain technology is used in this work along with the deep learning model. The diagnosis support is assisted by the DL model for rendering accurate predictions for which the SBTM model is designed, which improves the prediction accuracy with better maintenance of intensification and diversification, thereby minimizing the training loss. The research’s major contributions are:

**_Smart Healthcare Monitoring using Blockchain Technology:_** The patients are monitored from a remote location to provide on-time medical assistance to promote the survival rate. In this instance, the sensors engaged in collecting the patient information are communicated over the hospital portal for the doctor’s perusal, and for ensuring the secure transmission and storage of the sensitive medical data, Blockchain technology is employed that ensures double-layer protection against unauthorized data access.

**_Spizella Optimization:_** The Spizella optimization hybridizes the unique foraging characteristics of the Spizella by considering the alarm indication and the striving behavior of the cougar to reach the optimal solution. Further, the Spizella optimizer effectively explores the large search space using the global searching ability and offers the global optimal solution for tuning the SBTM model, improving the epileptic seizure prediction.

**_Proposed IoT-assisted Blockchain-enabled Spizella Optimized BiLSTM Network (SBTM):_** In the proposed research, the BiLSTM model effectively gathers the temporal dependencies and nonlinear dynamics of EEG signals in sequential data by exploiting both the forward and backward flow of information. Further, the Spizella Optimization adaptively fine-tunes the hyperparameters of the SBTM classifier, resulting in enhanced prediction accuracy.

The remainder of the research is arranged as follows: The related studies, along with research gaps, are presented in [Motivation](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Sec2), and [System model of IoT-blockchain based epileptic seizure prediction](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Sec5) elucidates the proposed methodology. The evaluations are represented in [Result and discussion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Sec21), whereas [Conclusion](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Sec40) concludes the research work with future directions.

## Motivation

The review of the conventional Epilepsy seizure prediction techniques based on machine learning and smart healthcare faces several challenges that limit the performance enhancement, which motivates to development of a novel smart healthcare-based epilepsy seizure prediction technique.

### Related works

Dhanalekshmi Prasad Yedurkar et al.[17](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR17 "Yedurkar, D. P., Metkar, S., Al-Turjman, F., Yardi, N. & Stephan, T. An IoT-based novel hybrid seizure detection approach for epileptic monitoring. IEEE Trans. Industr. Inf. 20(2), 1420–1431 (2023).") implemented the IoT-enabled EEG monitoring system utilizing the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) method for identifying EEG seizures. In addition, the epileptic information obtained from the multichannel EEG data associated with many brain regions offers valuable information for improving performance. Further, the system leveraged critical spectral verge (CSV) features obtained using the spike-statistical (SS) flower pollination algorithm (FPA) for improving the epileptic seizure prediction. Banu Priya Prathaban et al.[18](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR18 "Prathaban, B. P., Balasubramanian, R. & Kalpana, R. ForeSeiz: An IoMT-based headband for Real-time epileptic seizure forecasting. Expert Syst. Appl. 188, 116083 (2022).") introduced the IoMT-based headband ForeSeiz for epileptic seizure prediction. Specifically, the ForeSeiz involves the Enhanced Convolutional Neural Network (ECNN) model, optimally tuned utilizing the Fletcher Reeves Algorithm for enhancing the convergence and reducing the model complexity. However, the IoT-constrained device hardware and a simple architecture with less complexity were required for this framework to work with real-time scenarios.

Kuldeep Singh and Jyoteesh Malhotra[19](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR19 "Singh, K. & Malhotra, J. IoT and cloud computing-based automatic epileptic seizure detection using HOS features-based random forest classification. J. Ambient. Intell. Humaniz. Comput. 14(11), 15497–15512 (2023)."), implemented the automatic epileptic seizure detection system utilizing communication technologies in association with ML and cloud computing for improving the detection of epileptic seizures. Specifically, the Random Forest (RF) technique was applied for the EEG signal classification. For highlighting the performance of the RF model, other ML algorithms, including the Bayes Net and Multilayer Perceptron, were utilized for analyzing the performance. However, the RF often struggles in analyzing the high-dimensional data and was observed with slower inference times for processing the large number of trees. Ankur Goyal et al.[20](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR20 "Goyal, A., Kaushik, S. & Khan, R. IoT IoT-based cloud network for smart health care using an optimization algorithm. Informatics in Medicine Unlocked 27, 100792 (2021).") introduced the Internet of Things (IoT) framework utilizing the Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and PSO algorithm for boosting the physiological sensor-data fusion. Besides, the PSO-ANN approach assisted in the automatic identification of epilepsy and brain fatalities from the EEG signals received by the health center. In addition, the particle swarm computation assists in optimizing the propagation of neural networks and EEG. Further, the healthcare services were extremely delay-sensitive services, and required an energy-efficient IoT-based cloud network.

M. Ramkumar et al.[21](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR21 "Ramkumar, M., Jamaesha, S. S., Gowtham, M. S. & Kumar, C. S. IoT and cloud computing-based automated epileptic seizure detection using optimized Siamese convolutional sparse autoencoder network. SIViP 18(4), 3509–3525 (2024).") presented the IoT-enabled automated epileptic seizure detection framework utilizing the Siamese Convolutional Fire Hawk Sparse Autoencoder Network (SCFHSAN) model. In the SCFHSAN model, the preprocessing for artifact removal was carried out using adaptive filtering and multi-resolutional analysis. In addition, the dandelion tunable Q-wavelet transform was applied for decomposing the signals into frequency sub-bands. Ultimately, the fire hawk optimization algorithm was utilized for optimally tuning the hyperparameters of the network. Kunpeng Song et al.[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR22 "Song, K. et al. An intelligent epileptic prediction system based on synchrosqueezed wavelet transform and multi-level feature CNN for smart healthcare IoT. Sensors 22(17), 6458 (2022).") developed the Intelligent Epileptic Prediction System utilizing the Synchrosqueezed Wavelet Transform (SWT) and Multi-Level Feature Convolutional Neural Network (MLF-CNN) for a smart healthcare IoT network. Additionally, the MLF-CNN model was recognized for automatically extracting the features from different dimensions. Nevertheless, the model showcased poor performance for a few patients. Although the MLF-CNN model offers better performance, with a small sample size, which possibly limits the generalizability for the diverse dataset.

Ali Kadhum Idrees et al.[23](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR23 "Idrees, A. K., Idrees, S. K., Couturier, R. & Ali-Yahiya, T. An edge-fog computing-enabled lossless EEG data compression with epileptic seizure detection in IoMT networks. IEEE Internet Things J. 9(15), 13327–13337 (2022).") introduced the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) based epileptic seizure prediction, which forwarded the huge volume of sensed data to the data centers of the cloud for treatment. In addition, the method of epileptic seizure detector-based Naive Bayes (ESDNB) algorithm was applied, which improved prediction. Specifically, the model minimized the size of IoMT EEG data distributed to the cloud via the application of the same lossless compression algorithm. Furthermore, the lossless compression technique would be enhanced to improve the compression power. Hisham Daoud et al_._[24](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR24 "Xin, Qi., Shaohai, Hu., Liu, S., Zhao, L. & Zhang, Y.-D. An attention-based wavelet convolution neural network for epilepsy EEG classification. IEEE Trans. Neural Syst. Rehabil. Eng. 30, 957–966 (2022).") suggested the IoT framework using a deep learning network for precise epileptic seizure prediction. In the deep learning model, both the feature extraction and classification stages were integrated for processing the raw EEG signals without any preprocessing, minimizing the computation complexity. More specifically, the CNN-based model captured the significant spatio-temporal features from the EEG signals. Besides, the channel selection algorithm was utilized, which minimized the complexity and the memory required for the system to accomplish the real-time application.

Jagadeesh Basavaiah et al.[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR25 "Basavaiah, J., Anthony, A. A., Mahadevaswamy, S. & Naveen Kumar, H. N. An efficient approach to an epilepsy seizure alert system using IoT and machine learning. Journal of Reliable Intelligent Environments 10(4), 449–461 (2024).") introduced the Machine Learning (ML) based remote monitoring system utilizing several sensors and equipment, including the ECG sensor, tilt, GPS, and GSM module, and vibration sensors for improving the prediction of epilepsy. In addition, the system provides alerts when the patient is undergoing a seizure, allowing timely intervention and treatment. However, the model requires enhancing the ML model by incorporating additional features and fine-tuning the hyperparameters. Nevertheless, the model requires combining blockchain technology to increase the security and confidentiality of the patient’s information.

Mohamadreza Khosrav_,_ et al_._[26](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR26 "Khosravi, M., Parsaei, H., Rezaee, K. & Helfroush, M. S. Fusing convolutional learning and attention-based Bi-LSTM networks for early Alzheimer’s diagnosis from EEG signals towards IoMT. Sci. Rep. 14(1), 26002 (2024).")_,_ presented an attention-based model for processing the EEG signals in a medical support system. To facilitate targeted analysis, the EEG signals were transformed to distinct frequency bands, and the dynamic nature was handled using smaller windows. The distribution over frequency and time was visualized; however, the computational requirements were higher, which hindered the applicability in real-time clinical practice. Rezaee Kh_,_ et al_._[27](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR27 "Rezaee, K., Azizi, E. & Haddadnia, J. Optimized seizure detection algorithm: a fast approach for onset of epileptic seizures in EEG signals using GT discriminant analysis and K-NN classifier. Journal of biomedical physics & engineering 6(2), 81 (2016).")_,_ suggested an optimized algorithm for seizure detection implemented using discriminant analysis. The wavelet transform was employed to visualize the temporal and spectral spaces, providing more adaptability in determining the mapping matrix. Furthermore, the feature vectors capable of discriminating different classes were acquired from the high-dimensional space, nonetheless, the error rates were higher for samples with subtle abnormalities.

Shabnam Hesari_,_ et al_._[28](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR28 "Nemati, N., Meshgini, S., Rezaii, T. Y. & Afrouzian, R. Neonatal seizure detection from EEG using inception ResNetV2 feature extraction and XGBoost optimized with particle swarm optimization. Sci. Rep. 15(1), 41493 (2025).")_,_ presented an ensemble feature learning method that supported multi-faceted processing in EEG signal analysis. The waveform was transformed to relevant subbands, and the non-stationarity of the signals was handled through signal windowing. The subbands of the signal were interpreted individually to obtain intrinsic and high-dimensional representations. However, the lack of data diversity affected the model’s generalization to unseen samples.

### Challenges

The challenges faced by conventional seizure prediction methods are.

- Although the MLF-CNN model provides better performance, the small size of the sample affected the generalizability of the diverse dataset[22](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR22 "Song, K. et al. An intelligent epileptic prediction system based on synchrosqueezed wavelet transform and multi-level feature CNN for smart healthcare IoT. Sensors 22(17), 6458 (2022).").
    
- In addition, the ML-based remote monitoring system requires improving the ML model by integrating additional features and fine-tuning the hyperparameters. Nevertheless, the ML model requires combining blockchain technology for the enhancement of security and confidentiality related to patient information[25](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR25 "Basavaiah, J., Anthony, A. A., Mahadevaswamy, S. & Naveen Kumar, H. N. An efficient approach to an epilepsy seizure alert system using IoT and machine learning. Journal of Reliable Intelligent Environments 10(4), 449–461 (2024).").
    
- The classification complexity increased with the increasing dimension of the features. In addition, the existing techniques do not consider the unique spatial–temporal features related to EEG, resulting in limited performance[15](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR15 "D. Połap, G. Srivastava, A. Jolfaei, and R. M. Parizi. \"Blockchain Technology and Neural Networks for the Internet of Medical Things,\" IEEE INFOCOM 2020 - IEEE Conference on Computer Communications Workshops (INFOCOM WKSHPS). 508–513, 2020.").
    
- Epileptic seizures were found to exist in various complex patterns, making it challenging to accurately detect all types of seizures[29](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR29 "Kode, H., Elleithy, K. & Almazedah, L. Epileptic Seizure detection in EEG signals using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques. IEEE Access. 12, 80657–80668 (2024).").
    
- Another issue related to capturing irrelevant details and noise happens when the model is overfitting using the training data. This results in a high number of trainable parameters[30](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR30 "Daoud, H., Williams, P. and Bayoumi, M., “IoT-based efficient epileptic seizure prediction system using deep learning,” 2020 IEEE 6th World Forum on Internet of Things (WF-IoT)1–6, 2020").
    

Most of the existing seizure prediction models suffer from the need for high computational time and substantial memory resources. Also, there is a risk of overfitting due to a high number of trainable parameters. In addition, the existing model requires combining blockchain technology to boost the security and confidentiality level of patient information. Specifically, the existing methods faced complexity with the increasing dimension of the features. In addition, the existing techniques fail to consider the unique spatial–temporal features of EEG, resulting in limited performance. Epileptic seizures were found to exist in different intricate patterns, making it challenging to accurately detect all types of seizures. In contrast, the proposed model leverages Blockchain with Spizella BiLSTM predictor to address these issues. More precisely, the proposed model exploits the BiLSTM architecture in capturing temporal dependencies and nonlinear dynamics of EEG signals, making the model highly efficient for learning the variability in the complex patterns associated with epileptic seizures. Besides, the Spizella Optimization is applied for fine-tuning the hyperparameters of the classifier, resulting in improved prediction accuracy.

## Result and discussion

In this section, the results obtained with the implementation of the proposed smart healthcare-based Epilepsy seizure prediction is discussed in detail.

### Experimental setup

The proposed smart healthcare-based Epilepsy seizure prediction is implemented using the MATLAB tool running in the Windows 11 Operating system with 16GB RAM and 0.34ms processing time. The hyperparameters of the proposed model and the optimization are provided in Tables [5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Tab5) and [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Tab6) below.

### Experimental results

The experimental results obtained with the proposed IoT-assisted epileptic seizure prediction using the SBTM model are shown in Fig. [6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Fig6). Initially, the input sample EEG signals used for the epileptic seizure prediction, followed by the preprocessed signal using the bandpass filter, and the final epileptic seizure prediction output is obtained with SBTM model.

### Dataset description

The dataset used to assess the effectiveness of the developed Spizella-based Bi-LSTM for disease prediction is done through the CHB-MIT dataset[34](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#ref-CR34 "CHB-MIT Scalp EEG Database, 
https://archive.physionet.org/physiobank/database/chbmit/
, Accessed on 2023."). The dataset is collected from the Children’s Hospital Boston, which consists of EEG recordings from young patients who had uncontrollable seizures. Following the discontinuation of anti-seizure medication, the subjects were observed for a few days at most to assess their suitability for surgical intervention and to define their seizures. 22 subjects’ recordings (five males, ages 3–22, and seventeen females, ages 1.5–19) were compiled into 23 cases. Every signal was sampled with 16 bits of resolution and 256 samples per second. Figure [7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Fig7) shows the proportion of the Focal and Non Focal classes in the CHB-MIT dataset. The majority of files have 23 EEG signals (sometimes 24 or 26). In the CHB-MIT dataset, there exist the focal and non-focal classes, accommodating about 19.4% and 80.6% respectively. For assessing generalizability, the research utilizes real-time dataset for external testing on this experiment.

### Performance analysis

This section describes the performance analysis of SBTM model in terms of varying training percentage and K-fold values.

#### Performance analysis based on training percentage

The superiority of the SBTM model evaluated in terms of varying the training percentages from 40 to 90% is discussed in this section. The performance is analyzed for a range of iterations from 20 to 100 epochs using CHB-MIT Scalp EEG and Real-time dataset as represented in Figs. [8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Fig8) and [9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Fig9), respectively.

Using the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG database for epochs 20, the SBTM model attains an accuracy of 92.28%, which is further improved to 97.52% for 100 epochs. Using a real-time dataset for 90% training, the accuracy of SBTM is measured as 79.86% and 84.40% for 20 epochs and 100 epochs, respectively, indicating the capability of the model in learning the training data. Moreover, SBTM gains F1-scores of 97.74% and 84.81% at iteration 100, using CHB-MIT Scalp EEG and real-time dataset, respectively. Furthermore, using the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG database, the sensitivities of 91.41% and 97.50% are evaluated at iterations 20 and 100, correspondingly. Meanwhile, using the real-time dataset, maximum sensitivity values of 79.12% and 84.39% are obtained at iterations 20 and 100. Furthermore, the SBTM gains specificities of 98.50% and 85.26% at iteration 100 for the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG and real-time dataset, respectively. The higher sensitivity indicates that the SBTM minimizes the false alarm rates through exhibiting a deeper understanding on seizure occurrence.

#### Performance analysis based on K-fold

The performance of the SBTM model evaluated in terms of varying the K-folds from 10 to 11 is discussed in this section. The performance is analyzed for a range of iterations from 20 to 100 epochs using CHB-MIT Scalp EEG and real-time dataset as represented in Figs. [10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Fig10) and [11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-36425-1#Fig11), respectively. Using the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG dataset, SBTM gains F1-scores of 90.39% and 96.85% at iterations 20 and 100, respectively. For the real-time dataset, the SBTM model showcases F1-scores of 78.23% and 83.82%, correspondingly for iterations 20 and 100. Using the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG database for epochs 20, the SBTM model attains an accuracy of 89.85% that is further improved to 96.39% for 100 epochs. Using real-time dataset for K-fold 10, the accuracies of SBTM is 77.76% for 20 epochs and 83.42% for 100 epochs, respectively, indicating the accurate prediction of epileptic seizures. Furthermore, for K-fold 10, the SBTM gains specificities of 98.17% and 84.96% at iteration 100 using the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG and real-time dataset, respectively, indicating the lower false positives. The SBTM achieves 89.67% and 97.51% sensitivities at iterations 20 and 100, correspondingly using the CHB-MIT Scalp EEG dataset. Meanwhile, using the real-time dataset, maximum sensitivity values of 77.61% and 84.39% are obtained at iterations 20 and 100 for K-fold 10.
```
